title: the agent writes new work to @any by default (S5), so a fix for one build line reaches lines nothing built: replace S5 with a scope decision table
description:
Under S5 the patch agent writes new ops and patches to target @any. It
only ever builds one line, so an @any change reaches lines nothing
tested.

Live case, 2026-10-06: job 20261006-130821Z-main-devel_glib20-623223-patch
(@main) added `file materialize dragonfly/patch-glib_glib-unix.c` in @any.
The patch edits g_unix_fd_query_path, new in glib 2.88. @main has 2.88.3,
@2026Q3 has 2.86.4. A dry run applies on 2.88.3 and fails on 2.86.4, so
@2026Q3 glib20 would fail in do-patch. Neither .8 (silent on all-@any
ports) nor .26 (does not see dragonfly/ patches) would catch it, and the
operator rejected checks that need sources outside the agent's env.

This bead replaces S5 with a decision table for where the agent's work
goes.
design:
DECISION TABLE (operator, 2026-10-06). Rows are checked in order; the
first match wins. "Op" means any overlay op (mk, text, file, patch apply)
and its payload, not only dragonfly/ patches.

| # | Situation at job start | Where the work goes | Operator? |
| 1 | No overlay (bootstrap) | new overlay, ops in target @any | no; accepted risk: the port may have built on other lines without one |
| 2 | Overlay exists; the fix is a new op or patch | target @<ours>; patch in dragonfly/@<ours>/ | no |
| 3 | The op to change is in our line's block | change it there | no |
| 4 | The op needed is in another line's block (filtered_out) | share it: target @<other>,@<ours>, not a second copy | no |
| 5a | A shared dragonfly/ patch (@any) fails on our line: re-cut | never overwrite the shared file; re-cut to dragonfly/@<ours>/X + materialize op in target @<ours> | no |
| 5b | Another @any op applies on our line but is wrong at build time (mk value ops) | override in target @<ours>, @any untouched (D4); the review page names the override | no |
| 6 | An @any op fails at compose on our line | stop; operator decides: drop everywhere, or move to the other lines' blocks | yes |

Row 1 is the bootstrap case only: no overlay.dops and no compat artifacts
(overlay_state.bootstrap_decision; ensure_bootstrap_overlay writes a
header with zero ops). A compat port has an overlay, so its new fix is
row 2. Ops a convert flow translates from compat artifacts stay @any,
because compat applied them on every line already.

DECIDED 2026-10-06, row 5a: patches in @any are never overwritten; a
re-cut goes to our line's own copy. Enforced in install_patches, not in
the prompt: the agent sees one line and cannot know an overwrite is safe
for the others. Today the overwrite makes the lines ping-pong: a @main
re-cut breaks @2026Q3, whose re-cut lands on the same shared file and
breaks @main again. Cost: once every live line has its own copy nothing
reads the shared one; .25 promotes or removes it at quarter bring-up.

DECIDED 2026-10-06, row 5b: option A, override in our block (D4).
Examples: lang/rust BOOTSTRAPS_DATE (a version pin), a MESON_ARGS flag a
newer release dropped. Only our line's composed tree changes, and the
agent needs nothing it lacks. Rejected: B, the split lang/rust got by
hand in 251d8df7756 (needs the list of live lines, which is not
configured, and edits text other lines read); C, a handoff. A and B
compose the same tree on every live line; they differ only on a future
line, which inherits the @any value under A. For a version pin both are
wrong for a quarterly cut from main, so .25's bring-up copies @main's
values either way.
With it: the review page names each override ("overrides @any
BOOTSTRAPS_DATE=1.95.0 on @main") so the operator can split it by hand;
and the playbook prefers relative ops (mk add/remove, mk bump) to an
absolute mk set in @any, since a relative op is right on every line.

WHY THIS REVERSES S5. S5's reason is written in the code
(worker._payload_destination, steps' build-line brief): "a wrongly shared
patch fails loudly on the other line; a wrongly scoped one is silently
absent there". The table takes the other side. A missing fix leaves the
other line as it was: no regression, and that line's own job fixes it.
A wrong shared fix breaks a line that was building, and nothing that
line built ever tested it (glib20).

CODE FINDINGS, 2026-10-06 (master d0fce69, as deployed).

F1. Rows 5 and 6 split on compose, not on op kind. One failed op makes
    apply_result.ok false and compose reports E_COMPOSE_APPLY_FAILED for
    the origin (compose_stages.py, dops stage). @any ops run first
    (models.order_ops_for_target), so a later @<ours> op cannot rescue an
    @any op that failed. Only an @any op that applies cleanly but is
    wrong for our line can be overridden.

F2. Which ops can fail on a missing subject, from the executors:
    - Never on our line (insert or write; fail only on a missing Makefile
      or ambiguity): mk set, mk add, mk eval, mk shell, mk bump,
      mk target set, mk block set, file materialize (its source is
      overlay payload, the same on every line).
    - Fail when the subject is missing on our line (on-missing error):
      mk remove, mk unset, mk target append/remove/rename, mk disable-if,
      mk replace-if, text replace-once/line-remove/line-insert-after,
      file remove, file copy (reads the composed port), patch apply.
    A dragonfly/ patch that no longer applies is row 5: materialize
    succeeds at compose and do-patch fails at build.

F3. Row 5 overrides validate. The dead-op rule
    (semantic._validate_dead_ops) lets an @any op die only to a later
    @any op, so an @<ours> op rewriting the same file is accepted.

F4. S5 is implemented in three places; each must follow the table:
    - install_patches scope_note for a new patch: "Add to the
      `target @any` block" (worker.py, the needs_op branch). This is the
      text the glib20 agent followed.
    - The job brief (steps.py, "You are building one build line"): "Put
      a change in `target @any` ... unless you can show it is this line's
      alone". The agent can never show that.
    - flow-patch.md "Scoping" and dops_quickref.md (the @any default).
      .4 already calls this text a wrong steer.

F5. A second live hazard, row 5a not implemented. When our line's winner
    for dragonfly/X is the @any op, _payload_destination returns
    (dragonfly/X, "existing") and install_patches copies the re-cut over
    the shared file. A re-cut made on one line changes every line,
    untested. Under the table it goes to dragonfly/@<ours>/X, with a
    materialize op in our block.

F6. Row 4 has its data: get_effective_overlay returns filtered_out,
    the ops scoped to other lines (tools.py).

F7. Row 6 today. The build-line brief (steps.py, only for ports that
    already have per-line blocks) says an @any op that fails here "itself
    has to change", so the agent edits the shared op and every line
    changes, untested. Ports with only @any get no guidance, with the
    same result. The same brief already states row 5b (undo or replace
    in the target block), again only for multi-line ports.

F8. No early handoff exists. The agent can end an attempt with
    "Rebuild Status: gave-up", but attempt_loop stops only on rebuild_ok
    or the token budget, so the next attempt starts anyway, up to
    max_iterations; manual_handoff.md is written when the loop ends
    (needs-help). Row 6 needs a real exit: end the job at once and write
    the handoff naming the op and the two choices.

F9. Convert writes @any, as the operator wants. The convert agent is
    gone (runner: bootstrap-or-abort; a port with compat artifacts goes
    to a manual handoff). The CLI, dportsv3 migrate convert, emits
    emit.header(target="@any") (migration/convert.py, citing the
    liblz4 @main bug). absorb_makefile/absorb_remove default to @main
    only as the targets they verify against, not as scope.

F10. poly-fklo has not started: 5 open children, no code, no branch.
    The table goes in now through the brief, install_patches and the
    playbooks; fklo.3/.5 enforce it later in the editor.

AFFECTS: S5 (replaced); .4 (playbook/quickref text); .25 (quarter
bring-up: @main-scoped work must reach a new quarterly, so it is no longer
optional); poly-fklo (enforce the table in the editor, not only the
prompt).
notes:
EVIDENCE BEYOND glib20 (DeltaPorts, read 2026-10-06). 8 overlays carry per-line blocks. 6 of them were split on 2026-10-05 because an @any op written by a September fix on @2026Q3 failed compose on @main after an upstream bump: devel/libbson 728d77e6cc8, devel/mongo-c-driver 919ab93fa6f, shells/bash-completion 762798fc331, devel/meson b1b18617555, devel/llvm12 94036bd64a7, cad/librecad 5247870c063 (all row 6: E_APPLY_MISSING_SUBJECT). Row 5b example, resolved by hand: lang/rust BOOTSTRAPS_DATE was @any 1.95.0 (08dd56cd0cb); 251d8df7756 moved it into target @2026Q3 and put 1.97.1 and LLVM_VERSION 22 in target @main, i.e. a split, not a D4 override.

LANDED 2026-10-06, 744dc5d (not pushed). Row 1 = no overlay OPS at job start (HEAD overlay absent or header-only; review F5: the preflight can commit a bootstrap header). Row 6 is in the patch preflight, not the attempt loop: a shared op (@any, or a target-list twin) failing in the preflight compose escalates with patch_scope_decision before any model call; a mid-job @any failure can only be the agent's own change. Row 5b overrides counted only for replacing ops (+ mk remove of a shared mk add token). Reviewed twice (Fable); follow-ups .28 (manual-queue row), .29 (put_file shared-payload guard), .30 (preflight refuses own-block compose failures).
close_reason: landed in 744dc5d

title: carry the reviewed commits onto poly-7pwa, land fix-ups 3a/4a/6a/9a and rows 11-14 in order, gate at row 15, merge
description:
The epic's first ten commits sit on backup/poly-7pwa-multitarget. Carry them
onto a fresh branch from master one at a time, each only once approved, and
do the rework there. This bead is the list; each row's state is updated in
the notes as it moves.

RULES FOR EVERY PICK.
  - Leave out .beads/issues.jsonl hunks: Dolt is the source, the jsonl is a
    passive export, and eight of the ten commits would conflict on it.
  - Run the commit's own tests, then the full suite with DPORTS_DELTA_ROOT
    set -- 14 whole-tree tests skip silently without it.
  - Verdicts come from the 2026-10-01/03 review, which tested premises
    against the real tree and the spec.

CHERRY-PICKS, in branch order:

  1  4af6339  .11  apply order is by scope; effective-overlay guard
                   SOUND: equivalent on every reachable target            -> pick
  2  7c6a823  .10  operator context per build line
                   SOUND: the flagged legacy-row regression does not hold -> pick
  3  5c35255  .7   a skipped port's report says what and why
                   READ ONLY, never tested                                -> test, then decide
  4  8e58057  .1   tell the attempt its edits missed its build line
                   SOUND: real-tree tests cover both directions           -> pick
  5  a417e00  .3   refuse two ops writing one destination
                   WRONG RULE: refuses the normative @any+@T override     -> skip, replaced by row 11
  6  221c4eb  .2 .13 .12  re-cut lane, re-cut procedure, PORTREVISION
                   lane right on 155/155 destinations; .12 verified;
                   new-patch fallback defaults to scoped (wrong);
                   re-cut paragraph cites .3's refusal                    -> pick + rows 12, 13
  7  0a15d97  .5   the brief names the build line
                   WORKS; one line carries the "@any is uncheckable" bias -> pick + row 14
  8  955e809  (.4 review)  "a duplicate destination is refused"
                   WRONG; dropping it restores 4af6339's correct sentence -> skip
  9  53a298a  .9   compat port's scoped payload warning
                   SOUND: diffs are applied, not copied                   -> pick
 10  861cdb4  --   beads export                                           -> skip

NEW WORK ON THE BRANCH:

 11  .3 + .20  the dead-op rule replaces a417e00's check; `file remove`
               counts as a writer. After poly-bz7n.1 lands on master.
 12  .2   a brand-new patch with no op defaults to flat dragonfly/; the
          resolver for existing destinations stays.
 13  .13  the re-cut paragraph keeps its advice (put the file where the
          existing op reads; do not add an op) but drops "refused outright":
          a second op in the same block is a dead op (rejected once row 11
          lands); a second op in @any is overridden on this build line and
          changes the others. Its test assertion changes with it.
 14  .5   drop "`@any` is the scope nothing here can check, so put a change
          there on the strength of an argument you can state."
 15  gate: full suite with DPORTS_DELTA_ROOT set, both before and after the
          whole series.

COMMANDS. Code blocks here are indented 4 spaces; strip that indent when
pasting (a heredoc's EOF has to start its line). Shell functions do not
persist between calls, so write the first block, and the cost() function
from PROMPT COST without its last line (cost "$W"), once to carry.sh in
the session scratchpad, and begin every call with
". <scratchpad>/carry.sh &&". It works in zsh and bash. Run bd from
/Volumes/Personal/s/polytropos, never inside the worktree: pick refuses
a dirty worktree.

    W=/Volumes/Personal/s/polytropos-poly-7pwa
    PY=/Volumes/Personal/s/polytropos/.venv/bin/python
    t() { (cd "$W" && PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONPATH="$W:$W/dev-env" \
        DPORTS_DELTA_ROOT=/Volumes/Personal/s/DeltaPorts \
        "$PY" -P -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider "$@"); }
    pick() {
      [ -z "$(git -C "$W" status --porcelain)" ] ||
        { echo "STOP: $W is not clean"; return 1; }
      git -C "$W" cherry-pick --no-commit "$1"
      bad=$(git -C "$W" diff --name-only --diff-filter=U |
            grep -vxF .beads/issues.jsonl)
      [ -z "$bad" ] || { echo "STOP: $1 conflicts in: $bad"; return 1; }
      git -C "$W" restore --staged --worktree --source=HEAD \
        -- .beads/issues.jsonl
      a=$(git -C "$W" diff --cached HEAD | git -C "$W" patch-id --stable)
      b=$(git -C "$W" show "$1" -- . ':(exclude).beads/issues.jsonl' |
          git -C "$W" patch-id --stable)
      if [ -z "${a%% *}" ] || [ "${a%% *}" != "${b%% *}" ]; then
        echo "STOP: $1 staged diff is not the reviewed diff;" \
          "nothing committed"
        diff <(git -C "$W" diff --cached HEAD) \
          <(git -C "$W" show --format= "$1" -- . \
            ':(exclude).beads/issues.jsonl')
        return 1
      fi
      git -C "$W" commit -q -C "$1" \
        --trailer "Carried-from: $(git -C "$W" rev-parse "$1")" || return 1
      echo "picked $1 as $(git -C "$W" rev-parse --short HEAD)"
    }

Gate before row 1, one call:

    if [ "$(git -C "$W" rev-parse HEAD)" != \
         "$(git -C "$W" rev-parse master)" ]; then

      git -C "$W" rev-parse --short HEAD && t tests/
    pick 53a298a && t tests/

Six of the seven picks print a CONFLICT on .beads/issues.jsonl and "error:
could not apply". That is expected: pick keeps HEAD's export, which is
newer than the backup's, and Dolt is the source. Row 7's amend drops the
"Separately in this commit" paragraph, which describes 955e809's change;
it changes only the message. Note the sha the amend prints, not the one
pick printed.

title: delete the 4473 file materialize ops that restate the folder convention
description:
Once compose installs by folder, the 4473 `file materialize` ops that restate
the convention are noise, and agents copy whatever pattern they see. Delete
them in one mechanical DeltaPorts commit. Explicit materialize stays in the
language for what the folder cannot say (a custom destination -- zero uses
today).

AGENT SIDE. install_patches and the playbooks say: a patch is installed by its
folder, and the folder is the scope -- dragonfly/ for every build line,
dragonfly/@<target>/ for that line only. Flat by default: every merged agent
fix so far was @any, and a wrongly shared patch fails loudly on the other
line where a wrongly scoped one is silent (poly-7pwa.4's notes).

GATE. The same whole-tree parity compose as the rule's bead, @main and
@2026Q3, byte-identical; every overlay still validates.

2026-10-06, from poly-7pwa.25: migrate branch-line (dportsv3/migration/line_branch.py) copies only the payload a copied op reads (file materialize src, patch apply path under <lane>/@<line>/). Once the folder is the install and these ops are gone, it must copy dragonfly/@<from>/ whole to dragonfly/@<new>/, or a new line loses @main's own patches.

title: compose installs dragonfly/ by folder for DSL ports, behind a whole-tree parity gate
description:

build line, dragonfly/@T/* on line T as dragonfly/* (the @T file wins a name

  - the I_COMPOSE_MODE_DOPS_SUPPRESSES_COMPAT note stops being true for

GATE (Step 47 6.2). Compose the whole tree for @main and @2026Q3 with and
without the rule. Byte-identical output on both. Depends on the eight-file
cleanup -- without it the gate shows exactly those eight.

title: payload: the dragonfly/ folder is the install -- dragonfly/* on every build line, dragonfly/@T/* on line T, no op
description:
In a DSL port a payload file under dragonfly/ reaches the build only through
an explicit `file materialize` op. Compose ignores the folder itself
(compose_stages.py:479, I_COMPOSE_MODE_DOPS_SUPPRESSES_COMPAT), and a
`target` block never picks the folder: file_text_patch.py:69 resolves the
source path literally, so the folder has to be spelled into every op.

MEASURED, all 5087 overlays, 2026-10-03:

    4473 file materialize ops
      4442  dragonfly/X -> dragonfly/X, in @any
        31  dragonfly/@T/X -> dragonfly/X, in a `target @T` block (lang/rust, ports-mgmt/pkg)
         0  custom destination; folder that disagrees with the block; scoped op reading a flat file
         0  ops that later read or edit a dragonfly/ file
    0 file copy ops. Subfolders under dragonfly/: only @main and @2026Q3 (two ports each).

Every op restates what the folder already says. They are boilerplate, and
agents pay for them: 143 of the 291 ops added by merged agent fixes are
materialize lines, and poly-ov2b records three runs where a patch was written
without its op and the fix silently never reached the build (one cost two
hours of firefox rounds).

ALREADY DECIDED, NEVER BUILT. Step 47's "convention-driven additive lane"
(docs/agentic-architecture-backlog.md:2057; a locked decision in DeltaPorts'
step47-diffs-absorption-plan.md, Phase 6, not started): compose
auto-materializes dragonfly/, explicit ops are still honoured and win, files
an explicit op claims are skipped. Step 47 left target scoping to explicit
ops. The @T folder rule below is the original v3 architecture's
(docs/architecture-v3.md:203 and :313).

THE RULE, for DSL ports:

  - dragonfly/* installs on every build line.
  - dragonfly/@T/* installs on line T only, as dragonfly/*; on a name clash
    the @T file wins.
  - a file an explicit `file materialize` reads is skipped -- explicit wins.
  - runs before the ops, so a later op can edit an installed file.
  - compat ports (23 still carry a dragonfly/) keep their script-parity path.

WHAT IT REMOVES. For payloads: poly-ov2b's failure (no op to forget),
poly-7pwa.3 (no two ops to collide), and most of poly-7pwa.2/.13 -- placing a
patch becomes choosing its folder, which IS the scope decision, flat by
default.

ORDER. The cleanup child first (eight files would otherwise start being
installed), then the compose rule behind a whole-tree parity gate, then
deleting the boilerplate ops.

Measured during the poly-7pwa.3 review.
notes:
2026-10-04 (poly-7pwa round 2). Correction to WHAT IT REMOVES, 'poly-7pwa.3
(no two ops to collide)': .3's dead-op check (E_SEM_DEAD_OP, which lands as
poly-7pwa.21 row 11) is kept after u9n4.3, not superseded. It still guards the
34 file remove ops, the 316 text ops and any custom-destination materialize,
and tests/test_dead_ops.py::test_no_overlay_in_the_tree_has_a_dead_op must
still pass once the 4473 ops are deleted.

title: nothing checks a job's build line against its env's: hold or refuse triage, patch, verify and confirm work in an env that composes another target
description:
Nothing verifies that the target a job says it is for is the target the env will
actually compose.

- resolve_env_for_job (agent/env_resolver.py) picks the env by job.dev_env, then
  the tracker's active env, then --env, then a sole env on disk. Target is not
  an input at any step.
- runner.py:4687 then stamps the JOB's target into the worker cache:
  _worker.set_env_target(_38a_env, job.get("target") or None)
- but reapply composes with the ENV's own $DPORTS_TARGET
  (dev-env/dports_dev_env/helpers.py), which comes from dev-env state.target.

If those disagree, everything downstream disagrees quietly and consistently:
get_effective_overlay filters ops for the job's target while compose,
make_extract, make_patch, dsynth and proposed_fix.md all use the env's. The
agent would be told which ops are effective for a target it is not building,
write its fix into that scope, and watch a build that never included it. It is
the poly-7pwa.1 failure again, from the other end, and with no line of output
naming the discrepancy.

env_verify already round-trips to the dev-env and returns its status, so the
comparison is available at the one place the attempt begins.

WHY IT IS FILED AS LATENT RATHER THAN BROKEN: today one host runs one env with
one target, and jobs are created by that env's own dsynth hooks, so job.target
and state.target agree by construction. The topology this epic exists for --
several envs, one per build line, on one host -- is exactly what removes that
guarantee. env_resolver's precedence rule #2 is "the env the operator selected
in the tracker UI", which has no relationship to the target of a job created by
a different env's hooks.

FIX SHAPE: at attempt start, compare job["target"] with the resolved env's
compose target and refuse the job rather than run it, naming both. A refusal
costs one queue cycle; running it costs a full attempt budget and produces a
misleading result. Cheap, and it turns the whole class into an error message.
design:
STATE, verified 2026-10-04. Open, not started; new work, not a .21 row.
Prototyped on a copy of the post-carry tree (master ab725ac plus .21 rows
1-9): every code, docstring, comment, help and doc edit below was applied
there, and the tests below were run there. Line numbers are on that tree.
The picks touch none of runner.py, lifecycle.py, env_resolver.py,
verify_fix.py, tests/conftest.py or docs/AGENTIC_BUILDS.md, so in those
files they equal master's. Of the files the picks touch, only worker.py
is edited, at its cache comment (worker.py:1771-1775), above every
worker.py hunk the picks bring.

DECISION, user, 2026-10-04: HOLD. An unpinned job whose build line the
selected env does not compose stays QUEUED at claim time until an env of
its line is selected, and the runner status names the waiting lines. A
confirm build waits unclaimed and uncounted. A verify request for another
line fails with a reason. Only a job pinned to an env of another line, a
job that races a selection change, and a line no env on the host composes
are refused.

PREMISE, verified 2026-10-04. Holds, and is stronger than filed.
- The target is never an input to env resolution. resolve_env_for_job
  (dportsv3/agent/env_resolver.py:109-190) takes job.dev_env, then the
  tracker's active env (per builder since poly-fij.13), then --env or the
  runner.dev_env setting, then a sole env on disk. "target" appears only
  in a refusal message.
- Hook-created jobs carry no dev_env. hook_common.sh
  (dev-env/dports_dev_env/dsynth-hooks/hook_common.sh:260-270) writes
  created_ts_utc, profile, target, origin, flavor, bundle_id, run_id,
  type, snippet_round and has_snippets; a job claimed from the DB has the
  same keys (runner._job_meta_from_row, runner.py:2762-2781). Only
  enqueue_patch_job (runner.py:2986) and enqueue_verify_job (:3048) write
  dev_env. So precedence 1 never binds a hook job, and
  env_resolver.py:9-11 ("Hook-driven jobs are bound to the env where
  dsynth failed") is false.
- Triage stamps the env it resolved onto the patch job (steps.py:813-817),
  which then resolves to it by precedence 1.
- process_patch_job caches job["target"] (runner.py:4684-4687), while
  reapply, regen and dbuild compose the env's state.target, exported as
  DPORTS_TARGET (dev-env/dports_dev_env/helpers.py:151-153).
- Readers of that cache: get_effective_overlay (worker.py:1850), and after
  the picks install_patches' lane (worker.py:3624), the build-line brief
  (steps.py:1228) and the scope-drift check (steps.py:1374,
  attempt_loop.py:228): four features, five call sites. is_slave_port
  (worker.py:2290) reads it too but has no caller. The patch brief's
  compose-root path reads job["target"] directly (context.py:534-542).
- Verify and confirm have the same unchecked pairing. verify-fix's own
  --env help says the env should be "target-matched to the bundle"
  (verify_fix.py:463-470) and nothing checks it; the tracker's verify
  picker lists every env name it knows (tracker/routes/pages.py:1103-1125);
  a confirm build resolves its env like an auto job (runner.py:5058).
- Measured: an @2026Q3 confirm built in an env composing @main is recorded
  GREEN today. Method: drive process_build_requests -> process_job
  (confirm) -> run_verify_fix over a state.db holding one resolving
  @2026Q3 issue, with the env's target stubbed to @main and only the HTTP,
  branch and handoff edges stubbed. Result: "confirm GREEN 1/2 for k1 ...
  env=main", one build, last_confirmed_build_generation 1.

CORRECTIONS TO THE DESCRIPTION.
- "env_verify already round-trips ... at the one place the attempt
  begins" is wrong. env_verify is an agent tool (tools.py:52; prompts.py
  :214, :394) and the runner never calls it. The authoritative value is
  state.target in the env's env.json: set once by dev-env create, printed
  by dev-env status and dev-env list. Read it with dports_dev_env's
  EnvironmentStore.load, a file read; do not shell out to dev-env status.
- "jobs are created by that env's own dsynth hooks, so job.target and
  state.target agree by construction" holds only when every hook feeding
  the runner builds the env's line. See REACHABILITY.
- "A refusal costs one queue cycle": a refused job is retired, as a
  WORKTREE_UNAVAILABLE job is. Holding is what costs a queue cycle.

REACHABILITY.
- One env, and every hook feeding this runner builds its line: not
  reachable. dev-env hooks-install writes DPORTSV3_TRACKER_TARGET from
  state.target (dev-env/dports_dev_env/hooks.py:52-70).
- A host dsynth whose profile builds another line, writing into
  paths.queue_root (default /build/synth/logs/evidence/queue,
  settings.py:140-142), or another line's hooks posting to the same
  tracker (claim_stranded_db_jobs claims queued triage rows with no target
  filter, runner.py:2738-2746): every such job runs in the wrong env. A
  hook conf that sets no target derives @<profile> (hook_common.sh
  :411-417), which no env composes. Which of these the deployed builder
  runs is UNVERIFIED; see PRE-DEPLOY CHECK.
- A second env on the host: every job for an unselected line runs in the
  selected env, every time. poly-fij.10's notes record a live builder
  carrying 2026Q1, 2026Q2 and 2026Q3 envs.

CHANGE.
1. dportsv3/agent/env_resolver.py: four functions after
   list_available_envs_detailed. They are the one comparator; no caller
   spells '@' + target.lstrip('@') itself.

       def build_line(target: str | None) -> str:
           t = (target or "").strip()
           return "@" + t.lstrip("@") if t else ""

       def env_compose_target(env: str) -> str
           # imports dports_dev_env.config.load_config and
           # dports_dev_env.store.EnvironmentStore inside the function
           # ImportError -> LookupError(
           #     f"dports_dev_env is not importable ({exc})")
           # any exception from load_config() or store.load(env) ->
           #     LookupError(f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
           # returns build_line(state.target)

       def other_build_line(env: str | None, target: str | None)
               -> str | None
           # env's line when it differs from build_line(target); None
           # when they match, when env or target is empty, or when
           # env_compose_target raises LookupError

       def envs_by_build_line(envs: Iterable[str] | None = None)
               -> dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]
           # {line: env names} over envs (default list_available_envs());
           # an env whose line raises LookupError is left out

   state.target is never empty (dev-env's loader rejects it,
   dev-env/dports_dev_env/state.py:101-105), so env_compose_target has no
   empty branch. All four look up env_compose_target and
   list_available_envs as module globals, so the conftest stubs apply.
   Replace docstring item 1 (env_resolver.py:9-11), quoting names as
   items 2-3 do:

       1. job.dev_env -- the job carries its own env: a patch job the
          env its triage ran in, a verify job the env the operator
          picked, a confirm build the env its feed checked. Hook-created
          jobs carry none (hook_common.sh writes no dev_env), so they
          resolve through 2-4, none of which looks at the job's target.
          The runner matches the two: it leaves such a job queued while
          the selected env composes another build line, and checks again
          at job start (poly-7pwa.14; other_build_line).

   The same false claim survives as the step-1 comment in
   resolve_env_for_job (env_resolver.py:124, "# Step 1: job carries its
   own env (hook-driven)."). Replace it with:

       # Step 1: the job carries its own env (patch, verify and confirm
       # jobs; a hook-created job never does).

2. dportsv3/agent/lifecycle.py.
   - JobEvent.ENV_TARGET_MISMATCH = "env_target_mismatch", after
     WORKTREE_UNAVAILABLE, commented: its own event for the same reason
     as WORKTREE_UNAVAILABLE, neither the agent giving up (counted against
     the patch cap) nor a broken env (feeds the health contract).
   - TRANSITIONS: (TRIAGING, ENV_TARGET_MISMATCH) -> DEAD and (PATCHING,
     ENV_TARGET_MISMATCH) -> DEAD, nothing else. The check runs after
     TRIAGE_START / PATCH_START (runner.py:4822-4826, :4854-4858). No
     CLAIMED entry: nothing fires it from there.
   - _TERMINAL_REASONS: ENV_TARGET_MISMATCH -> "env_target_mismatch".
   - RETIRE_INTERRUPTED (lifecycle.py:371-373) gains
     "env_target_mismatch"; unlisted, it would be derived into
     RETIRE_FAILED.
   - Not in _EVENT_TO_RESOLUTION: the bundle keeps resolution NULL, so
     fix_status reads "unknown" and Retry is offered
     (tracker/fix_state.py:195-201).
   - reap_stale_queued (lifecycle.py:611-663) gains the keyword
     "keep: Collection[str] = ()" (import Collection from
     collections.abc): job ids it leaves queued however old, checked right
     after the pending/ file check (:655-657). Add to its docstring: "keep
     names rows to leave queued however old: the runner's DB claim takes
     them once an env of their build line is selected (poly-7pwa.14)."
     Its only caller, runner.main(), passes keep through CHANGE 5a.

3. Verify requests: runner.process_verify_requests (runner.py:1158).
   Import build_line and other_build_line inside the function. After
   target is read (:1210), before enqueue_verify_job (:1212):

       env_line = other_build_line(env, target)
       if env_line:
           reason = (f"bundle {bundle_id} is for {build_line(target)} "
                     f"but env {env} composes {env_line}; verify it in "
                     f"an env of {build_line(target)}")
           _mark_verify_request(req_id, "failed", error=reason)
           activity_log(
               queue_root, "verify_refused_env_target_mismatch", reason,
               extra={"request_id": req_id, "bundle_id": bundle_id,
                      "env": env, "job_target": build_line(target),
                      "env_target": env_line})
           continue

   No job, no throwaway verify branch, bundles.verification_status
   untouched. The tracker already shows a failed request as "verify never
   started" with "The verify could not be enqueued: <reason>."
   (tracker/fix_state.py:413-418).

4. Confirm builds: runner.process_build_requests (runner.py:1780).
   Import build_line inside the function.
   - After the issues are read (:1806-1811): return when there are none,
     so a pass with nothing to build reads no env state; then
     gate_env = resolve_env_for_gate() and
     held = _lines_held_back(gate_env) (CHANGE 5).
   - After the "if not bundle_id: continue" guard (:1818), before
     _claim_issue_build (:1824):

         if build_line(target) in held:
             continue    # unclaimed, uncounted: it waits for its line's env

   - Pass dev_env=gate_env to enqueue_confirm_build_job (:1827). That
     function (runner.py:3072) gains "dev_env: str | None = None" and
     appends the line dev_env=<env> to the job file when it is set.
     In its docstring, replace only the sentence that begins "dev_env is
     deliberately omitted" and ends "exactly as auto triage/patch jobs
     do." (:3091-3093; names in double backquotes, as the docstring
     writes them) with: "dev_env is the env process_build_requests
     checked the issue's build line against, so the build runs where it
     was checked even if the selection moves while the job waits
     (poly-7pwa.14)." Keep the sentence that follows it ("generation is
     carried so the verdict can be matched to the exact C1 intent.").
   - Add to process_build_requests' docstring: "An issue whose build line
     the selected env does not compose, while another env on this host
     does, waits here, unclaimed and uncounted, until an env of its line
     is selected; the job is then pinned to the env it was checked
     against (poly-7pwa.14)."
   This keeps the feed's contract (runner.py:1793-1796: a busy env never
   costs an issue retry budget). A confirm refused at build time instead
   would count three could-not-run failures and then reopen the issue
   through _record_confirm_failure: delivery_bundle_id NULL and a
   confirm_build_red handoff, for a fix nothing built.

5. The claim-time hold: runner.py, beside claim_stranded_db_jobs.

       _HELD_FOR_LINE: dict[str, int] = {}

       def _lines_held_back(gate_env: str | None) -> frozenset[str]
           # frozenset() when gate_env is falsy or
           # env_compose_target(gate_env) raises LookupError (nothing is
           # held on a guess); else
           # frozenset(envs_by_build_line()) - {gate_env's line}

       def _waits_for_its_line(meta: dict, held: frozenset[str]) -> bool
           # False when meta has dev_env (a pinned job's env cannot
           # change, so it would wait forever) or when
           # build_line(meta.get("target")) is not in held; else
           # _HELD_FOR_LINE[line] += 1 and True

       def _idle_stage() -> str
           # "waiting" when _HELD_FOR_LINE is empty, else
           # "waiting: queued jobs need an env of their build line
           # (<n> for <line>, <n> for <line>)", sorted by line

   - claim_next_job_batch (runner.py:2870): clear _HELD_FOR_LINE, compute
     held = _lines_held_back(resolve_env_for_gate()) once per pass, skip
     a lead when job_held_back(meta) or _waits_for_its_line(meta, held)
     (:2895), and pass held to claim_stranded_db_jobs (:2932).
   - claim_stranded_db_jobs (runner.py:2811) gains the keyword
     "held: frozenset[str] | None = None" (None: compute it). After its
     runs.profile filter (:2833-2838) and before "if not rows: return
     None" (:2840), it drops rows for which
     _waits_for_its_line(_job_meta_from_row(r), held). A row with no
     profile is never claimed, so it is not counted as waiting. DB rows
     carry no dev_env.
   - The main loop's idle branch (runner.py:5609) passes
     stage=_idle_stage(). With --once, a pass that claims nothing logs
     _idle_stage() instead of "no jobs in queue" (:5589) when
     _HELD_FOR_LINE is not empty.
   Never held: a job with dev_env; a job with no target; a line no env on
   this host composes, such as an old hook conf's @<profile> (it goes on
   to the refusal); anything while the selected env's line cannot be
   read. Siblings are not checked apart from their lead: they share its
   profile, and a profile is one env's.
   Cost: _lines_held_back reads the selected env's env.json, lists the
   env store (which reads every env.json) and reads each env's env.json
   once more, about 2n+1 small local reads for n envs. The claim pass
   runs it once per loop pass (every 5 s when idle);
   process_build_requests runs it once more, only on a pass where some
   issue needs a confirm build.

5a. The startup reap. runner.main() reaps, once at startup, every QUEUED
    row whose .job file is not in pending/ and whose last transition is

          A job runs only in an env of its own build line. A dev-env
          composes one target, and a job, a verify and a confirm build
          are each for one. Hook-created jobs name no env, so a queued
          job whose line the selected env does not compose, while another
          env on this host does, waits in the queue, also across a runner
          restart: the runner status says how many, and for which line,
          and the job runs once an env of that line is selected. A
          confirm build waits the same way and spends none of its retry
          budget. A verify asked for in an env of another line never
          starts; its request says why. Before triage or a patch attempt
          the runner checks the pairing once more, and a job pinned to an
          env of another line, or for a line no env on this host
          composes, is retired with retire_reason env_target_mismatch and
          an activity row naming both lines. The port is triaged again
          the next time it fails on its line, or through Retry, which
          waits like any queued job until an env of its line is selected
          (for a line no env here composes, create that env first);
          Retry's required note reaches the agent and lets a MANUAL
          decision run an attempt. dportsv3 verify-fix --env refuses an
          env of another line.

EDGE CASES.
- A bare target ("main", only from a hand-set DPORTSV3_TRACKER_TARGET;
  hook_common.sh and hooks.py always add the '@') matches "@main".
- A job with no target is never held or refused; its scope cache now
  holds the env's line instead of None.
- An env whose state cannot be read: nothing is held and nothing refused.
- The selection moves between claim and job start (the gate's 1 s cache):
  the job is refused, not requeued. Rare; the port is triaged again on
  its next failure.
- A held job is QUEUED: fix_status shows it in progress, and
  _has_active_same_origin_job (runner.py:1862-1887; QUEUED is in
  lifecycle.ACTIVE_WORK_STATES) blocks an operator-context retriage of
  that origin on its own build line while it waits. The guard matches
  jobs of the run's target, or with no target, so a held @2026Q3 job
  does not block a retriage from a @main run.
- A runner restart keeps a held job queued (CHANGE 5a). It also keeps a
  DB-only triage row of the selected line that went stale while the
  runner was down: the DB claim takes it instead of the reap retiring it,
  as a pending/ file of any age is already kept. A stale queued row for a
  line no env here composes is still reaped.
- A refused patch job: process_job still calls
  _drop_bundle_branch_for_job in the pinned env; no worktree exists and
  the call is soft-fail.
- decision.py's patch cap counts only patch_gave_up and
  patch_budget_exhausted (decision.py:117-126), so a refusal never costs
  the port an attempt.
- A verify request naming an env this host does not have (the tracker's
  picker lists the union of all builders' env names): its line cannot be
  read, so the request is enqueued as today.
- A confirm build for a line no env here composes is not held: it is
  enqueued pinned and the backstop refuses it. After
  runner.confirm_max_failures (default 3) the existing policy for a fix
  that cannot run reopens the issue and writes a confirm_build_red
  handoff, with the refusal as the reason. Before this change it was
  built in the wrong env and its verdict recorded.

acceptance_criteria:
ACCEPTANCE.
- A job that names no env, and whose build line the selected env does not
  compose while another env on this host does, is not claimed, from the
  file queue or from the DB. It stays QUEUED, and the idle runner status
  reads "waiting: queued jobs need an env of their build line (<n> for
  <line>)"; a --once pass that holds every job logs the same text. The
  first pass after an env of its line is selected claims it.
- A runner restart does not retire a held job: the startup reap leaves a
  queued triage row the DB claim can take, for a line some env here
  composes. Other stale queued rows whose file is gone are reaped as
  before.
- A confirm build for such a line is neither claimed nor counted: the
  issue stays resolving, building_generation NULL, confirm_failure_count
  unchanged. Once an env of its line is selected it is enqueued with
  dev_env=<that env>, and it runs there even if the selection moves.
- A verify request whose env composes another line than its bundle's is
  marked failed with a reason naming both lines, plus an activity row
  verify_refused_env_target_mismatch. No verify job, no verify branch,
  bundles.verification_status untouched; the bundle page reads "verify
  never started".
- A triage or patch job that reaches job start in an env of another line
  builds no payload, creates no worktree and never reaches the model. It
  and its siblings end DEAD with retire_reason env_target_mismatch,
  counted as interrupted by job_outcome_counts and not counted by
  decision.py's patch cap; jobs.dev_env is filled. One activity row,
  triage_ or patch_refused_env_target_mismatch, names the origin, the env
  and both lines, with a hint that names the tracker UI or dev-env create
  and never --env or retry.
- dportsv3 verify-fix --env with an env of another line raises
  VerifyFixError naming both lines before apply-and-build runs.
- A patch job's scope cache (worker.peek_env_target) holds the line its

title: the drifted-patch re-cut procedure promises 'same path' overwrite, which is false for scoped ports, and reconcile then deletes the re-cut
description:
error-prefer-dops-over-static-patches.md:118-127 documents the drifted-patch
procedure: re-cut with genpatch, write the refreshed patch back under
`dragonfly/`, KEEP the existing `file materialize` line, and -- quoted --
"overlay.dops is not edited at all ... overwrites the old one at the same path".

For a target-scoped port the old one is NOT at that path. rust/pkg keep it at
`dragonfly/@main/patch-X`; install_patches writes `dragonfly/patch-X`
(poly-7pwa.2). So the procedure's central promise, same path, silently fails and
the three outcomes are all bad:

1. The kept materialize line keeps staging the STALE file. The build sees the
   unrefreshed patch, fails the same way, and the refreshed one is inert.
2. If the build then passes for any other reason, reconcile_orphaned_artifacts
   DELETES the refreshed patch as an orphan -- it is unreferenced by any op
   (reconcile.py:64-67, success-only, steps.py:1760). The agent's work is
   removed as part of the fix.
3. If the agent instead appends its own materialize op, poly-7pwa.1 scopes it to
   the file's last block, poly-7pwa.3 lets it collide with the existing
   `@main/patch-X` op with no diagnostic, and poly-7pwa.11 decides which wins --
   differently per target.

So this one paragraph of guidance routes into three other beads at once, which
is why it is filed separately from the playbook bead (.4): .4 is about absent
and mis-steering advice, this is a specific named procedure that is actively
wrong for these ports and needs rewriting in place.

IT ALSO QUALIFIES A "SOUND" FINDING. reconcile_orphaned_artifacts was cleared
during the audit for the right reason -- it plans UNFILTERED, so it will not
delete another target's patches. That still holds. What it does do is delete the
agent's own flat re-cut when the referenced source is scoped. Sound for the
sibling target, hazardous for the current one.

FIX SHAPE: rewrite the procedure to derive the destination from the op that
already references the patch, rather than assuming `dragonfly/<basename>` --
which is also exactly what .2's fix computes, so the two should land together
and the doc should cite the mechanism rather than restate a path.

title: the playbook prescribes PORTREVISION in @any, which silently downgrades package identity on every build line it was not computed from
description:
flow-patch.md:187-189 tells the agent to keep PORTREVISION bumps in @any:

  "PORTREVISION is an exception: it's part of the port's package identity, so a
   bump scoped to one build line ships an un-bumped package on the others. Keep
   PORTREVISION bumps in @any."

and :334 tells it to compute the new value from the current one -- read from the
Makefile of the branch this job is building.

mk.var.set REPLACES an existing assignment and INSERTS when absent
(engine/executors/mk_ops.py:172-200); there is no missing-subject row, so it
never errors and never warns. Branch Makefiles legitimately carry different
PORTREVISION values. So `mk set PORTREVISION "1"`, computed correctly on
@2026Q3 where the port sits at 0, silently rewrites @main's PORTREVISION= 3
down to 1 -- a package identity DOWNGRADE on a build line nobody built.

The advice is not silly; its stated rationale is real (a scoped bump ships an
un-bumped package elsewhere). But it trades a missing bump for a wrong one, and
a wrong PORTREVISION is worse than an absent one: pkg upgrade ordering depends
on it, so the downgraded line stops offering the rebuild to users.

AND IT IS THE CASE A CROSS-TARGET COMPOSE CANNOT CATCH (see poly-7pwa.8). The
second-target compose check catches ops whose subject is MISSING, because
on-missing defaults to error. mk set inserts instead, so it composes clean on
every target and produces a different, wrong value on the ones not built.

WHAT THE GUIDANCE SHOULD PROBABLY SAY -- flagging that this is a decision rather
than an obvious fix: either (a) `mk add`-style relative bump semantics, if the
engine can express "increment whatever is there", or (b) keep it scoped per
target and accept that each build line's bump is that line's business, which is
what the branch Makefiles already assume by carrying different values, or (c)
refuse PORTREVISION in @any outright in the semantic layer and make the author
choose. (c) is cheapest and loudest; (b) matches the data.

Verified: mk_ops.py:172-200 read; the differing-value premise is what the
playbook itself asserts in the sentence quoted above.

title: scope decides apply order, not file position, so the op that reads last wins on one target and loses on another
description:
engine/apply.py:275-277 orders ops for an apply run as: every @any op in source
order, THEN every op for the run's target, THEN the rest (skipped). So scope,
not file position, decides what runs last -- and last-wins is how mk/text ops
resolve.

PROVEN. Declaration order @main-then-@any, one variable:

  target @main
  mk set FOO "from-main"
  target @any
  mk set FOO "from-any"

  apply order on @main   : [@any from-any, @main from-main]  -> FOO= from-main
  apply order on @2026Q3 : [@any from-any]                   -> FOO= from-any

The op that reads LAST in the file wins on @2026Q3 and loses on @main. One
edit, two different composed Makefiles, and no build can show you the second.

THE AGENT IS TOLD THE OPPOSITE. flow-patch.md:36 describes
get_effective_overlay's output as "declaration order"; :137 says ops "play in
declaration order, last-wins". Both true within one scope and wrong across
scopes. get_effective_overlay itself returns plan order (worker.py:1898-1912),
i.e. declaration order, so the tool the playbook points at for "what will
actually apply" presents the ops in an order the engine will not use.

This is documented behaviour, not an engine bug: docs/dsl-v0.md:129-131 states
the three-phase order explicitly, and DeltaPorts' own ports-mgmt/pkg commit
(c030e103838) relies on it -- "@any ops always run first regardless of where the
block sits in the file, so @any keeps the autosetup form for every quarter and
only main diverges." The overlay author knows. The agent's guidance does not.

IT ALSO DECIDES EVERY COLLISION IN poly-7pwa.3. Two ops writing one
materialize destination resolve by apply order, so a scoped op beats an @any op
on its own target and loses everywhere else. Any diagnostic written for .3 must
describe the winner in these terms, not in file terms.

FIX SHAPE, two parts and the second matters more:
- correct flow-patch.md and dops_quickref.md: within a scope, declaration
  order; across scopes, @any always first, then the target's own. An op that
  must beat an @any op has to be in the target's block, not merely below it.
- make get_effective_overlay return ops in APPLY order for the env's target
  (or carry an explicit order index), so the tool that exists to answer "what
  will the engine do" stops answering in the engine's non-order.

title: install_patches writes to a flat dragonfly/ whatever the target is, so a re-cut patch for a target-scoped port is inert and the old one keeps building
description:
worker.py:3472, in install_patches:

    dst = paths.deltaports / "ports" / dest_origin / "dragonfly"

Always the flat lane, whatever target the job is for. A port whose source
patches are target-scoped -- lang/rust keeps 15 under dragonfly/@2026Q3/ and
14 under dragonfly/@main/, pkg keeps one under each -- therefore receives the
agent's freshly cut patch BESIDE the scoped ones, at a path the target's own
`file materialize dragonfly/@main/patch-X -> dragonfly/patch-X` op does not
read.

WHAT THE AGENT SEES: install_patches returns ok with the file listed as
installed. materialize_dports composes, and composes the OLD scoped patch,
because that is what the op names. dsynth_build reproduces the original
failure. The new patch is inert -- dops mode suppresses the compat auto-copy,
so an unreferenced file under dragonfly/ reaches nothing.

THIS IS poly-lt5q's THIRD CASE. That bead's own docstring names the class:
"install into a directory the build never reads", found for slave ports where
DFLY_PATCHDIR resolves into the master's tree. The remedy chosen there is the
one available here, and the reasoning transfers verbatim -- redirect the
destination and SAY SO in the result rather than refusing, because the model
has no way to know the convention and telling it to retry elsewhere just
costs a turn.

THE TARGET IS ALREADY IN HAND. install_patches takes `env`, and
worker.peek_env_target(env) returns the job's compose target (set by
runner.py:4687 from job["target"]). The destination for a target-scoped port
is dragonfly/@<target>/.

HOW TO DECIDE WHETHER A PORT IS TARGET-SCOPED: do not guess from the
filesystem alone. The overlay is the authority -- build_plan on
ports/<origin>/overlay.dops returns every materialize op with its src and its
scope, so "this port keeps its dragonfly payload under @<target>/ for the
scope I am building" is a question about the plan, not about which directories
happen to exist. A port may have a scoped dir for one target and flat files
for another (pkg does: four libpkg patches are flat and @any, one is scoped
per target).

RELATED, SAME TREE: tools/mass_convert.py:47 detects target-scoped dragonfly
payloads and ESCALATES TO A HUMAN rather than emitting ops for them. The
repo's own batch converter treats this case as out of scope; the agent
currently has less guidance than the thing that gave up.

       def _payload_destination(plan, target: str, filename: str,
                                port_dir: Path, patched: str | None
                                ) -> tuple[str, str]:
           import posixpath
           from pathlib import PurePosixPath
           from dportsv3.engine.models import order_ops_for_target

           def payload_file(op) -> str | None:
               if op.kind != "file.materialize":
                   return None
               src = posixpath.normpath(str(op.payload.get("src") or ""))
               parts = PurePosixPath(src).parts
               if (len(parts) < 2 or parts[0] != "dragonfly"
                       or ".." in parts):
                   return None
               return src

           winners = {}
           for op in order_ops_for_target(plan.ops, target):
               if (op.kind in ("file.materialize", "file.copy")
                       and op.target in ("@any", target)):
                   dst = posixpath.normpath(
                       str(op.payload.get("dst") or ""))
                   winners[dst] = op
           wanted = f"dragonfly/{filename}"
           op = winners.get(wanted)
           if op is None and patched:
               same = [src for dst, w in winners.items()
                       if dst.startswith("dragonfly/patch-")
                       and (src := payload_file(w)) is not None
                       and _patched_path(port_dir / src) == patched]
               if len(same) == 1:
                   return same[0], "existing"
           if op is None:
               return wanted, "new"
           src = payload_file(op)
           if src is None:
               return wanted, "unsafe"
           return src, "existing"

   The kinds, for its docstring:
   - "existing": the op that fills dragonfly/<filename> last on this line
     is a file.materialize reading a file under dragonfly/; the path is
     that file. When nothing fills that name: the one dragonfly/patch-*
     destination on the line whose file changes the same single path (the
     header key; none or several, no match). The destination is the key,
     not the layout: pkg keeps four libpkg patches flat under @any and one
     scoped per line.

     @any op. A wrongly shared patch fails loudly on the other line; a
     wrongly scoped one is silently absent there (poly-7pwa.4's notes).
   - "unsafe": the winner does not read a file under dragonfly/: a
     file.copy (it reads the composed port, not the payload), or a source
     that is absolute, contains "..", or lies outside dragonfly/. Never
     followed.

   WHY dragonfly/ AND NOT THE ENGINE'S RULE. apply accepts any relative
   source inside the port dir; that is a rule for reading. install_patches
   writes. The op "file materialize overlay.dops -> dragonfly/patch-x"

title: an overlay op appended at end of file silently inherits the last target block, so a fix for one build line is written into another
description:
The agent has no scope-aware write primitive for overlay.dops. It hand-edits
with put_file/edit_file, and the natural edit -- append the new op -- inherits
whatever `target` directive was last named in the file. Scope is therefore
assigned by BYTE POSITION, and the agent is never told that.

MEASURED against both multi-target ports in DeltaPorts today, by appending
`file materialize dragonfly/patch-NEW -> dragonfly/patch-NEW` at end of file
and re-planning:

  lang/rust:      op lands in scope @main
                    working @2026Q3: FILTERED OUT -- fix never composes
                    working @main:   EFFECTIVE
  ports-mgmt/pkg: op lands in scope @main
                    working @2026Q3: FILTERED OUT -- fix never composes
                    working @main:   EFFECTIVE

CONSEQUENCE. A job on @2026Q3 for either port writes its op, validate_dops
passes (the overlay is well-formed), materialize_dports composes WITHOUT the
op because get_effective_overlay's filter drops it, dsynth_build fails exactly
as it did before the fix, and the agent spends its remaining attempts on a
tree that never received the change. Nothing in any result says the op was
filtered out of its own plan. On @main it is accidentally right, which is
worse: it will pass review until someone builds the other line.

This was safe for as long as overlays were single-scope -- appending at EOF
inherited @any and @any is universal. The DeltaPorts convention changed what
"append" means without anything on this side noticing.

TWO NOTES FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS:

- worker.py:1826 cites `_append_overlay`'s "@current path" in a docstring.
  That helper no longer exists. Whatever replaces it is the natural home for
  a scope argument, and the docstring is a stale pointer to delete either way.
- get_effective_overlay ALREADY returns `filtered_out` with a per-op reason
  (worker.py:1908-1913), so the information needed to catch this at the end of
  an attempt is already computed. A fix could be as small as: after the agent
  declares done, re-read the effective plan and refuse if an op the attempt
  wrote is in filtered_out.

VERIFICATION SHAPE: break it deliberately. A test that appends an op to a
fixture whose last block is @main, asks for the @2026Q3 plan, and asserts the
op is absent must FAIL against the fixed code and pass against today's.

title: an overlay op must land in the scope the fix is for: the agent is single-target in a tree that is not
description:
DeltaPorts has started carrying two build lines per port, and the convention
is now in the tree: ports-mgmt/pkg (2.8.4 on @main, 2.7.5 on @2026Q3) and
lang/rust (1.98.1 / 1.96.1, where none of the fourteen source patches common
to both sets is identical across the two versions). Both use per-target
blocks plus target-scoped payload directories -- `dragonfly/@main/patch-X ->
dragonfly/patch-X` -- so the composed name stays flat and only the source is
scoped.

THE ENGINE IS READY. Verified by building real plans against both ports:
pkg plans clean with 7 materialize sources, 2 of them target-scoped; lang/rust
with 86 and 29; both carry ops in @any, @2026Q3 and @main. `target @any`, the
comma list `@2026Q3,@main`, `dragonfly/@T/` and `diffs/@T/`, and the invalid-
@dir check in validate_target_scoped_payloads all work. So do three things
that looked like likely casualties and are not:

- reconcile_orphaned_artifacts calls build_plan UNFILTERED, so its reference
  set holds every target's sources; it will not delete @2026Q3's patches
  while a job works on @main.
- make_patch / dupe / genpatch operate on the COMPOSED tree, already flattened
  for the job's target, so the baseline a patch is cut against is target-
  correct for free.
- the dsynth-busy gate is host-wide via pgrep (dsynth_active's env_name is
  deliberately unused, runner.py:2676) -- right for several envs on one host.

THE AGENT IS NOT READY, and the shared invariant it breaks is: AN OVERLAY OP
MUST LAND IN THE SCOPE THE FIX IS FOR, AND A PATCH FILE MUST LAND WHERE THAT
SCOPE READS IT. Five children, each violating it at a different layer:

- install_patches writes to a flat `dragonfly/` whatever the target is
- an op appended at end of file inherits the last `target` block, silently
- two ops may materialize the same destination with no diagnostic
- the playbooks never mention the convention and steer toward @any
- the job brief never states the target as a fact the fix depends on

WHY THIS IS URGENT RATHER THAN TIDY. Each of the first two lets an attempt
run to completion, report a fix, and leave the tree unchanged for the target
it was working on -- the failure reproduces identically and nothing says why.
That is the poly-lt5q shape (a patch installed into a directory the build
never reads) on a new axis, and lt5q cost a full attempt budget per occurrence
before it was found.

NOT AUDITED HERE: the tracker's multi-target views, and whether two envs on
one host can hold concurrent jobs at all. The engine, agent write path,
playbooks and job brief are what this epic covers.
design:
AIM. DeltaPorts now builds some ports on more than one build line: @main
and the current quarterly. lang/rust and ports-mgmt/pkg do it with
per-target blocks and dragonfly/@T/ payload folders. The engine composes
these ports correctly. The patch agent, which works one build line per
env, does not respect the layout.

THE INVARIANT. An overlay op must land in the scope the fix is for, and a
patch file must land where that scope reads it. Each env builds exactly
one target, so no part of the system may rely on a build to catch damage
to another line.

The epic makes the agent's write path, the engine's checks, the guidance
the agent reads and the runner's pairing of jobs with envs enforce it:
- a re-cut goes where its line's op reads it (.21 row 12);
- a dead op is reported (.21 row 11);
- the brief names the build line (.21 rows 7 and 14);
- a job never runs in an env of another line (.14);
- an attempt can show which lines its change reaches (.8).
New agent-authored patches and ops default to flat/@any, and scoping
answers a measured divergence (S5). The reviewed commits from
backup/poly-7pwa-multitarget are carried first (.21). The remaining beads
are ordered around poly-u9n4 (folder install) and poly-fklo (overlay
editor), so that no mechanism is written twice.

title: master is red: the progress entry grew a flavor key and its exact-shape test was not updated
description:
tests/test_progress_logfile_link.py::
test_the_entry_shape_is_dsynths_plus_what_the_tracker_knows fails on
master:

  assert set(entry) == {"entry", "elapsed", "ID", "result", "origin",
                        "info", "duration", "recorded_at"}
  E  Extra items in the left set: 'flavor'

3bfecca ("tracker: preserve build results and status per flavor") added a
flavor key to the progress entry; the test asserts an EXACT key set and was
not updated with it. Verified pre-existing, not caused by poly-1v7l's
changes, by stashing those and re-running: still fails.

THE FIX IS ONE LINE EITHER WAY, and which line is a decision the author of
3bfecca should make, which is why this is a bead and not a drive-by edit:

  a) `flavor` belongs in the entry -> add it to the expected set and to the
     docstring, which currently enumerates "the TWO fields the tracker adds
     because it has them and dsynth did not". It would become three.
  b) `flavor` does not belong -> the entry shape is deliberately
     dsynth-progress' own plus a named few, and an internal column leaking
     into it is the defect the exact-set assertion exists to catch. Drop it
     from the entry instead.

The test is doing its job in either case. Note the exactness is the point:
a subset assertion would not have noticed, and this is the surface
dsynth-progress consumers read.
notes:
FIXED 2026-09-27, option (b): the flavour comes out of the entry, and the
exact-shape test passes unchanged. Master is green -- 4429 passed, 1
skipped, 0 failed.

IT WAS NOT THE COIN FLIP THIS BEAD MADE IT. Three things decide it, all
already in the tree:

1. The adapter's own module docstring states the contract: "Entries carry
   one field dsynth-progress never had: bundle_id". The payload documents
   its additions one by one, which is the whole reason the assertion is an
   exact set.
2. THE LIFTED progress.js NEVER READS A FLAVOUR. run.js renders and
   searches `origin` and nothing else -- originCell(b.origin) at :162,
   r.origin at :248, the search filter at :216. A "flavor" key was dead
   weight in a payload whose purpose is to let that UI run unmodified.
3. THE FLAVOUR WAS ALREADY THERE. 3bfecca also made origin read
   "devel/glib20@bootstrap" -- dsynth's own spelling, the one db.py
   already parses (the `"@" in origin` branch of the port query) and the
   one originCell turns into a port link. The separate key was a SECOND
   copy of information the payload was already carrying.

So nothing was lost by removing it, which is the part that makes (b) safe
rather than merely tidy.

WHAT 3bfecca GOT RIGHT, and should not be confused with this: the flavor
fields it added to models.py -- ResultItem, PortStatusOut, BuildResultRow,
DiffEntry, DiffSideEntry, BuildCompareEntry, QueueItem -- are the
TRACKER'S OWN vocabulary, where a flavour is its own field and the
templates read it as one (build_compare.html, diff.html, port_detail.html,
builds_dashboard.html). That commit was right everywhere except the one
payload that is not the tracker's own shape. This is a boundary bug, not
a wrong idea.

ALSO FIXED, and it had no test at all: _active_builders carried the same
duplicate key. summary.json's builder rows have no exact-shape assertion,
so that copy would have sat there indefinitely.

THE CONTRACT DOC WAS ALREADY DRIFTING. It said "one field
dsynth-progress never had" while the payload carried two -- recorded_at
arrived with poly-0e02.4 and the sentence was never updated. The test
docstring says two, the module said one, and the payload had three. Now
the module names both, says a flavour is not a third, and says where a
flavour does live.

TESTS, four, in tests/test_progress_contract.py, and they pin BOTH
directions because each is a plausible next change:

  two flavors of one port are two entries        -- the information is
  an unflavored port keeps a bare origin            still in the payload
  the flavor is not also its own field           -- and only once
  a flavored builder row names the flavor

Verified by breaking it each way. Restoring the extra key fails
test_the_flavor_is_not_also_its_own_field AND the exact-shape test in
test_progress_logfile_link; dropping the "@flavor" from origin instead
fails the other two. Removing the key without the first pair would have
left "just delete the @flavor too" looking like a tidy-up.

ONE FIXTURE TRAP, recorded because it cost a red run and looked like a
code bug: a 'building' row is EXCLUDED from the history chunk by design
(it belongs in summary.builders). The first fixture marked one of the two
glib20 flavours building, which silently took it out of the very payload
the test was asserting about. The in-flight row needs its own port.

NOT DONE: mypy. The four new tests add three errors of the two classes the
file already has ten of -- a fixture annotated `-> tuple[...]` rather than
`Iterator[...]`, and indexing `run_summary(...)["builders"]` which is
typed Optional. Matched the surrounding twelve tests rather than diverging
on four; nothing gates on mypy here and the file is not clean today.
close_reason: Fixed with option (b): the flavour rides in origin as dsynth spells it, and the redundant key is gone from both the history entry and the builder row. Not a coin flip — the adapter's own contract documents its additions one by one, run.js never reads a flavour, and the information was already in origin. Master green: 4429 passed, 0 failed.

title: tracker and runner race to migrate on startup; the loser's raise kills the tracker, and busy_timeout cannot cover a lock upgrade
description:
The tracker and the runner both run schema migrations from init_db at
startup, and `deploy install` restarts them back to back. On a deploy that
carries a migration they race for the write lock, the loser raises, and in
the tracker that raise is inside the uvicorn startup lifespan -- so the
service does not degrade, it EXITS.

HAPPENED IN PRODUCTION 2026-09-26, deploying 41eecf4 (the flavor migration,
3bfecca) to 192.168.5.101. Verbatim, from /var/log/polytropos/tracker.log:

  File ".../dportsv3/tracker/server.py", line 210, in _startup
    conn = init_db(app.state.db_path)
  File ".../dportsv3/db/schema.py", line 782, in init_db
    _add_build_flavor_dimension(conn)
  File ".../dportsv3/db/schema.py", line 745, in _add_build_flavor_dimension
    conn.execute(definition)
  sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked
  ERROR:    Application startup failed. Exiting.

The runner won the race, completed the migration cleanly (2749
build_results and 1731 port_status rows, both keys rebuilt, no leftover
_flavored tables -- the SAVEPOINT rollback worked), and went on serving.
The tracker was simply down, with HTTP dead, until restarted by hand. A
plain restart then worked, because the migration was already applied and
the idempotence check skips it.

BUSY_TIMEOUT IS SET AND DOES NOT HELP. tracker/db.py:83 sets
`PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` on every connection open_db hands out, which
is why this looks impossible at first. The reason it does not apply is the
shape of the migration:

  conn.execute("SAVEPOINT build_flavors")     # opens a transaction
  PRAGMA table_info(<table>)                  # a READ
  conn.execute(definition)                    # CREATE TABLE -- a WRITE

That last line is a LOCK UPGRADE: the transaction is already open holding a
read lock, and sqlite returns SQLITE_BUSY for an upgrade IMMEDIATELY
without invoking the busy handler, because waiting on an upgrade can
deadlock. The timeout is honoured only when the lock is taken cleanly.

MEASURED, both directions, against a WAL database with busy_timeout=5000
on both connections and another writer holding the lock:

  SAVEPOINT, read, then write   -> raises "database is locked" at 0.000s
  BEGIN IMMEDIATE, then write   -> waits 1.55s for the other writer, then
                                   succeeds

So the fix direction is to take the write lock up front rather than
upgrade into it. That is one line at the top of the migration, and it
makes the existing 5s timeout do the job it was already configured for.

WORTH DECIDING WITH IT, and bigger than the one line: SHOULD TWO PROCESSES
MIGRATE AT ALL? runner.py:616 ("Always run init_db -- it's idempotent and
applies any pending") and tracker/server.py:210 both do. Idempotent is not
the same as concurrent-safe, which is exactly what this proved. A single
owner -- the deploy running migrations explicitly before either service
starts, with both services then only verifying -- removes the race instead
of making it survivable. The deploy runbook already has a natural place for
it, between phase 2 (install) and phase 4 (restart).

ALSO WORTH A LOOK: the tracker treating any startup DB error as fatal is
defensible on its own, but combined with the above it turns a transient
lock into an outage that nothing retries and nothing alerts on. The failure
was found by a human reading a deploy report, not by the system.

WHY IT WILL RECUR AND HAS NOT BEFORE: it only bites when a deploy carries a
schema migration that actually has work to do. Every deploy since the
services were split has been migration-free, so the race has been latent.
The next schema change hits it again.

NOT URGENT FOR THE HOST: 192.168.5.101 is fully up on 41eecf4, migration
applied, config check rc=0, both services running. The snapshot taken
before the deploy is at
/build/synth/logs/evidence/state.db.pre-flavor-20260926T195838Z and can be
removed once someone is satisfied the flavor data is right.
notes:
FIXED 2026-09-27. THE LOCK IS TAKEN FOR THE WHOLE MIGRATION PHASE, not
per-migration as this bead proposed.

_migrate() now wraps everything between the PRAGMAs and
executescript(SCHEMA) in one BEGIN IMMEDIATE: the MIGRATIONS ALTERs and
_add_build_flavor_dimension together. Three reasons it is the phase and
not the one migration that failed:

1. EVERY migration in the phase is protected, including the next one
   somebody writes. The defect was not in _add_build_flavor_dimension; it
   was in doing a read and then a write inside an open transaction, which
   any rebuild does.
2. THE PHASE IS NOW ATOMIC, which it was not. Only the flavor migration
   carried a SAVEPOINT; an ALTER that succeeded before a later migration
   raised was committed and stayed. test_a_migration_failure_leaves_no_
   half_built_table fails against the old code for exactly that reason --
   it is a behaviour change, not only a locking fix.
3. _add_build_flavor_dimension keeps its SAVEPOINT untouched. Inside the
   outer transaction it is a nested savepoint, so its own rollback
   semantics still hold and the lock is already held when it reads.

A CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES THIS, and it is measured, not assumed:
conn.executescript() COMMITS ANY PENDING TRANSACTION before it runs. So
the lock cannot be held across executescript(SCHEMA) -- an outer
transaction would be committed halfway and silently. Verified:
in_transaction True before, False after. SCHEMA is CREATE ... IF NOT
EXISTS, which takes its locks cleanly and is covered by the ordinary busy
handler, so it does not need the window.
_add_env_health_runner_dimension uses executescript too and runs after
SCHEMA, so it is outside the window for the same reason; its read-then-
write is not inside a transaction, so the plain handler applies to it.

TIMEOUT: MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000 for the phase, restored to
5000 in a finally. This bead's own note said BEGIN IMMEDIATE alone "makes
the existing 5s timeout do the job" -- true, but 5s is a ceiling for a
query and a poor one for a table copy on a bigger database than this one.
test_the_connection_is_left_on_the_ordinary_timeout pins the restore,
because leaving 30s on the connection would make every later query wait
half a minute on a lock it should report at once.

NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY: single-owner migration. This bead asks whether two
processes should migrate at all, and the answer is still probably no --
but it moves migrations into the deploy, between install and restart,
which means the runbook and the deploy agent change too, and both services
need a "verify, do not migrate" mode with something sensible to do when
the schema is older than they are. That is its own piece of work with its
own failure modes, and it should not ride in on a lock fix. What is done
here makes the race survivable and correct; single-owner would make it
absent. Worth filing when someone wants to spend the deploy-path risk.

ALSO NOT CHANGED: the tracker treating a startup DB error as fatal. With
the transient case now waiting instead of dying, what is left is a lock
held for 30 seconds or a genuinely broken DB, and neither is a thing to
serve through. The bead was right that it turned a transient into an
outage; the transient is what got fixed.

TESTS: tests/test_migration_lock.py, seven. Three fail against the old
code -- waiting instead of dying, the wait being bounded and the handler
actually engaged, and the atomicity above. The other four pin the parts
that must not drift: the fixture really is unmigrated, the loser skips
work already done, the timeout is restored, and a caller that already
holds a transaction keeps it rather than being raised at.

ONE TEST FOLLOWED THE CODE: test_migrations_run_before_the_schema_script
asserted on init_db's source containing "for stmt in MIGRATIONS", which
moved into _migrate. It now checks init_db's call order AND that the loop
is where it moved to -- the second half matters, or the assertion would
pass on a _migrate that had quietly stopped running them.

FOUND WHILE TESTING, filed as poly-xhg6: the rebuild copies rows with
foreign_keys=ON, against sqlite's documented rebuild procedure, so one
orphan row now fails a service start instead of being reported. Latent
today -- nothing writes the FK-declared tables on a connection without
the pragma -- but the enforcement a row is written under is not the one
it is copied under, and the place that finds out is a boot.
close_reason: Fixed: the whole pre-SCHEMA migration phase runs under one BEGIN IMMEDIATE with a 30s timeout, so the loser waits for the winner instead of raising, and the phase is atomic. Cannot extend over executescript(SCHEMA), which commits pending transactions (measured). Single-owner migration deliberately left open. 7 tests, 3 fail against the old code.

title: config check reports every dev-env setting as a key nobody reads: claimed= exempts the section, not its subtree
description:
`Schema.unknown_keys(claimed={"dev_env"})` exempts the literal string
"dev_env" and nothing beneath it, so every dev-env setting written into the
shared config file is reported as a key nobody reads.

FOUND ON THE BUILDER, 2026-09-26, during the poly-atq9 deploy. `dportsv3
config check` exits 1 there with:

  warning: dev_env.dsynth_ccache is not a setting anything reads
           (check the spelling)

The setting is real, correctly spelled, and actively read:
dev-env/dports_dev_env/config.py:101 declares it, dsynth.py:38,46 reads it
to choose between /work/dsynth/ccache and `disabled`. The host has
`dsynth_ccache = true` set on purpose -- it is poly-dei7's remedy, the
difference between a one-file edit costing ~45 min on firefox and ~13 h on
chromium.

So the warning tells an operator to check the spelling of a correctly
spelled key, and the obvious way to make `config check` exit 0 is to delete
it, which silently turns ccache back off. That is the whole hazard: the
message argues for the change that breaks the thing.

THE MECHANISM. confschema.py:351 builds `known = set(self._by_path) |
claimed`, then walks the file. The walk yields BOTH the section and each
leaf under it:

  dev_env                 -> in known  -> skipped
  dev_env.dsynth_ccache   -> NOT in known, no table setting covers it, and
                             nothing in known starts with it + "." -> reported

The docstring says what was meant: "``claimed`` lets a caller pass the
paths another schema owns, so sharing one file does not make every key look
unknown to everybody." A section name is how both callers spell it
(commands/config.py:155, settings.py:765), so the intent is the subtree.

WHY IT SURVIVED. tests/test_settings_unification.py:294 tests only the
section header:

    assert "elsewhere" not in s.unknown_keys(claimed={"elsewhere"})

which is the one case that works. Reproduced with the same schema by
loading {"elsewhere": {"x": 1}}: unknown_keys(claimed={"elsewhere"})
returns ['elsewhere.x'].

FIX: treat a claimed path the way a `table` setting is already treated two
lines down -- `dotted == c or dotted.startswith(c + ".")`. The table branch
is the same idea and is already written.

WORTH DECIDING WITH IT: whether a false unknown-key warning should be
exit-1 at all. It counts into `problems` alongside a world-readable
credential and an unresolvable setting, so one stale key makes `config
check` fail as loudly as a leaked secret, and a deploy's verify step cannot
distinguish them. The deploy that found this reported the row as FAIL and
had to reason about it by hand.
notes:
FIXED 2026-09-26, BUT NOT THE WAY THIS BEAD PRESCRIBED. The description
says to make a claimed path own its subtree, "the way a table setting is
already treated two lines down". Reading the callers says otherwise, and
the divergence is the substance of the fix, so it is recorded here rather
than left to be re-derived.

WHY NOT THE SUBTREE. It fixes the false positive by destroying the true
one. Claiming `dev_env` as a subtree exempts dev_env.dsynth_ccache -- and
equally exempts dev_env.dsynth_cache, a typo no schema declares, which
then keeps its default in silence. That is the precise failure
unknown_keys exists to catch; the module docstring calls a silently
ignored key the reason the whole settings table was built.

Not argued, measured. With the bead's proposal applied on top of the
original callers, the new test
test_config_check_still_fails_on_a_misspelled_dev_env_key fails: the
misspelling stops being reported. Two tests fail in total, and both are
the ones that exist to pin this exact trade.

WHAT WAS DONE INSTEAD. The callers were wrong, not unknown_keys. The
docstring already said `claimed` takes "the paths another schema owns" --
paths, plural -- and both call sites passed a section name. So:
