2. THE BILLABLE RING NEEDS NO NEW DATA. render/nowbar.py already computes spend
and budget, and _spend carries a careful scope argument: budget is the JOB
budget (tier.max_tokens, enforced across attempts) while a turns
cumulative_billable_tokens counts THIS ATTEMPT only, so the job figure is what
the attempt opened with plus what it has spent since. That reasoning is the
denominator this ring needs and it is already right.

3. CONTEXT NEEDS ONE FIELD CARRIED. The turn card is built in
render/activity.py and pulls cumulative_billable_tokens but NOT prompt_tokens,
even though tool_loop emits it on every llm_turn row. One field added to the
card, then the newest turns value is the context occupancy.

4. THE WINDOW SETTING HAS AN OBVIOUS HOME: llm.patch.context_window, beside
llm.patch.context_keep_turns -- the masking knob that exists precisely to keep
the context down. Default 0 meaning "not declared", which satisfies this beads
own acceptance criterion 4: omit the ring rather than invent a denominator. The
patch role is the one that runs the agent loop, so a single global window would
have been wrong anyway with triage and chat on different models.

5. NO ENTRY ANIMATION, despite the sketch having one. The now-bar is re-rendered
by the live fragment on every poll that has rows, so a fill animation would
replay every three seconds, and a CSS transition cannot apply to an element
that is recreated. The ring fills as the VALUE grows, which is what was asked
for; it does not need to animate on arrival.

SO BOTH RINGS LAND, not one: the context ring is gated on a declared window
rather than deferred. A deployment that declares none sees exactly what it sees
today plus the billable ring.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-24. 4313 -> 4341 tests (28 new).

  settings.py            llm.patch.context_window, int, default 0
  render/nowbar.py       gauge(value, ceiling) -> {pct, level, value, ceiling}
                         GAUGE_WARN_PCT 75 / GAUGE_HOT_PCT 90
                         now_bar gains spend_gauge, context, context_window,
                         context_gauge
  render/activity.py     the turn card carries prompt_tokens
  _macros.html           gauge_ring(g, cap, title)
  _now_bar.html          both rings, with the figures kept beside them
  progress.css           .nb-gauge / .gauge-ring, conic-gradient, no library

Verified end to end on a seeded job: the PAGE and the live FRAGMENT both
render billable 66 green and context 93 red from the same `now`.

THREE THINGS THE REVIEW CAUGHT.

1. A TEST HOLE, found by mutation rather than by reading. Every context test
monkeypatched _context_window, so making the DEFAULT 200,000 -- inventing the
ceiling this beads AC4 forbids -- passed all of them. Two tests added that go
through the real settings read, and they fail under that mutation.

2. THE TEMPLATE EXPLODED ON A `now` DICT THAT PREDATES THESE KEYS.
test_render_now_bar renders the partial with a hand-built dict; a missing key
is Undefined, which is falsy in a condition but raises inside format(). Now
now.get() throughout. Worth keeping: this partial is rendered from whatever
dict it is handed, by two callers.

3. THE CUSTOM PROPERTIES ARE DEFAULTED ON THE ELEMENT. --gauge: var(--muted)
and --pct: 0 on .gauge-ring itself, so a ring that arrives without a level
class draws neutral and empty rather than as an unpainted disc. The design
token test also requires every var() to be defined, and a value set inline in
a selector does not count as a definition.

WHAT DID NOT HAPPEN, deliberately:
- no entry animation. The live fragment re-renders this bar on every poll with
  rows, so a fill would replay every three seconds, and a transition cannot
  apply to an element that is recreated. The ring fills as the value grows.
- no invented context ceiling. Undeclared shows the occupancy figure with no
  ring, and the tooltip names the setting that would give it one.
- the absolute figures were not replaced. 264,110 / 400,000 is what an
  operator quotes; the ring is the glance.

poly-0g0 REMAINS OPEN and this does not close it -- but it no longer makes it
worse: every figure on the line is captioned with its quantity, which is what
the dependency was recorded for.

title: The worktree version pill reloads the page and lands at the top
description:
Operator report 2026-09-24: clicking an attempt pill (A1, A2...) in the
working-tree version selector "takes you up to the job detail page".

CAUSE: wt_link builds a query-param URL and the pills are plain anchors.

  pages.py:1498     request.url.include_query_params(attempt=n)
  agentic_api.py    lambda n: f"?attempt={n}"

Both are correct as URLs -- the pin has to be linkable into a bead or a handoff
(poly-5tgc UI 8) -- but following one is a full navigation that lands at the top
of a long page, and the working-tree band is near the bottom. The operator
clicks a version and appears to be thrown somewhere else.

FIX: anchor the link at the band. _worktree.html already stamps
id="worktree" on the section, so appending #worktree to both link builders
makes the browser land on the band it just changed, and the URL stays
shareable. No JS needed.
close_reason: Closed

title: Attempt strip: narrow segments clip their label to a misleading number
description:
Operator report 2026-09-24: "the timelines look weird when compared among
attempts". Screenshot shows A1 (rebuild failed, 51m27s, 165 turns) above A2
(running, ~5m, 11 turns), sharing one scale.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG, from the code:

1. LABELS CLIP TO A MISLEADING NUMBER. .seg has overflow:hidden and a 7px left
pad, and the label is printed inside the segment whatever its width. A2 shows
"1m52s | 55 | 2m18s" -- the middle one is dur_ms rendering "55.0s" into a
segment a few percent wide, clipped after two characters. "55" beside "1m52s"
reads as a quantity in the same unit. A segment too narrow for its label should
carry none; the title attribute already has the full value.

2. dur_ms IS INCONSISTENT BELOW A MINUTE. _macros.html:102 renders
(ms/1000)|round(2), so a sub-minute segment reads "55.0s" or "2.35s" while
every longer one reads "1m52s". Two decimal places on a wall-clock segment is
false precision.

NOT A DEFECT, RECORDED SO IT IS NOT "FIXED" BY ACCIDENT: segments are grouped
by KIND and ordered by _KIND_ORDER = llm, run, tool, build, test, fail -- not
chronologically. Its comment says that is deliberate, "stable across attempts
so two rows can be compared". The design (specimen 01) describes "one track per
attempt, segmented by what consumed the wall clock" and does not require
chronological order.

OPEN QUESTION FOR THE OPERATOR, since it may be what actually looked wrong: the
leading segment changes MEANING between rows. On a finished attempt the
remainder is "llm" (violet, "model turns + overhead, not timed"); on a running
one the same leading slot is "run" (in progress). A1s 41m53s violet block and
A2s leading block are the same position and similar weight but mean different
things. Options if that is the complaint: label the remainder differently per
state, or split it out of the track entirely.
notes:
CLAIM 2 WITHDRAWN 2026-09-24, before implementing. I called dur_ms rendering
"55.0s" / "2.35s" below a minute "false precision". The design source does the
same -- its own samples read "1.74s", "462ms", "44m02s" -- so two decimals under
a minute is the house style, not a defect, and changing it would be a new
divergence rather than a fix.

That leaves ONE defect here: the clipping. "55" in the screenshot is "55.0s"
cut off by a segment a few percent wide, which is why it reads as a bare
number next to "1m52s".
FIXED 2026-09-24, the clipping half. Segments carry a label only at or above
_LABEL_MIN_PCT = 5.0 percent of the track; below that the title attribute is
the only carrier, which it already was for every segment. Mutation-checked:
labelling every segment regardless fails two tests.

LEFT OPEN DELIBERATELY: whether the leading segment changing meaning between a
finished attempt (llm, "model turns + overhead") and a running one (run, "in
progress") is what actually looked wrong when comparing rows. That is a design
question rather than a defect, and it needs the operator to say which reading
they expected before anything moves.

title: The tracker and its UI treat dev-envs as one global set with one active: no host dimension
description:
PREREQUISITE FOR THE REST OF THIS EPIC, and it needs no HTTP work: this is a
data-model and UI change, and the runner already writes env_health_status
directly today.

Multiple dev-envs per host already work at the DEV-ENV layer -- env_resolver's
list_available_envs enumerates <cache_root>/envs, and a live builder carries
2026Q1, 2026Q2 and 2026Q3. The tracker does not model that. It enumerates env
NAMES globally and selects exactly one, which is single-host thinking in all
three layers:

  SCHEMA
    tracker_active_env   singleton INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (singleton = 1)
    env_health_status    env TEXT PRIMARY KEY
  QUERY
    get_active_env(conn)        -> one value for the deployment
    env_health_statuses(conn)   -> "Latest persisted health probe per dev-env",
                                   ORDER BY env, no host anywhere
  UI  (agentic_runner.html, "Environment health")
    "Active env (runner default + verify-fix fallback): <one value>"
    "none -- runner will auto-pick if exactly one env exists"
    a [set] button per row, radio semantics: exactly one active

There is no builder column in any of it, and no way to say that 2026Q3 is
healthy on one builder and broken on another.

TWO FAILURE MODES, and the quiet one is worse:
* tracker_active_env hands every builder the same answer. Fails visibly --
  a builder without that env simply cannot work.
* env_health_status is keyed by env NAME, so two builders carrying 2026Q3
  share one row and overwrite each other's probes. Fails SILENTLY: an
  operator reads a green 2026Q3 probed on a different machine, and the
  runner's dsynth gate believes it.

SCOPE: give env selection and env health a host/runner dimension, and make
the UI show envs per builder rather than as one global list. The runner
already reports health per env; what is missing is who reported it.

OPEN DESIGN QUESTION, and it decides how disruptive this is: per-runner rows,
or keep the singleton as the operator's DEFAULT that a builder's own set
overrides. The second preserves today's single-host workflow exactly -- one
builder, one active env picked in the UI, nothing changes until a second
builder enrolls -- and is the reason to prefer it.

SEQUENCING: first. poly-fij.10's capability dispatch cannot match a job to a
builder that has the right env until the tracker can record which builder has
which env, and poly-fij.6's per-runner UI is the same question asked about
presentation. This does NOT depend on poly-fij.12: no HTTP conversion is
needed to add a column and a host-aware UI.
notes:
AFTER READING THE CODE, 2026-09-24. Three things the description did not know.

1. THE COLLISION IS LITERAL, at runner.py:415:

     INSERT INTO env_health_status (env, status, ...)
     ON CONFLICT(env) DO UPDATE SET status=excluded.status, ...

   Two builders probing 2026Q3 do not merely share a row, they actively
   overwrite each other on every probe cycle.

2. env_health_status IS ALSO THE UI'S LIST OF AVAILABLE ENVS, not just health.
   stub_unprobed_envs() (runner.py:356) inserts a placeholder row per env on
   disk at runner start, and says why: "brand-new envs are invisible to the
   tracker UI (the dropdown sources from this table) until the runner's first
   health probe touches them". So the host dimension matters twice over --
   with N builders the dropdown becomes the union of every builder's envs with
   no indication of who has which. Worse, its INSERT OR IGNORE keys on (env),
   so builder B's brand-new env is silently skipped when builder A already
   stubbed that name, and B's env stays invisible.

3. THE TRACKER ALREADY KNOWS IT CANNOT PROBE. set_active_env's docstring:
   "No server-side validation against the envs that actually exist ...
   Validation here would couple the tracker to filesystem state it can't
   reliably read (tracker runs unprivileged)." That is the same root cause as
   poly-paee, and it settles the direction: the RUNNER reports which envs it
   has, the tracker never looks.

DESIGN DECIDED, the second option from the description: the singleton stays as
the operator's DEPLOYMENT DEFAULT, and a per-builder selection overrides it
when set. Today's single-host workflow then behaves exactly as it does now --
one builder, one env picked in the UI -- and nothing changes until a second
builder enrolls. Per-runner selection goes on `runners` as a column, which is
the extension pattern poly-fij.3 already chose for that table.

env_health_status needs its PRIMARY KEY changed, which sqlite cannot ALTER, so
it is a table rebuild: legacy rows carry runner_id = '' meaning unattributed,
and the UI says so rather than pretending they belong to anyone.

ALSO IN SCOPE, found while reading: env_resolver.py:135 reads get_active_env
at precedence step 2 and is one of the six agent->tracker read imports
(poly-fij.12). It has to pass its own runner_id or a per-builder override can
never take effect.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-24.

SCHEMA. env_health_status is keyed (runner_id, env); runners gained
active_env. A fresh DB gets both inline -- the column had to go in the CREATE
as well as MIGRATIONS, because MIGRATIONS runs BEFORE the schema script and
the ALTER hits "no such table" on a fresh DB, exactly as that tuple's own
comment says ("every column lives in its CREATE above").

An existing DB is REBUILT, not altered: the fix is to the PRIMARY KEY, which
sqlite cannot alter in place. Not in MIGRATIONS either -- that list is the
tolerant ADD COLUMN path and swallows OperationalError, which is the last
thing a multi-statement rebuild should have. It sits with
_RETIRE_STORED_REGRESSED and _DROP_DEAD_TABLES, runs untolerated after SCHEMA,
and is idempotent by inspecting PRAGMA table_info rather than by IF NOT
EXISTS.

LEGACY ROWS ARE DISCARDED, which was a decision, not laziness. Keeping them
as runner_id '' looked conservative but is worse: a runner stamping its real
id never matches them, so every env would carry a permanent unattributable
ghost beside its real row. Safe because every column is a PROBE CACHE, not a
record -- status, probed_at, operator_action and detail_json all come from the
probe object (runner.py getattr(env_health, ...)), and there is no operator
input in the table. The runner stubs at start and re-probes on its cycle, so
the cost is one cycle of "unprobed".

SELECTION IS A DEFAULT PLUS OVERRIDES, as decided. tracker_active_env stays
the singleton deployment default; runners.active_env overrides it when set.
get_active_env(conn, runner_id=None) and set_active_env(conn, name,
runner_id=None) both default to the old behaviour, so a single-builder install
is unchanged. set_active_env with a runner_id UPDATEs rather than upserts: a
runner row comes from enrollment and the heartbeat, and inventing one here
would put a builder in the table that never reported.

WRITERS. Both runner writers stamp runner_id(), and the probe's
ON CONFLICT(env) -- the literal cause of two builders overwriting each other
-- is now ON CONFLICT(runner_id, env). env_resolver passes runner_id() at
precedence step 2, or a per-builder choice could never take effect.

UI. The builder column and the per-builder env table appear only when there is
more than one builder, so a single-builder page renders exactly as it did.
That kept test_the_page_shows_one_runner's intent intact -- its assertion had
to move off the string "runner_id", which now legitimately appears in the
page's own fetch payload, and onto the rendered markup.

TWO THINGS THE RE-REVIEW CAUGHT that tests had not:
* the verify-fix env picker (pages.py) builds a list of env NAMES from these
  rows, so two builders carrying 2026Q3 would have listed it twice. Now
  de-duplicated, order preserved, with the reason: verify-fix is a CLI on some
  host and the tracker cannot know which, so the union of names is right there
  rather than one builder's.
* PUT /api/config/active-env now echoes {"name", "runner_id"} because "name"
  alone became ambiguous. Three tests asserted exact equality on the old
  shape; only they consume it -- the page's script checks r.ok.

15 new tests in tests/test_env_per_builder.py; 4239 pass.

NOT DONE HERE, deliberately: nothing yet MATCHES work to a builder's envs.
That is poly-fij.10, which now has the representation it needs.
close_reason: Closed

title: Convert the runner's direct DB access to the tracker's HTTP vocabulary
description:
THE HOLE EVERY OTHER BEAD IN THIS EPIC WAITS ON. poly-fij.4 says "Converting
those is Step 21's centralization work, and this bead depends on it rather
than duplicating it" -- and Step 21 (poly-39v) was rescoped on migration with
21b "dropped, not deferred". So poly-fij.4 waits on cancelled work,
poly-fij.7 builds a pipe with nothing scheduled to flow through it,
poly-fij.9 sizes a load nothing is scheduled to produce, and poly-fij.1
converts one call site out of roughly fifty.

WHY THIS IS NOT A REVIVAL OF 21b. 21b was dropped because "centralize every
write into typed helpers" across 232 execute sites in 22 files is not one
unit of work, and the drift it targeted is better caught by tests. That was a
STYLE judgement about the whole codebase. The runner's writes are a
BOUNDARY: they are exactly the set that has to cross a network for a remote
dev-env, and nothing else is. The tracker keeps its own ~200 writes exactly
where they are. Scoped to the boundary it is a unit of work again.

MEASURED 2026-09-24, in dportsv3/agent/:

  31 write statements across 10 tables
    issues 9 · jobs 4 · bundles 4 · runners 3 · user_context_requests 3
    env_health_status 2 · activity_log 2 · runner_status 2
    job_events 1 · verify_requests 1

  PLUS 4 statements that live in the TRACKER's modules and run on the
  runner's connection because the runner imports them, touching an 11th
  table:
    runner.py:161   take_pending_operator_notes    operator_notes (UPDATE)
    runner.py:1597  resolve_issue_build_confirmed  issues
    runner.py:1470  reopen_issue_build_failed      issues
    runner.py:1616  reopen_issue_build_failed      issues

  Three of those import dportsv3.tracker.routes.issue_actions -- the runner
  executing the tracker's HTTP ROUTE HANDLERS as library functions.

  PLUS THE READS, which conversions like this routinely forget: 13 on the
  runner's connection, and 6 imported tracker query functions --
  green_head_watermark, issues_needing_build, is_origin_skipped,
  issue_for_bundle, list_user_context_history, and get_active_env in
  env_resolver.py:135. A remote runner cannot read the DB either, and
  get_active_env is per job while is_origin_skipped is per port.

HOW: ONE SEAM, TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS. Not 31 call sites rewritten as requests
-- that is a big-bang cutover with no safe intermediate state. Introduce one
interface for the runner's state access with LocalStore (today's
_state_db_conn, byte-for-byte the same behaviour) and HttpStore. Move call
sites through the seam one at a time with no behaviour change, tests green
throughout, then flip the implementation by config. One place for auth
headers, retries and batching; a fake store for the runner's tests; and the
agent->tracker imports die as a side effect because the seam replaces them.

ENDPOINT VOCABULARY, grouped by meaning rather than by table. The vocabulary
belongs to the TRACKER; the runner is a client of it, pointed at loopback
exactly like the hooks.

  activity_log                 POST /v1/activity      NEW, and must BATCH
  runner_status + runners      POST /v1/runners/heartbeat   NEW
  jobs + job_events            /v1/jobs/transition    ALREADY EXISTS
  issues (+3 handler imports)  /v1/issues/...         NEW
  bundles                      /v1/bundles/upsert     extend
  user_context_requests        /v1/user-context       extend
  env_health_status            POST /v1/env-health    NEW
  operator_notes               claim-and-return       NEW

jobs + job_events needs no design at all: ArtifactStore.apply_transition is
"Hook-side entry point for the lifecycle state machine ... a thin wrapper"
around dportsv3.agent.lifecycle, so POST /v1/jobs/transition already routes
transitions through the same state machine and the HOOKS ALREADY USE IT. The
runner is the only caller taking the shortcut. lifecycle.apply does not move;
it becomes the server-side implementation with two callers.

ORDER, easiest proof first:
1. Seam + LocalStore. No behaviour change. Most of the work, all of the
   safety.
2. Heartbeat. One call per 5s, self-contained -- proves the path end to end
   at trivial volume.
3. activity_log. The volume test: 2,130 llm_turn rows in one observed day, a
   row per tool call. Second, so the performance truth arrives early.
4. issues. The semantics test, and where the route-handler imports die.
5. Reads.
6. Then poly-fij.4's auth, by then a header in one place.

FOUR THINGS THAT WILL BITE:
* Telemetry must never block the agent loop. Batch, fire-and-forget, spool
  locally (poly-fij.7). A tracker outage must not slow a build.
* Batching must preserve order. Rows are read back by id and the turn cards
  pair tool_start with tool_call by call_id.
* The 5000-row prune currently runs INSIDE the runner's write
  (runner.py:1877). Server-side once writes are HTTP -- and it is the cap
  that caused poly-a162.
* take_pending_operator_notes is a read-modify-write, and it gets BETTER
  over HTTP: atomicity moves server-side instead of resting on the runner
  holding _state_db_lock.

DONE WHEN, and these two facts are the test: the runner holds no sqlite
connection at all, and dportsv3/agent/ imports nothing from
dportsv3/tracker/.
notes:
DOWNSTREAM CONSUMER, 2026-09-24: poly-pvs2 (the dsynth tail in the job-detail cards) now depends on this bead and needs only steps 1 and 2 -- the seam, then POST /v1/runners/heartbeat. The tail rides the heartbeat call as a field, because that is the one call happening at the right cadence with the right identity. Steps 3-5 are not on its path.

That makes step 2 worth more than 'proves the path at trivial volume': it is the step that unfreezes a user-visible feature.
CODE READ 2026-09-24, four findings that constrain step 1.

1. THE SEAM IS ONE FILE'S CONCERN. All 123 _state_db_conn references are in
runner.py. Nothing else in dportsv3/agent/ touches it.

2. LOCALSTORE MUST RESOLVE THE CONNECTION AT CALL TIME, NOT AT CONSTRUCTION.
Eight test files plus demo/drive_demo.py assign runner._state_db_conn after
import (monkeypatch.setattr or direct assignment) and expect writes to land in
their own sqlite. A store that captured the connection in __init__ would
silently stop seeing those, and the failure mode is a test that passes while
asserting nothing. 'Byte-for-byte the same behaviour' includes this.

3. THE FIRST GROUP IS RUNNER PRESENCE, AND IT IS FIVE STATEMENTS, NOT TWO.
The measurement above counts runner_status 2 + runners 3. As operations:
  register_runner()      INSERT INTO runners ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, clears
                         stopped_at -- re-enrollment on restart
  _heartbeat_loop()      UPDATE runner_status.updated_at
                         UPDATE runners.last_heartbeat_at
  update_runner_status() upsert the runner_status singleton, with a CASE that
                         preserves started_at unless job_id changed
  deregister_runner()    UPDATE runners.stopped_at on clean shutdown
So 'POST /v1/runners/heartbeat' in the vocabulary above is under-specified:
presence needs register / heartbeat / status / deregister, and the status
upsert carries the started_at CASE which a naive endpoint would drop.

4. ERROR HANDLING IS NOT UNIFORM AND THE DIFFERENCE IS DELIBERATE.
_heartbeat_loop swallows silently (it runs 12x a minute; a warning per tick
would bury the log). register_runner, update_runner_status and
deregister_runner print a warning. Step 1 preserves each as it is; unifying
them is a separate decision, not a free side effect of introducing a seam.
STEP 1 LANDED 2026-09-24. dportsv3/agent/state_store.py: StateStore protocol, LocalStore, a process-wide store() with set_store() for the flip and for tests. Runner presence is the first group across -- register_runner, heartbeat, set_runner_status, deregister_runner. No direct write to runners or runner_status is left in dportsv3/agent/. 4239 -> 4251 tests, the 12 new ones in tests/test_state_store_seam.py; no behaviour change, which is the bar for this step.

TWO TESTS WERE MUTATION-CHECKED rather than trusted for passing first try:
- capture the connection in __init__ instead of per call -> the
  assigned-after-construction test fails. That is the silent-writes-nowhere
  failure mode from finding 2.
- drop the started_at CASE -> the same-job test fails. That is the clause step
  2's endpoint is likeliest to lose.

STEP 2 IS NEXT and its shape is now fixed by the protocol: HttpStore plus the
endpoints. Note that presence needs FOUR calls, not the one the vocabulary
table names -- register / heartbeat / status / deregister -- and the tail
(poly-pvs2) rides the heartbeat one as a field.
ENDPOINT SHAPE DECIDED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-09-24: ONE endpoint, event-shaped.

  POST /v1/runners/presence   {runner_id, event, ...}
  event in register | heartbeat | status | deregister

This SUPERSEDES the vocabulary table's 'runner_status + runners POST
/v1/runners/heartbeat', which was both under-specified (presence is four
operations, not one) and, as four separate routes, more surface than the
meaning needs. Rationale: it follows /v1/jobs/transition, which is already
event-shaped and already the precedent this bead cites for having one
implementation with two callers. The tail (poly-pvs2) then rides the heartbeat
event as a field rather than needing a route of its own.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE OTHER GROUPS: the same question will come up for issues and
env-health. Not pre-deciding it here -- but the reason given above (follow the
existing event-shaped precedent, one route per resource rather than per verb)
applies to them too.

runner_id travels on EVERY event, including status, whose handler does not use
it yet because runner_status is still the id=1 singleton. It is the caller's
identity, not a speculative feature: poly-fij.4 binds a token to exactly that
field, and an endpoint that cannot say who called it cannot be authenticated
later without a wire change.
STEP 2 LANDED 2026-09-24.

  db/presence.py            one implementation: register / heartbeat /
                            set_status / deregister, plus apply(conn, payload)
  LocalStore                builds the payload and calls presence.apply
  HttpStore                 builds the SAME payload and POSTs it
  ArtifactStore.apply_presence  server side, no emit_event
  POST /v1/runners/presence event-shaped, 400 on a bad payload
  runner.state_transport    'local' | 'http', refused if it is neither
  select_state_store()      called from main() before anything writes

4251 -> 4267 tests. The shipped config sample is generated from the settings
table and had to be regenerated (deploy/polytropos.toml.sample); two tests
guard that and caught it.

WHAT THE PARITY TEST DOES AND DOES NOT PROVE, since it would be easy to
over-trust. Both transports build the same payload and call the same
presence.apply, so parity holds BY CONSTRUCTION. Mutation-checked all three
ways: breaking the shared SQL (the started_at CASE) fails the two behaviour
tests and parity still PASSES; dropping a field inside apply() fails only the
local behaviour test; dropping a field in the ROUTE fails parity. So parity
guards the architecture -- a second code path appearing -- and the over-the-wire
tests carry the behaviour.

TWO THINGS THE REVIEW CHANGED, not the tests:
- HttpStore was silent on every failure in the first version. Wrong: a builder
  pointed at the wrong URL would fail to enroll and report nothing, which is
  the one deployment where a log line is worth most. It now warns where
  LocalStore warns, from the same table, and stays silent on the heartbeat.
- The timeout is HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL - 1, not artifact_store_put's 20s. A call
  that can outlive its slot leaves ticks overlapping and the thread behind the
  cadence it defines. Pinned by a test.

STILL OPEN AND DELIBERATE: runner_status is the id=1 singleton, so the status
event's runner_id is carried and not used. With N builders, 'what is the runner
doing' becomes per-runner -- that is poly-fij.6's read model, not this bead's.

title: A dumb hook's failed POST is lost: nothing retries and the failure is swallowed
description:
The hooks are deliberately dumb and must stay that way -- stdlib shell,
posting to loopback, no intelligence, no knowledge of topology. poly-fij.7
keeps them unchanged: "the artifact-store-client is unchanged and still
points at 127.0.0.1".

That makes the DELIVERY GUARANTEE somebody else's job, and right now it is
nobody's. Two legs, and only one is covered:

  hook --loopback--> relay        THIS BEAD. Nothing retries.
  relay --------> tracker         poly-fij.7's disk spool.

artifact_store_put catches every exception and returns False
(runner.py:548). hook_common.sh calls the client and does not inspect the
outcome. So a tracker restart, a blip, or a relay that is not listening
loses a bundle upsert, an artifact, or a job transition with no record that
it existed. poly-fij.7 names this for its own leg -- "silently loses
evidence with no record it existed" -- and it is equally true one hop
earlier.

WHY IT CANNOT BE FIXED BY MAKING THE HOOK RETRY: that is intelligence in the
hook, which is the thing being kept out. A retry loop needs backoff, a
bound, and somewhere to put what it could not deliver -- a spool -- and a
spool in a hook is a spool inside the build sandbox.

SO THE FIX IS ON THE RECEIVING SIDE, and it is a property, not a feature:
SPOOL BEFORE ACK. The local listener writes to its disk spool and only then
returns 2xx. Then the hook's dumb single POST is enough: a 2xx means the
bytes are durable, and the only loss window is a crash between accept and
spool-write, which is identical whether the listener is a thread in the
runner or its own process. Getting the order backwards -- ack then spool --
is what makes the process boundary matter.

The hook should still SAY SOMETHING on a non-2xx rather than swallowing it.
It cannot fix it, but a line in the build log is the difference between lost
evidence and lost evidence nobody can explain later.

LIVE TODAY, INDEPENDENT OF REMOTE BUILDERS OR AUTH. This is a defect on a
single LAN host now -- poly-fij.7's own notes say the durability half should
be split out so it can land, and this is the other half of that split.

title: Dispatch has no notion of what a builder can build, and the active env is a singleton
description:
The tracker will have work FOR a runner -- "build this" -- and which builder
can take which work depends on the host. Nothing in this epic accounts for
it: poly-fij.1's claim endpoint picks work without asking who is asking, and
poly-fij.3's enrollment extends `runners` with display_name, enrolled_at,
token_sha256 and revoked_at -- identity and auth, no capabilities.

THE FIRST BLOCKER IS SCHEMA-LEVEL, not a missing feature:

  CREATE TABLE tracker_active_env (
      singleton INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (singleton = 1), ...

One active dev-env for the whole deployment, operator-set, read by every
runner through get_active_env() -- "Source of truth for the runner's
per-job-dispatch env resolution (precedence step 2)". A builder has the envs
it has: a live host was observed carrying 2026Q1, 2026Q2 and 2026Q3, and a
job for @2026Q3 cannot run on a builder that lacks that env. With N builders
a single global answer is wrong for N-1 of them, and the CHECK forbids
recording a second.

SO THE DISPATCH AXES, smallest first:

1. WHICH ENVS A BUILDER HAS. This is the minimum and it is not optional --
   without it a claim can hand a job to a host that cannot run it. Reported
   at enrollment and refreshed on heartbeat, because envs are created and
   destroyed while a builder lives.
2. TARGET -> ENV. jobs.target is already recorded (@2026Q3) and jobs.dev_env
   since poly-qqx9.12, so the join exists; what is missing is the claim
   asking for it.
3. Everything beyond that is speculative until measured: architecture, disk,
   ccache presence, "big ports need a big machine". Do not design for it
   now; leave the capability record open-ended enough that adding an axis is
   a row, not a migration.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE RELAY ARGUMENT: this is the direction that stops the
builder-side component being a dumb forwarder. Writes forward without
interpretation (poly-fij.7), but the runner also PULLS work and must present
what it can do. So the runner is a real client with an identity and a
capability set, not a pipe -- and that is an argument for the relay living
inside it rather than beside it.

Where the singleton goes is the open design question: per-runner rows in
`runners` (an extension, like poly-fij.3's), or keep the singleton as the
operator's DEFAULT and let a builder's own set override it. The second keeps
today's single-host workflow untouched, which is worth something.
notes:
THERE IS NO SEPARATE MULTI-DEV-ENV BEAD TO DEPEND ON, checked 2026-09-24, and
the reason is that the capability already exists -- what is missing is only
the tracker's host-awareness. So this bead IS that work rather than waiting
on it.

ALREADY TRUE: the dev-env layer supports N envs per host
(worker/env_resolver list_available_envs over <cache_root>/envs; a live
builder carries 2026Q1, 2026Q2 and 2026Q3). poly-i7y, closed, was about the
runner losing its dsynth gate when it could NOT enumerate them. poly-l18e is
build economics, not env support.

ALSO ALREADY TRUE: the tracker models N envs, one row per env in
env_health_status. Multi-env is not absent from the tracker.

WHAT BREAKS UNDER N BUILDERS is that both tracker-side env tables are keyed
WITHOUT THE HOST:

  tracker_active_env   singleton INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (singleton = 1)
  env_health_status    env TEXT PRIMARY KEY

The second was missed in the description above and is the worse of the two,
because it fails silently. Two builders that both carry 2026Q3 share one
health row and overwrite each other's probes -- so an operator reads a green
2026Q3 that was probed on a different machine, and the runner's gate believes
it. The singleton at least fails visibly, by handing every builder the same
answer.

So the scope is: env selection and env health both become per-builder, and
the claim matches jobs.target to a builder that actually has the env. Whether
selection lives as per-runner rows or as an operator DEFAULT that a builder's
own set overrides is still the open design question in the description --
keeping the singleton as a default is what preserves today's single-host
workflow unchanged.
RESEQUENCED 2026-09-24. The singleton/host-dimension half of this bead moved
out to poly-fij.13, which this now depends on, and the wrong dependency on
poly-fij.12 was removed.

Two corrections behind that:
* Multi-env awareness in the tracker does NOT need the HTTP conversion. It is
  a schema and UI change, and the runner already writes env_health_status
  directly. Making this wait on poly-fij.12 put it behind the largest piece of
  work in the epic for no reason.
* An earlier note here claimed "the tracker models N envs, one row per env in
  env_health_status. Multi-env is not absent from the tracker." That is wrong
  and it is withdrawn: one row per env NAME with no host column is a global
  list of names, not a model of N envs on M hosts. The UI is the same -- it
  lists names and picks exactly one, globally.

What is left in THIS bead is the matching: the claim endpoint asking who is
asking, and handing a job only to a builder that has the env its target
needs. That wants poly-fij.13 for the representation and poly-fij.1 for the
claim, and nothing else.
2026-10-04 pointer (poly-7pwa). (1) poly-7pwa.14 holds an unpinned job at
claim time while the selected env composes another build line
(runner._lines_held_back and _waits_for_its_line, over
env_resolver.envs_by_build_line). This bead's claim, matching jobs.target to a
builder's envs, replaces that hold: delete it then, and keep .14's job-start
backstop (runner._check_env_build_line) and its startup reap's keep set
(runner._reap_stale_queued_at_startup). (2) This claim is the first thing that
runs two lines' jobs in parallel, which is poly-7pwa.15's revisit trigger.

title: The attempt strip never refreshes: it is not in the live fragment at all
description:
Reported from a running job, 2026-09-24: the timelines do not update.

api_job_activity_fragment returns three bodies -- html (raw rows),
cards_html, nowbar_html -- and the strip is not among them. agentic-job.js
never touches #attempt-strip. So it is whatever the full page render
produced and never changes again: a running attempt's remainder segment
does not grow, and a second attempt does not appear, until a reload.

IT MUST NOT BE GATED ON NEW ROWS, unlike the cards. attempt_strip's
running attempt carries `total_ms = max(elapsed_ms, measured)` and its
remainder is the `run` segment -- that advances with the WALL CLOCK, not
with activity rows. Gating it on `rows` would leave it frozen for the whole
of a long build, which is the same bug in a smaller window.

So it re-renders every poll while the job is active: attempt_boundaries +
attempt_tool_totals + attempt_turn_totals, three GROUP BY queries over one
job's activity rows, every 3s per open page. That cost is the point of the
bead -- the alternative is recomputing segment percentages client-side,
which is more code and another copy of the scale logic.
notes:
FIXED 2026-09-24.

The strip is now in the fragment and swapped through a slot -- the same
pattern the bar already used, <div id="attempt-strip-slot">, because
_attempt_strip.html renders the #attempt-strip element itself and swapping
that element's own innerHTML would have nested it.

SENT ON EVERY POLL, and it is the only body that is. The bar is omitted
when nothing is new (poly-qqx9.15) because its content cannot have changed;
the strip's CAN, without any row arriving, since a running attempt's
remainder is its `run` segment and total_ms = max(elapsed_ms, measured).
Gating it on rows would freeze it for the whole of a long build.

The cost is three GROUP BY queries per poll, and it is bounded on both
sides: they filter by job_id through idx_activity_log_job, and the table
is capped at runner.activity_log_max rows globally -- the same cap that
caused poly-a162. Polling only happens while #live-indicator is active.

The alternative -- advancing the running segment client-side -- was
rejected: it needs a second copy of the scale logic in JS, and every
attempt's track is a percentage of the longest, so the whole chart has to
be recomputed when the running one grows past it.

An empty body empties the slot, which is right: a triage/verify/confirm job
writes no boundaries, and a stale chart is worse than none.

Tests: the strip survives a quiet poll while the bar is absent from the
same response, the body is empty for a job with no attempts, and the page
renders the slot. 4213 pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: Runner publishes the overlay diff per attempt, so a running job can show its working tree
description:
The replacement for the live read poly-paee deletes. The tracker must not
reach into a build env, so the runner emits and the tracker reads.

NO NEW TRANSPORT IS NEEDED. The runner already POSTs artifacts over plain
HTTP -- runner.artifact_store_put -> POST /v1/artifacts/put -- and that is
how analysis/changes.diff already arrives (289 of them on a live builder).
It is the one runner->tracker path that survives the runner going remote:
activity_log writes go straight into the shared state.db
(runner.py:1837, _state_db_conn), which does not.

The runner ALREADY COMPUTES THIS. attempt_loop._current_diff() reads the
carried overlay diff at the top of every retry and hands it to the model;
the operator could not see what the model could. Publishing the same text
costs one POST per attempt.

Per attempt, at a per-job relpath, so a retried bundle does not overwrite
a sibling job's: analysis/worktree/<job_id>.attempt<n>.diff or similar.
That also gives the band real per-attempt attribution instead of the
first-write-wins query poly-qqx9.7 settled for.

Cadence is the open question. Per attempt is cheap and correct but goes
stale during a long attempt; the agent's own emit_diff calls are a natural
extra trigger. Start with per attempt.

/v1 is unauthenticated today, which is poly-fij.4's problem, not a reason
to avoid the channel: the diff of a port overlay is not a secret and the
same endpoint already carries every other artifact.
notes:
DESIGN SETTLED 2026-09-24, with the UI requirements. Measured on a live
builder throughout.

CADENCE: on every edit, upserting ONE relpath per attempt --
analysis/worktree/<job_id>.attempt<N>.diff. put_blob upserts on
(bundle_id, relpath) and is content-addressed, so republishing unchanged
bytes costs a row update and no new blob. Triggers: attempt start (the
carried diff attempt_loop already computes), after each successful WRITE
tool (PatchEventDispatcher already intercepts tool_call, steps.py:234), and
attempt end. The agent's own emit_diff results are a free extra trigger.

Publishing on every edit LOSES NOTHING, which was a confusion worth
recording: the diff is cumulative against HEAD, so every publish is a
complete snapshot rather than a delta, and each one correctly supersedes
the last. Overwriting costs only the ability to REPLAY intermediate states
within an attempt -- a forensic question, not a watching one.

SNAPSHOTS, NOT DIFFS-OF-DIFFS. Considered and rejected on two grounds that
outrank the storage saving:
- A diff of two diffs is not renderable. parse_diff_files keys on
  "diff --git a/... b/..." and counts +/- inside hunks; in a delta those
  headers arrive as CONTENT lines prefixed +/-. Nothing can be drawn
  without reconstructing the full diff first.
- Best-effort publishing plus a delta chain is a fragile chain.
  artifact_store_put swallows every error and returns False by design, so
  a cosmetic feature can never break an attempt. One dropped POST costs one
  snapshot; with deltas it costs everything after it, including the current
  tree.
The saving does not exist anyway: 290 changes.diff artifacts measured at
avg 2.6 KB, max 68 KB, min 0. The bundle already carries a 118 KB session
dump per attempt.

"WHAT ATTEMPT N CHANGED" IS A READ-TIME COMPUTATION, not a storage format.
The overlay accumulates across attempts (reset_attempt_workspace clears
only genpatch-out and WRKDIR, poly-dq5), so comparing two parsed snapshots
gives it exactly -- structurally, as file sets and counts, which is what an
operator reads. render/compare.py already does this shape for occurrences.

THE SESSION DUMP IS NOT THE MECHANISM, though it often contains a diff.
Checked one on a live builder: emit_diff tool results, 2 non-empty in 214
message rows. Rejected because runner.dump_session DEFAULTS TO FALSE (true
on that host only), the diff is present only if the model chose to call
emit_diff, and it is a 118 KB gzipped JSONL whose payload is a
JSON-escaped string inside a content field. A band built on it would
appear for some jobs and not others for reasons no operator can see -- the
same trap poly-qqx9.1 found in the turn card's sentence.

PER-ATTEMPT COMMITS IN THE WORKTREE: considered, WITHDRAWN. The bundle's
branch is scratch and is deliberately destroyed at terminal job end
(_drop_bundle_branch_for_job, Step 30 slice 4), whose own comment says the
diff artifact is captured first "so the branch's purpose is done". Git here
is what the diff is rescued FROM, not a durable store, and the tracker
cannot run git regardless. The existing architecture already made this
call; per-attempt snapshots take the same decision more than once per job.

COST: 54.4 artifacts per bundle already, so ~1-3 more per job is a 2-5%
increment; ~730 rows across 364 patch jobs. Empty attempts publish 0 bytes
and dedupe to one blob.

-- UI, job detail ------------------------------------------------------

1. THE VERSION IS SELECTABLE. One control per published attempt. Follow the
   file list's existing role="tablist"/role="tab" pattern rather than
   inventing a second idiom.

2. THE LATEST IS ALWAYS DISPLAYED BY DEFAULT, and stays latest as new
   versions arrive -- UNLESS the operator has selected an older one, which
   the live poll must not steal back. This is the same problem the turn
   cards already solve by carrying open <details> across the swap by
   data-key; the selection needs the same treatment or the band will yank
   the reader to the newest every 3s.

3. SAY WHICH VERSION AND HOW FRESH. It is a snapshot, not a live read:
   "attempt 3 · as of 06:41:12". And mark whether the selected version is
   the current one or historical -- reading attempt 2 while attempt 3 runs
   must not look like the current tree.

4. AN EMPTY VERSION IS SHOWN, NOT OMITTED. An attempt that changed nothing
   publishes 0 bytes, and "this attempt changed nothing" is a finding --
   especially on an attempt that then failed. Skipping it would read as
   "this attempt does not exist".

5. A MISSING VERSION IS A GAP, NOT A RENUMBERING. Publishing is
   best-effort; if attempt 2's POST failed the selector shows A2 as not
   published rather than silently presenting A3 as the second version.

6. CUMULATIVE AND DELTA ARE BOTH WANTED. "The tree as of attempt N" and
   "what attempt N changed" are different questions and the second is the
   whole point of per-attempt storage. Needs a place in the band; which is
   the default for a historical version is an open question -- delta is
   probably right for history, cumulative for the latest.

7. PER-FILE ATTRIBUTION COMES FROM THE SNAPSHOTS NOW. "attempt not
   recorded" should disappear: it exists because attribution is inferred
   from write-tool args, and those rows are evicted by the activity cap
   while artifacts never are.

8. DEEP-LINKABLE. ?attempt=N in the URL, through the existing query_for
   helper, so a version can be pasted into a bead or a handoff.

9. IT MUST WORK WITH ZERO ACTIVITY ROWS. Artifacts outlive the 5000-row
   global cap (poly-a162), so the band will routinely be the only surface
   left on an older job -- after the now-bar, strip and turn cards have all
   aged out. It cannot depend on cards being present.

-- OPEN ---------------------------------------------------------------

What _current_diff costs per call, in-chroot. On every write tool that is
~128 added git invocations in a long job (measured: 221 edit_file, 81
genpatch, 59 install_patches, 15 make_patch, 9 put_file across 3 jobs). If
it is material the same artifact gets a floor -- republish at most every N
seconds -- and nothing else in the design changes. Measure before wiring
the per-edit trigger; the attempt-boundary trigger is unconditionally safe.

ACCEPTANCE: a running patch job shows a working tree that advances as the
agent edits; an escalated job shows one version per attempt, selectable,
with what each attempt changed; no tracker process runs anything; a dropped
publish costs one version and nothing else.
REVISITED AGAINST THE CODE 2026-09-24. Two corrections to the note above,
and the work is smaller than it said.

CONFIRMED: THE RUNNER DOES ALL OF IT. Both trigger sites are runner-side --
attempt_loop for the boundaries and steps.py's PatchEventDispatcher for the
per-edit case, and both run in the runner process, which is root and owns
the chroot. The tracker has no chroot and executes nothing; poly-paee
removed its last two attempts to.

CORRECTION 1 -- THE PRODUCER IS ALREADY WRITTEN, AND IT IS NOT emit_diff.
runner._write_changes_diff(bundle_dir, bundle_id, env, origin, *,
only_if_nonempty, extra_relpaths) already computes the diff and POSTs it:

    for rp in ("analysis/changes.diff", *extra_relpaths):
        artifact_store_put(bundle_id, rp, diff_bytes, "text")

The rescue path already uses extra_relpaths for a per-JOB path
(analysis/rescued/<job_id>.diff). So per-attempt publishing is this call
with extra_relpaths=("analysis/worktree/<job_id>.attempt<N>.diff",). No new
publish helper.

And its diff is BETTER than the one the note above proposed. It is
branch-vs-base, not HEAD-relative: "Includes both convert commits on the
bundle branch and the patch agent's uncommitted working-tree edits"
(Step 30 slice 5). attempt_loop._current_diff -> worker.emit_diff is
HEAD-relative and would silently drop a convert bundle's commits. Use
_write_changes_diff. Two diffs exist in the runner and they are not
interchangeable.

ONE SMALL CHANGE IT NEEDS: the canonical relpath is hardcoded as the first
element of that tuple, so calling it per-edit would rewrite
analysis/changes.diff on every edit -- turning the canonical FINAL diff
into a rolling current one, and on a retried bundle letting a sibling job
overwrite it repeatedly. It needs the canonical write to be optional
(canonical: bool = True, or a relpaths override).

CORRECTION 2 -- EMPTY AND UNREADABLE MUST NOT COLLAPSE, and neither
existing mode keeps them apart for our purposes. With
only_if_nonempty=True a failed read RAISES (good: catch and publish
nothing) but an empty diff returns 0 and publishes nothing (bad: we want
an explicit zero-byte artifact, because "this attempt changed nothing" is
a finding). With only_if_nonempty=False a failed read publishes a
"# failed to capture diff:" tombstone, which would render as a diff.

The function's own comment states the stake: "'the agent changed nothing'
-- the one answer we cannot tell apart from a real loss." So the
per-attempt caller wants a third behaviour: publish 0 bytes when the diff
is genuinely empty, publish NOTHING when the read failed. UI requirement 4
(show empty versions) and 5 (show gaps) depend on that separation holding.

WIRING, all in scope already. At the dispatcher's construction site
(steps.py:1554) ctx.bundle_id, env and origin are all live -- bundle_id is
used 30 lines later at 1584 -- and artifact_store_put is ALREADY imported
ten lines below, next to take_operator_notes. The dispatcher itself holds
only queue_root/job_id/origin and no bundle_id or env, so pass an injected
publish_worktree(attempt) closure: that follows the class's own documented
convention ("Callables are injected (not module imports) so the class is
decoupled from runner internals and trivial to unit-test") and mirrors
runner.take_operator_notes(job_id), which returns exactly this shape and is
imported at exactly this spot.

tool_call events already carry "attempt" and "turn" (steps.py:239-240), so
the attempt number needs no new plumbing.

OPEN, unchanged but now aimed at the right function: what
_write_changes_diff costs per call. It shells git in-chroot too, so the
per-edit trigger adds one invocation per write tool (~128 in a long job).
The attempt-boundary trigger is unconditionally safe; measure before wiring
the per-edit one, and if it is material give it a time floor.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-24.

THE CONVENTION IS NOW SHARED. dportsv3/common/artifacts.py owns the relpaths
the runner publishes and the tracker reads -- worktree, rescued and
canonical. It was spelled twice before: steps.py built the rescue path with
an f-string while tracker/worktree_source.py had its own rescued_relpath.
Both now delegate. ``common`` because the agent must not import the tracker
and the tracker must not import the runner.

RUNNER SIDE. runner.publish_worktree_snapshot(bundle_id, env, job_id,
attempt) POSTs one snapshot. The capture was factored out of
_write_changes_diff as _capture_branch_diff so both callers get the same
branch-vs-base bytes -- which includes the convert commits that
emit_diff's HEAD-relative read would have dropped -- under different
failure semantics.

The three states are kept apart, as the bead required: an empty diff
publishes 0 bytes, a capture that could not look publishes NOTHING, and
nothing tombstones. The whole body is inside the guard: a test that stubbed
artifact_store_put to raise walked straight through a narrower version that
only guarded the capture.

_write_changes_diff was NOT given an optional-canonical flag after all --
the snapshot publisher does not go through it, so the canonical artifact is
untouched by per-edit publishing and keeps its end-of-job meaning.

TRIGGERS: all three are events PatchEventDispatcher already received, so
attempt_loop needed no change at all -- attempt_start, every successful
WRITE tool (_WRITE_TOOLS reused from attempt_loop rather than a third
copy), and attempt_end. Injected as a publish_worktree closure, per the
class's own convention and mirroring take_operator_notes; it defaults None
so every existing construction and test is unaffected.

TRACKER SIDE. worktree_versions() lists a job's snapshots, filtered by job
id as well as bundle so a retried bundle's sibling is not read as an earlier
attempt, and sorted numerically (attempt10 sorts before attempt2 as a
string). The assembly moved out of pages.py into worktree_source, because
the live fragment renders it too and two copies would disagree about which
version is current.

Source order: snapshot, then rescued, then the bundle's changes.diff.

UI, against the numbered list:
1. Selectable -- a pill per published attempt, role=tab like the file list.
2. Newest by default, and a pinned ?attempt=N survives the poll: the JS
   reads it from the URL and sends it with every fragment request.
3. Header says "attempt N, as of <age>" and marks a non-newest version
   "historical -- a later attempt has its own".
4. An empty version renders "attempt N changed nothing" rather than
   falling through to the pending state.
5. A gap renders as a dashed A<n> saying the runner could not read the tree
   or the upload did not land.
6. PARTIAL. Files the selected attempt touched are marked "changed here",
   computed from the snapshots; there is no separate delta-only view. The
   bead left the default open and this answers the question inside the
   cumulative view. If a delta view is wanted it is a template change on
   data that is already there.
7. "attempt not recorded" is gone where snapshots exist:
   render.attribute_across_snapshots gives first-appearance exactly, since
   the overlay accumulates. The tool-args heuristic remains the fallback.
8. ?attempt=N, and the link is built by the renderer (the page preserves
   limit and stage_filter through request.url; the fragment emits a bare
   query) because the fragment has no request object.
9. It needs no activity rows: cards are used only to mark a file being
   written right now, and absent cards simply mean no marker.

LIVE. The band is in the fragment, gated on new rows -- correct here,
unlike the strip, because the band changes only when a write tool RETURNS
and that return is itself a row. The file-tab handler was rebound to
delegate from the document; bound to .wt-list it died with the first swap.
The open file is carried across by path and replayed through the same
handler so the diff panes follow.

The measurement the bead asked for is still not taken: what
_capture_branch_diff costs per call in-chroot. The per-edit trigger is
wired without a floor. If it proves material the floor goes in
_publish_worktree, which is the single place all three triggers pass
through.

4224 tests pass; 21 new in tests/test_worktree_versions.py.
close_reason: Closed

title: Confine the browser artifact resolver too, and fix the five fixtures that block it
description:
poly-zjtx removed the write path for 'fs' artifact refs and confined the
/v1 read (ArtifactStore.get_artifact -> contained_fs_path). The browser
resolver, render.resolve_artifact_path, still serves fs_path exactly as
recorded. It feeds /api/bundles/{id}/artifacts/{relpath}, the agentic
artifact route, and the artifact viewer.

Not a live hole: nothing can write an 'fs' row any more, so every row
reaching that resolver was written by the hook before it moved to
put-blob. This is defence against re-introduction, and it removes an
asymmetry worth removing -- two resolvers over one column, one confined.

WHAT IT COSTS, which is why it was not done inside poly-zjtx: the same
containment fails 42 tests in five files. Those fixtures write artifact
files into tmp_path while leaving paths.artifact_root at its production
default, so the recorded path and the configured root are unrelated by
construction and NO containment boundary can hold.

  tests/test_tracker_agentic_views.py   25
  tests/test_repairs_split.py           13
  tests/test_occurrence_compare.py       2
  tests/test_render_worktree.py          1
  tests/test_fix_chat_persistence.py     1

So the work is: set paths.artifact_root in those fixtures, place the
artifact files under it, then confine the resolver. Check the blob-backed
refs in the same fixtures while there -- a blob path is DERIVED from
artifact_root, so moving the root moves those too.

BEFORE PICKING THE BOUNDARY: no real fs row was available to read when
poly-zjtx chose one. The logs root is where the old hook's dsynth log
sat, and that is what the /v1 side confines to, but a deployed database
may hold rows pointing somewhere else (a bundle_dir, say) and confining
to the logs root would 404 those. Read a real state.db first:

  SELECT DISTINCT fs_path FROM artifact_refs WHERE backend = 'fs';
notes:
NARROWER THAN THE DESCRIPTION SAYS (2026-09-24).

The one backend='fs' row in the seeded bench.db is not evidence of a
production shape: it was hand-inserted while building poly-qqx9.7, and it
carries a sha256, which put_fs_ref never wrote (that column was always
NULL there).

Production stores the same artifact as a BLOB. The rescue path runs
steps.py -> services.write_changes_diff -> runner._write_changes_diff ->
artifact_store_put(bytes) -> POST /v1/artifacts/put, and put_blob is the
only writer of artifact_refs left.

So the fs rows a deployed database can hold are the pre-put-blob hook's
dsynth full logs and nothing else, which is what the logs-root boundary
was chosen for. Still run the DISTINCT fs_path query before confining the
browser resolver, but expect "dsynth logs, or empty" rather than an open
question.
THE OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED (2026-09-24). On a live builder's state.db:

  SELECT backend, count(*) FROM artifact_refs GROUP BY backend;
  blob|31606

ZERO fs rows, out of 31,606. So nothing legitimate is at risk from the
boundary, and poly-zjtx's confinement of the /v1 read cannot 404 anything
on that host.

WHICH SUGGESTS A BETTER FIX THAN THIS BEAD DESCRIBES. Confining the
browser resolver makes two resolvers symmetric over a backend that has no
production rows at all. Deleting the 'fs' read path outright -- both
branches, leaving the column for archaeology -- removes the asymmetry
instead of balancing it, and removes the primitive rather than fencing it.

Same blocker either way: the five fixtures use 'fs' refs as a convenience
to point at tmp files. The better target is to have them use blob refs,
which is what production writes; then the branch just goes. That is more
work than setting paths.artifact_root in each, so whoever takes this
chooses. Confining is still an acceptable outcome.

title: tracker.public_readonly does not cover /v1: the ingest surface has no gate
description:
Verified in code, 2026-09-23.

forbid_anonymous appears 19 times across tracker/routes/ and zero times
in tracker/routes/ingest_api.py. Every /v1 route plus /health is served
regardless of tracker.public_readonly:

  GET  /v1/artifacts/get
  POST /v1/artifacts/put
  POST /v1/artifacts/put-fs   (removed by poly-zjtx)
  POST /v1/bundles/upsert
  POST /v1/jobs/transition
  POST /v1/user-context

So the setting's own promise -- "every mutating control disappears from
the page AND is refused at the endpoint" -- is not true of the ingest
surface. An anonymous caller on a tracker serving public_readonly can
still write artifacts, upsert bundles, transition jobs, and set the
operator hint text that feeds a re-triage prompt.

This is a gap in the switch rather than in the machine-auth design: /v1
is the builder path, so it wants poly-fij.4 (17c, authenticated writes
from a builder), not forbid_anonymous. Until that lands, public_readonly
should either refuse /v1 or say in its own text that it does not cover
it -- the setting is documented as the switch for "a tracker that dozens
of people can reach but only a few should drive", which is exactly the
deployment where this matters.

title: Store tool args on the activity row, so a running tool reads as fields
description:
The turn card renders a tool call as fields — name, args, elapsed, outcome.
What reaches activity_log is one prose line per call from
_summarize_tool_call (runner.py:3896), whose own docstring says it is for the
at-a-glance message column, plus extra_json carrying attempt, turn, ok, and
on failure rc/stderr_tail/stdout_tail.

The args exist at the emitting end: the tool_call event carries them in full,
along with the whole result dict and duration_ms (tool_loop.py:450).
PatchEventDispatcher builds its extra dict and drops them (steps.py:152).

They are also persisted post-hoc — analysis/tool_trace.jsonl is every event
verbatim (runner.py:4006), written from the rescue path so it survives a
failed run. That is why this is not a data-loss bead. It is a LIVE
availability bead: the trace lands after the run, and the job page's whole
point is the job that is still going.

Do it in the dispatcher's extra dict, not as a new event. Cap what goes in —
a put_file's args carry the file CONTENT, and that must not land in
extra_json; store the path and the size, not the bytes.

OPTIONAL, and worth deciding here rather than later: add a capped (~300
character) assistant summary to the llm_turn event so the card can lead with
the model's own sentence. Today that text exists only in the session dump,
gated by runner.dump_session which defaults to false and is described as a
debug switch — and its artifacts land per attempt, so they are not live
within an attempt anyway. The card must degrade without it regardless: every
job that has already run has no such text, and that must not look broken.
close_reason:
Implemented, including the optional half.

ARGS. tool_call and tool_start both carry args to the dispatcher, which
stores them through _redact_tool_args: each value capped at 160 chars with
its true length declared, the whole dict capped at 1200, and anything past
the budget named in _dropped rather than silently missing. So put_file's
path survives intact and its content becomes '... (50000 chars)'. The row
renders a call as fields; analysis/tool_trace.jsonl remains the place the
bytes are reconstructed from.

THE MODEL'S SENTENCE — DECIDED YES, and cheaper than feared. The emitters
(tool_loop and triage) now carry the turn's text in the event, so
tool_trace.jsonl becomes self-sufficient: it holds what the model SAID as
well as what it did. The activity row stores a 300-char single-line excerpt
via _excerpt. runner.dump_session stays off by default and untouched.

An llm_turn with no text is left alone, so every job that already ran keeps
working and the card must degrade for it — tested.

Tests: 7 added (4 args, 3 text). Full suite 4072 passed.

title: Record dev_env on the jobs row, so the tracker can reach the workspace
description:
The tracker cannot tell which dev-env a job ran in, so it cannot call
worker.emit_diff(env, origin, relpath) for the working tree, and it cannot
resolve env_paths(env).writable/work/dsynth/logs/<stem>[@flavor].log for the
in-row build tail. Both are blocked on one missing column.

The env is not unknown — it is recorded in the wrong place. env_resolver's
top precedence is `job.dev_env` (env_resolver.py:126), and the runner writes
`dev_env=<name>` into the queue FILE for the job (runner.py:2840). The DB
never sees it: the jobs table has no such column and get_job is
`SELECT * FROM jobs`. Only verify_requests carries an env (schema.py:349),
which is why verify is the one flow that can already answer this.

Add the column and write it where the runner resolves the env for the job,
at claim time, so the value stored is the one the work actually used rather
than whatever tracker_active_env says later — the operator can change that
selection mid-job, and env_resolver's own precedence puts the job's env above
the tracker's for exactly that reason.

Backfill is not possible and not needed: an old job renders its working tree
from the stored diff (see poly-qqx9.7) and simply has no live tail.
close_reason:
Implemented. jobs.dev_env added to SCHEMA and to MIGRATIONS, written by runner._record_job_env from resolve_env(job) — the only moment that knows the answer, so the row holds what the tools were actually pointed at rather than what tracker_active_env says later. Best-effort like every other read-model write; a failure never breaks the job.

Tests: 7 in tests/test_job_dev_env_recorded.py (column present, write, re-resolution wins, no-op cases, write failure swallowed, migration onto a pre-existing table, init_db idempotent). Full suite 4080 passed, no skips.

ONE THING WORTH KNOWING: the column was first added LAST in the CREATE TABLE, which made 'ALTER TABLE jobs DROP COLUMN dev_env' fail — sqlite re-parses the stored CREATE and the trailing comment block left it incomplete. tests/test_schema_migration_ordering.py silently SKIPPED the new column as a result ('not droppable; cannot simulate'), i.e. the generalized migration guard stopped covering exactly the column that had just been added. Moving it above owner_id restored the coverage. Any future column here should be checked the same way: a skip in that test is the failure, not a pass.

title: Tell a running agent something: an operator note delivered on the next turn
description:
The only chat the tracker has is post-hoc: _bundle_chat.html on the occurrence
page, a fresh model seeded with the saved session, and its own copy says
"Read-only — no tools, no rebuild." Nothing can reach a job while it runs. The
only control on a running job is `Abandon job (mark dead)` — watch or kill.

An operator often knows one thing the agent does not, and knows it early:
that a path moved upstream, that a whole line of attack is wrong. Today that
knowledge can only be spent by killing the job and re-queuing it, which
throws away the attempt budget and the workspace.

THE SEAM IS THE NEXT TURN, NOT THE ATTEMPT BOUNDARY

  During a 44-minute dsynth_test the agent is sitting inside a turn, waiting
  on the tool. The next turn is composed when that tool returns, and its
  message is the natural carrier: append the operator note to the tool-result
  payload the loop is already assembling. That delivers in minutes rather
  than at the end of an attempt, and it never interrupts a provider call in
  flight.

  An earlier draft put it at the attempt boundary, next to the retry preamble
  that attempt_loop already assembles (_current_diff, "what that attempt
  already did"). That is simpler, and it is the fallback if turn-level
  injection turns out to disturb the loop — but it can be 40 minutes late,
  which is most of the value gone.

SHAPE

  - A composer docked at the foot of the job page. Disabled with a reason
    when the job is terminal; that case is the existing post-hoc chat.
  - The note appears IMMEDIATELY as an operator card in the transcript,
    marked queued, saying what it is waiting for ("dsynth_test still
    running"). No optimistic silence.
  - Once consumed it becomes a delivered card, stamped with the turn it
    landed in, and it stays in the transcript forever — the note is part of
    why the job did what it did next, and a later reader needs it in place.
  - Persist it: poly-pf4a is open precisely because the fix chat is not
    stored. Do not repeat that.

  Not in scope: the pause-after-attempt control and the approval gate, both
  drawn in specimen 05 of the design artifact.
notes:
AFTER READING THE CODE (second pass):

1. THE NOTE GOES IN AS ITS OWN MESSAGE, NOT FOLDED INTO A TOOL RESULT.
   The description names the tool-result payload as the carrier; the
   TIMING that argues for is exactly right and is what shipped -- the
   injection happens at the end of the turn body in tool_loop, so the
   note is in the messages the next model call sees, minutes after it
   was written rather than at the end of a 44-minute attempt. But
   putting operator text inside what the model has been told is a
   tool's own output blurs the provenance a note most needs to keep, so
   it is appended as a labelled user message instead. Deliberate
   divergence from the letter, not the intent.

2. CLAIM-THEN-RETURN, NOT READ-THEN-MARK. take_pending_operator_notes
   marks delivered before handing the rows back. A crash between the two
   loses a note; the other order delivers it twice, and a note costs
   tokens every time it reaches the model.

3. tool_loop NEVER SEES THE STATE DB. runner.take_operator_notes(job_id)
   returns a closure of (attempt, turn) -> rows, which is what the loop
   is handed. The loop asks "is there anything for me"; everything about
   storage stays on the runner side, where _state_db_conn already lives
   from poly-qqx9.12.

4. python-multipart is NOT a dependency of this project and
   request.form() requires it. The endpoint parses the body itself --
   urlencoded from the plain form, JSON from a fetch -- so the composer
   works without JavaScript and without adding a library for one
   textarea.

5. THE ACTIVITY SECTION WAS KEYED ON ROWS AND HAD TO MOVE TO CARDS. A
   note queued before the job's first turn is a card with no activity
   row behind it; the old `{% if activity %}` guard hid it, which is
   precisely the optimistic silence the description rules out.

6. window_cards already pinned undelivered notes above the window --
   built and tested in poly-qqx9.5 from the note on that bead, so
   nothing here had to reopen it.

Not in scope, as the description says: the pause-after-attempt control
and the approval gate from specimen 05.
close_reason: Closed

title: Cost that adds up: per attempt, per job, per port, against the tier budget
description:
Every ingredient exists and nothing adds up. Per turn: prompt/completion/
cached/cumulative_billable in extra_json. Per attempt: attempt_end carries
billable_tokens and tokens (steps.py:53, which deliberately drops the term
when it cannot tell which quantity it holds). Per job: token_usage_for_job.
Above the job: nothing — the Prior attempts table lists sibling bundles for
the same (origin, target) with no spend beside them, so "what has this port
cost me across four jobs" cannot be asked.

Make it add up: per-attempt on each attempt's header, per-job in the now-bar
against the tier budget, per-port across sibling jobs in the prior-attempts
band. Name the largest turn outright — that is what the sortable token column
was being used for (poly-9hjm).

Keep billable and total apart, and keep the sentence the console mock already
wrote for this: "Total re-counts the cached prefix every turn. Billable is the
real cost."

Money is out of scope unless a price table is introduced deliberately: there
is no usd/price anywhere in the repo today, and inventing one in a template
would be the wrong place for it. poly-cg6u is the epic that owns that
question.
notes:
PER-PORT IS THE ONLY MISSING AGGREGATE (poly-qqx9.1). Per turn, per attempt
and per job all exist — attempt_end carries billable_tokens and tokens
(steps.py:53), token_usage_for_job sums the job, and render/activity.py
already sums billable per attempt group. What nothing does is add up sibling
jobs for the same (origin, target): list_port_bundles returns the bundles
with no spend beside them. That aggregate is this bead's real work; the rest
is placement.

The budget denominator needs no tier lookup and no settings read: the
attempt_start event carries its own "budget" field (attempt_loop.py:512), so
it is already in the row's extra_json.
AFTER READING THE CODE (second pass):

1. THE NOTE ON THIS BEAD IS WRONG, AND IT WOULD HAVE COST A DUPLICATE.
   "Per-port is the only missing aggregate" -- but token_usage_for_port
   (jobs.py:311) already computes exactly that, and the BUNDLE page has
   rendered it since Step 9. I had written a second, near-identically
   named port aggregate before finding it; it is deleted.
   What is actually missing is narrower: (a) the port total never
   appeared on the JOB page, and (b) nothing splits it per bundle, so
   the prior-attempts band could show which sibling attempt spent what.
   One new query, token_usage_by_bundle, keyed by bundle_id, deriving
   billable the same way token_usage_for_port does so a row and the
   footer above it are the same quantity.

2. PER-ATTEMPT ALSO ALREADY EXISTED, TWICE, AND BOTH WERE WINDOWED.
   The attempt_end boundary card sums the rows in hand, which
   poly-qqx9.5 showed reads "66 turns" on an attempt of 75. The honest
   per-attempt figure is attempt_turn_totals, the SQL aggregate
   poly-qqx9.6 added over the whole job -- so the cost belongs on the
   attempt strip, next to the attempt it describes, not on a card built
   from a window.

3. The largest turn was already computed (token_usage.largest_turn) and
   already rendered -- inside a collapsed card. Finding it is what the
   sortable token column was for, and poly-qqx9.5 moved that table to
   the transcript, so it is now named in the card's summary line where
   it can be read without opening anything.

4. Per-job against the tier budget landed in poly-qqx9.3 (and needed the
   two-scopes correction recorded there).

5. Money stays out, as the description says. Nothing here introduces a
   price; poly-cg6u owns that question.
close_reason: Closed

title: The dsynth tail lives inside the tool row running it, not in a pane
description:
A build's output belongs to the tool row that is running it — not to a pane
of its own. The running dsynth_test row carries its own last lines, a
`last line Ns ago` counter beside them, and the byte cap stated rather than
silently applied. When the tool finishes the row collapses to its duration
and rc and the lines fold away; a FAILED build keeps them open, the same way
a rejected make_patch keeps its reject text.

That `last line Ns ago` is the liveness signal the page lacks today — it says
something about the JOB, unlike the current badge, which reports the poll.

Source is worker.dsynth_log(env, origin, tail_lines, flavor, max_bytes),
which already resolves the per-flavor log and is byte-capped — poly-9hjm put
that cap there after one call cost 690k tokens, and the same cap belongs on
this endpoint. Serve it by byte offset (?offset=N -> {offset, text, eof}).

TRANSPORT: no socket. Cheapest correct shape is a `tail` field on the
fragment the page already polls every 3s (agentic-job.js / dpLive), so the
tail costs no new connection. If a stream is ever wanted, the tracker already
speaks SSE at /api/events (bundle_actions.py:1666) and it must stay
`async def` — one uvicorn process, no workers, sync routes on Starlette's
threadpool (poly-0e02), so a handful of held generators would starve it.

Today the runner and the tracker share a host and this is a file read. Under
poly-fij it is not: shape the endpoint so the builder-side relay (poly-fij.7)
can feed it rather than baking in co-location.

Needs poly-qqx9.2 to know which log to tail, with which env and flavor, and
when to stop.
notes:
AFTER READING THE CODE (second pass):

1. worker.dsynth_log IS THE WRONG READER FOR THIS. It reads the whole
   file then keeps the last N lines -- right for a model asking "why did
   this fail", wrong for a page asking every 3s "what is new", because a
   build log runs to megabytes. New tracker/dsynth_tail.py seeks to an
   offset instead: (path, offset) -> (text, next offset, eof). It reuses
   worker's _dsynth_log_candidates for path resolution, because dsynth
   writes one log PER FLAVOR and a flavored port has no unflavored file
   at all -- the trap that helper exists for.

2. THE SWAP DECIDED THE TRANSPORT. The description offers "a tail field
   on the fragment the page already polls", and that is what shipped --
   but poly-qqx9.4's live update replaces the card container wholesale,
   so an appended tail would be erased every 3s. The tail is therefore
   re-read fresh each poll at offset=-1 (the newest screenful, 40 lines,
   32 KiB cap) rather than accumulated client-side. A 32 KiB seek-read
   beats making the client merge. The offset contract is still there and
   still exercised by /api/jobs/{job_id}/dsynth-tail?offset=N, which is
   what poly-fij.7's relay will implement.

3. THE LIVENESS SIGNAL IS THE LOG'S MTIME, not the poll. read_tail
   returns it and the row counts up from it: "last line 35s ago". A
   build that has printed nothing for four minutes now looks different
   from a healthy one, which was the point.

4. A mid-file read starts halfway through a line. Dropping that first
   fragment is not cosmetic -- showing half a word as though the build
   printed it is wrong.

5. dev_env (poly-qqx9.12) is what makes this reachable at all. Without
   it on the job row there is no env to resolve the log under, and the
   row gets no tail rather than a wrong one.
close_reason: Closed

title: Working-tree band: what the agent changed, with per-attempt attribution
description:
The page never shows what the agent changed, and never links to its own
occurrence — the summary card prints `Bundle dir` as a text path while
jobs.bundle_id sits in the schema and is joined the other way for the
cockpit's Jobs table. Meanwhile attempt_loop._current_diff() reads the carried
overlay diff at the top of every retry and hands it to the MODEL
(attempt_loop.py:211, via worker.emit_diff). The model can see the diff; the
operator cannot.

A band below the turn cards, full width: the file list on the left —
status letter (A/M/D), path, +/- counts, which attempt the file arrived in,
and a live marker on the file being written right now — and the diff on the
right. Placement was decided in specimen 07 against a sticky rail, an
inline-only variant and a drawer; band below won because the diff gets full
width and the rail's permanent ~330px tax buys something you look at
intermittently.

Render with render.render_diff (text.py:274) and the diff tokens the artifact
reader already uses; do not write a second diff renderer.

Two things the design says that a plain `git diff --stat` would not:
  - The overlay under ports/<origin>/ is NOT reset between attempts, so the
    tree is cumulative. _current_diff's own measurement: 0b, 1694b, 2116b,
    2204b across one four-attempt job. Without per-attempt attribution an
    operator reads attempt 1's edits as attempt 3's.
  - emit_diff catches untracked files through its --intent-to-add dance, so
    a newly added payload file shows as added rather than missing.

Also fix the link: job -> occurrence -> artifact reader.
poly-qqx9.1 settles how the tracker reaches emit_diff, which runs where the
workspace is.
notes:
PHASE IT — the terminal case needs no new data (poly-qqx9.1, second pass).

The rescue path in steps.py:841 already writes analysis/changes.diff, the
whole tree against the bundle base with the --intent-to-add bracket so
never-committed files surface as additions, AND analysis/rescued/<job_id>.diff,
the same bytes at a path no later job overwrites. Both are written when
