title: hook_common still disables tracking for a whole run on a 409
description:
poly-gd5 fixed the tracker side: a run that has recorded nothing for
tracker.stale_build_run_hours is superseded rather than defended, so an
interrupted dsynth no longer blocks later builds indefinitely.

WHAT IS STILL EXPOSED

The window before that bound elapses. Within it, start-build still 409s
and hook_common.sh still responds by setting TRACKING_DISABLED=1 for the
whole run — collecting nothing, quietly, until the operator notices. The
original incident lost 2.5 hours of builds that way, which is inside a
six-hour window.

poly-gd5's own note put it best: degrading to "collect nothing,
indefinitely" is the wrong default for a data-collection tool. Recording
against a fresh run would lose far less.

SCOPE

hook_common.sh, so it needs every env's hooks reinstalled — which
poly-440 records the documented upgrade path does not do. That is why it
was split out rather than done alongside the tracker fix.

Options:

- On a 409, ask the tracker to supersede explicitly and retry once, so
  an interrupted build self-heals on the very next build rather than
  after the inactivity bound.
- Or keep TRACKING_DISABLED but make it per-attempt rather than
  sticky for the whole run, so the next hook invocation tries again.

Either way the failure mode to remove is that the only trace is a line
in a log inside the chroot.

title: The tracker is one process with one writer, and Step 17 makes it the throughput path
description:
Step 17 makes every builder write through the tracker. Nothing in this
epic has yet asked whether the tracker can serve that, and the answer
depends on facts that are currently implicit.

THE MODEL, VERIFIED BY READING IT

- One process. commands/tracker.py calls uvicorn.run(app, host, port)
  with no `workers`.
- Every route is `def`, not `async def` (one exception in
  bundle_actions). Starlette runs each in the anyio threadpool, ~40
  threads. Those threads hold the GIL for pure-Python work, so they buy
  I/O overlap, not CPU parallelism.
- WAL on, busy_timeout 5000, a fresh connection per request
  (tracker/db.py:open_db).
- ArtifactStore is the exception: a long-lived connection plus its own
  threading.Lock, so every ingest serialises against every other ingest.

WHAT ALREADY SERIALISES, AND AT WHAT COST

- Ingest: sha256 over each artifact body, plus compute_fingerprint()
  in-process when the hook did not send error_signature
  (artifact_store.py:146). All under ArtifactStore._lock.
- Delivery: _CLONE_LOCK, one at a time. Measured 6.6-8.2s each; an
  operator accepting ~26 bundles lost 14 to the wait bound (poly-lt1).

WHAT STEP 17 ADDS ON TOP

- poly-fij.1: POST /api/jobs/claim is a write transaction per claim,
  now arriving from N builders instead of one local loop.
- poly-fij.4: 57 execute/commit sites across 9 tables stop being local
  sqlite and become HTTP requests to this process.
- poly-fij.7: the relay makes ingest retryable, so transient failures
  become repeat requests against the same store lock rather than
  silently dropped evidence.

THE LANDMINE

The obvious way to scale a slow uvicorn app is workers=2. Doing that
here silently breaks two correctness locks, not just performance:
_CLONE_LOCK and ArtifactStore._lock are threading.Locks, in-process,
and delivery/orchestrator.py documents that this is sound *because*
uvicorn.run() is invoked without `workers`. Two processes means two
locks means two deliveries in one clone_dir — poly-lt1, unguarded.

So "add workers" is not available until those become file locks or the
work moves out. Write this down before someone reaches for it under
load.

ALSO: SQLite HAS ONE WRITER REGARDLESS

Adding processes does not add write throughput. It would help reads and
rendering. If writes are the bottleneck the answer is fewer/larger
transactions, not more processes.

DECIDE (not build)

1. Does ingest get its own process or socket, separate from the
   operator UI? Ingest peaks during a farm build, which is exactly when
   the tracker is most watched.
2. If workers>1 is ever wanted: file locks for the clone and the store,
   or move delivery out of the request path entirely.
3. Threadpool sizing, and a bound on concurrent ingest.

MEASURE FIRST. Nothing here is a reported problem yet; it is a
precondition that has not been checked. The cheap experiment is one
farm build's hook traffic replayed against the tracker while an
operator drives the UI.

Related: poly-39v (Step 21) is about the SHAPE of write connections —
one constructor for the autocommit pattern. This bead is about how many
of them can run at once. Different question, same subsystem.

title: Fix-chat is not persisted anywhere: reload and the conversation is gone
description:
There is no chat table. POST /api/bundles/{bundle_id}/chat takes the
whole message list from the request body — the client is the only thing
holding the conversation.

So: reload the bundle page and the conversation is gone. Two operators
looking at the same failing port cannot see each other's questions. The
reasoning that produced a decision is not attached to the bundle that
was decided.

This is true of the current UI, not just the redesign. It surfaces now
because the new cockpit gives chat its own tab, which implies a
persistent thing.

DECIDE

- accept it, and say so in the UI ("this conversation is not saved")
- or persist: a table keyed on bundle_id with role, content, ts, and
  the assembled-context marker fix_chat.build_chat_messages already
  computes

If persisted, it becomes evidence and inherits the same questions as the
rest: does it belong to the occurrence or the issue, and does it survive
into the manual handoff.
notes:
Read against the code 2026-09-13: the bead's premise is half stale, and its option (a) was already shipped.

The chat DOES survive a reload -- agentic-bundle.js mirrored the history into localStorage keyed by bundle, and the panel said so: 'Kept in this browser only (server saves nothing) -- a reload restores it'. So 'reload and the conversation is gone' was wrong by the time this was filed. What stayed true is the rest of the bead, and it is the important part: two operators on the same failing port could not see each other's questions, and the reasoning that produced a decision was not attached to the bundle that was decided.

DECIDED: persist. Taking option (b).

The bead asks whether it belongs to the occurrence or the issue; the code answers it. fix_chat.build_chat_messages seeds the conversation with ONE bundle's frozen artifacts and THAT bundle's session dump, so a turn read beside a different attempt would be answering about evidence that attempt never produced. Occurrence-scoped, keyed on bundle_id.

- bundle_chat_turns(id, bundle_id, role, content, created_at, session_relpath, artifacts_included). The last two are the assembled-context marker the bead mentions: build_chat_messages already computed both and the endpoint reported them to the UI and then dropped them. Now a turn can be read back knowing what the model was shown. New table, so CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS on an existing state.db is the whole migration.
- POST /api/bundles/{id}/chat takes {'message': '...'} and assembles history FROM THE STORE, not from the request -- otherwise two operators diverge, with whoever asks next overwriting the thread from their own browser. The legacy {'messages': [...]} shape still works: the last user turn in it is the question.
- Both turns are written only after the model answers, so a question whose answer 502s does not sit in the thread with nothing under it.
- DELETE /api/bundles/{id}/chat for [clear]. A delete, not a soft-hide: an operator asking for it to be gone is asking for it to be gone. The confirm now says it clears for everyone.
- The thread renders server-side from the store; the JS no longer holds it and localStorage is gone.

BEYOND THE BEAD: chat_enabled required a session dump. The thread is evidence now and evidence gets pruned, so a stored conversation whose session dump had since gone would have disappeared with it. The panel now also opens when there are stored turns.

STILL OPEN, deliberately not decided here: whether the conversation survives into the manual handoff. That is the bead's other inherited question and it is about what the handoff carries, not about where the chat lives. Filed separately.

13 tests in tests/test_fix_chat_persistence.py.
close_reason: Closed

title: activity_log is capped globally, so the port's 'lifetime' token cost silently shrinks
description:
runner.activity_log() prunes on every write:

    DELETE FROM activity_log WHERE id NOT IN (
      SELECT id FROM activity_log ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?)

The cap is runner.activity_log_max, default 5000, and it is GLOBAL —
across every job, not per job. One chatty job evicts every other job's
history.

THE MISLABELLED METRIC

token_usage_for_port() sums llm_turn rows out of that table. Its
docstring says "Lifetime token usage across every job for
(origin, target)" and the bundle page renders it as a lifetime figure.
It is not lifetime. It is "whatever survives in the last 5000 activity
rows", so the number silently SHRINKS as unrelated jobs run. Two
operators looking a day apart see different totals for the same finished
port and neither is told why.

token_usage_for_job() has the same source, but is bounded by one job's
own rows, so it degrades to has_data=False instead of quietly
under-reporting. The per-port card is the one that lies.

KNOCK-ON: ATTEMPT HISTORY EVAPORATES

attempt_start / attempt_end rows carry extra.attempt and
extra.rebuild_ok, and render.group_activity_by_attempt folds them into
the job page's attempt blocks. For an older job those rows are gone, so
the timeline shows nothing and reads as "no attempts" rather than "no
longer recorded".

OPTIONS

- retain per job rather than globally (keep last N per job_id)
- keep the cap but persist a per-job token rollup at job end, so the
  aggregate does not depend on the firehose surviving
- at minimum, label the card with what it actually measures and return
  has_data=False when the window is known to have been truncated

Also worth noting for whoever picks this up: the prune runs a full
anti-join on every single activity write.

Sits with the token-accounting family: poly-0g0, poly-cwi, poly-9t9,
poly-5bl.

title: Per-occurrence attempts and furthest state need one aggregate over job_events
description:
The occurrence selector shows, per occurrence, an attempt count and how
far that attempt got. Both have durable sources; neither has a query.

FURTHEST STATE — job_events

job_events records every transition (from_state, to_state, event_name,
actor), is indexed (job_id, id), and is NEVER pruned. jobs.bundle_id is
indexed. So furthest-state-per-occurrence is one indexed join.

jobs.job_events_for_job() is per-job only. Needs a set-based version
keyed on a list of bundle ids.

ATTEMPT COUNT — two different questions

- how many jobs worked this occurrence: COUNT(*) FROM jobs WHERE
  bundle_id = ?. Durable, indexed. list_manual_requests already inlines
  the per-origin form of this as patch_attempts.
- which retry attempt within a job (attempt 2 of 3): only in
  activity_log as attempt_start/attempt_end rows carrying
  extra.attempt and extra.rebuild_ok. activity_log is pruned to a
  global rolling cap, so this is NOT durable — see the prune bead.

So the selector may show job count and furthest state for any
occurrence, and intra-job attempt detail only for recent ones. Do not
render a missing attempt count as 0; it means the rows were evicted, not
that nothing was tried.

Supersedes the earlier guess that this needed a new column at ingest.
notes: CLOSED 29c73d5. occurrence_attempts(conn, bundle_ids) -> {bundle_id: {jobs, furthest_state, furthest_at, outcome, outcome_at, last_event_at}}, one aggregate for a whole selector. Depth ranking is lifecycle.JOB_STATE_DEPTH (not a total order over the machine -- verify-fix/confirm jump from claimed to their own state -- so it ranks depth, and the three terminals are outcomes rather than depths). Ranking in Python so the state machine has one definition; a CASE in the SQL would be a second copy. Intra-job attempt detail deliberately excluded: activity_log is pruned, and a count that silently becomes 0 is worse than none. Measured against 320,000 job_events: 0.14 ms for 12 occurrences, 2.17 ms for 200, both indexes used. 11 tests.
close_reason: Closed

title: verify_requests is written and never read back
description:
The tracker writes verify_requests (agentic_api.py:539, the
POST /api/bundles/{id}/verify path) and never reads it back. The runner
reads and updates it (runner.process_verify_requests). There is no
verify.py in agentic_queries.

The row carries: bundle_id, env, requested_by, requested_at, status,
job_id, error.

So all of this is recorded and unsurfaced:

• is a verify build in flight for this occurrence (status, job_id)
• which env it ran in (env) — the cockpit wants "green in <env>" and
bundles has no env column, so this row is the source
• a verify that never started (status, error)

Related but distinct: poly-9az is that a verify FAILURE records no
reason. This is that the verify REQUEST is never displayed at all.

Also relevant to poly-s9m.3 (record the env a job ran in on the jobs
row): for the verify path specifically the env is already persisted
here, so the cockpit does not have to wait on that bead.

DONE 2026-09-06 -- and the row alone is not enough

READING IT BACK IS THE EASY HALF

agentic_queries/verify.py: latest_verify_request + verify_requests_for_bundle,
each carrying the job's state joined by job_id.

THE STATUS COLUMN STOPS AT `enqueued`

The runner sets pending -> enqueued, or -> failed if the enqueue raised, and
that is the whole vocabulary. The verification result posts back to
/api/bundles/{id}/verification, which updates five columns on `bundles` and
never touches the request -- it has no request id to close. So `enqueued`
does not mean "in flight"; it means "a job was created at some point", and
the row may be running, finished, or attached to a job that died.

fix_state.verify_state reconciles the three places it takes to say which:
the request's status, the job's state, and whether the bundle's
verification_at postdates the request. Nine states, from "nobody asked" to
"the job ended without recording a result".

DERIVED, NOT WRITTEN

Closing the request on post-back was the obvious alternative and is wrong:
the post-back carries no request id, so it would have to close "the newest
enqueued request for this bundle" -- and mis-close whichever second verify
an operator started in the meantime. Comparing verification_at against
requested_at is the same boundary reasoning issue_state uses for regression,
and it gets the re-verify case right: an older green does not answer a newer
request.
notes: CLOSED 29c73d5. agentic_queries/verify.py (latest_verify_request, verify_requests_for_bundle, each carrying the job's state) + fix_state.verify_state with nine states. Key finding: the request's status stops at 'enqueued' and nothing closes it, so the projection reconciles request status + job state + verification_at vs requested_at. Derived not written -- the post-back has no request id. 20 tests.
close_reason: Closed

title: No text search and no offset paging on issues, bundles or jobs
description:
Every operator list in the new design has a search box. The query layer
has no search and no offset.

• issues.list_issues: target and origin are exact match (=, not LIKE),
no free-text, LIMIT with no OFFSET
• bundles.list_bundles: same, plus no resolution/status filter
• jobs.list_jobs: state bucket + target, no origin filter, no OFFSET

So every search in the mock is client-side over a capped fetch: 500 on
/agentic, 300 on /agentic/issues, 200 on /agentic/jobs and
/agentic/bundles. A port outside the cap cannot be found by typing its
name — the box silently returns nothing rather than saying it only
searched the first N.

UI-5 needs at minimum origin substring search on issues. Decide whether
the same applies to bundles and jobs, and whether the answer is offset
paging or a "showing first N of M" honesty line.

Note the ordering: issues come back times_seen DESC, so the cap keeps
the loudest issues and drops the long tail — which is where a specific
port someone is looking for usually lives.

DECIDED 2026-09-06: all three lists, and both answers

Search AND offset paging on issues, bundles and jobs, plus the honesty
line -- which stops being a consolation once the count is real, because
"1-100 of 452" is the same sentence whether or not the tail is reachable.

Search is a case-insensitive substring with its LIKE wildcards escaped
(one definition, _util.like_contains, now shared with the Builds table).
Each list also matches its own id, because an operator types an origin and
pastes a key: issues on origin/issue_key/fingerprint, bundles on
origin/bundle_id, jobs on origin/job_id. `origin` stays an EXACT filter --
the port page passes it and widening it would have changed that caller
silently.

count_issues / count_bundles / count_jobs share one WHERE builder with
their list_ sibling, so a page and the total it is a page of cannot
describe different sets. A test asserts that over every filter combination.

MEASURED -- a leading-wildcard LIKE scans, and that is fine here

20,000 issues / 60,000 bundles / 60,000 jobs, far past current volume:

  list_issues search              1.95 ms      count 1.44 ms
  list_bundles search             6.91 ms      count 3.71 ms
  list_jobs search                5.51 ms      count 3.55 ms
  list_issues offset 19000        9.88 ms

The plan is SCAN, as it must be for a leading wildcard; no index changes
this and none was added. FTS would be the answer two orders of magnitude
from here, not now. The deep offset costs what it does because ORDER BY
times_seen needs a temp b-tree over the table.

THE DERIVED STATE FILTERS CANNOT PAGE IN SQL

`regressed` is derived from occurrences, so the rows it drops are
interleaved with the ones it keeps and SQL LIMIT/OFFSET would leave holes.
`resolved` and `regressed` page in Python over a bounded fetch (1000) and
the page says when that bound bit. Everything else pages in SQL.

The worklist keeps its cap rather than paging -- it groups by band, not by
row -- and now says "Reading the 500 most-seen of N issues" with a link to
the searchable list when the cap bites.

FOUND WHILE DOING IT

An issue with no occurrences 500'd the whole worklist: the leaf row
dereferenced g.latest, which is None. issue_bucket already bands such an
issue as needing a look, so the code path was anticipated and only the
template could not render it. Reachable whenever evidence is pruned out
from under an issue row. Fixed here with the rest.
close_reason: Closed

title: The progress JSON contract cannot feed the rewritten run view
description:
UI-3 keeps the summary.json + chunked NN_history.json contract and replaces
only the rendering. Three things the redrawn view wants are not in that
contract.

RECORDED_AT IS FETCHED AND THROWN AWAY

run_history_chunk selects br.recorded_at, then builds an entry dict of
(entry, elapsed, ID, result, origin, info, duration, bundle_id). The
timestamp never reaches the client. A "Recorded" column has no data.

QUEUED AND BUILDING ROWS ARE NOT IN THE CHUNKS

The chunk query is WHERE status NOT IN ('building','queued') by design --
in-flight rows belong to summary.builders. Consequence: a "Queued" status
filter on the results table is always empty, and "Building" requires
cross-referencing summary.builders, which carries origin but no version and
no timestamp.

THE BUILDERS TABLE IS SYNTHETIC, NOT JUST INCOMPLETE

_active_builders emits phase="build" as a literal for every row,
elapsed=" --:--:--", lines="", and ID = a zero-padded index over ports in
'building' state. There is no per-builder-slot model. Per-row duration and
ID in the history entries are "" and "00" for the same reason.

Only summary.stats.elapsed is a measured value. load and swapinfo are "  -",
pkghour/impulse/meta are 0.

So the run view may show: origin, version, result, and the run's own
elapsed. Everything else is absent and must render as absent.

DONE 2026-09-06 -- additive only, the lifted progress.js keeps working

* entry.recorded_at now reaches the client. It was selected all along.
* builders[] rows carry version, which enqueue_ports really wrote.
* stats.in_queue and stats.in_progress are the rows actually in those
  states. stats.queued stays as dsynth means it -- the WHOLE queue, ie
  total_expected -- and a view that read the dsynth name as "how many are
  waiting" would be wrong by the size of the build. That was the sharpest
  trap in this contract and it was not in the original bead.
* The module docstring now lists, field by field, what is measured and what
  is dsynth shape. tests/test_progress_contract.py pins both halves, so a
  placeholder cannot quietly be filled in with something plausible.

THE QUEUED ROWS STAY OUT OF THE PAYLOAD

A run starts with every origin queued -- 13,440 for #1842 -- so shipping
them in summary.json would put the whole tree in one response. stats.in_queue
is the count and the Builds dashboard is the paged list: /?run=N&state=queued
is server-paged, filterable and searchable as of poly-5ynj. UI-3 links there
rather than reimplementing it against a payload that cannot carry it.

builders[] is the in-flight list that IS bounded, so it keeps its rows.

FOUND WHILE DOING IT: THERE IS NO START TIME AT ALL

builders[].recorded_at was added and came back empty for every row.
enqueue_ports writes recorded_at='' and update_port_status only moves the
status column, so nothing anywhere records when a port started building.
That is why builders[].elapsed and entry.duration cannot be computed rather
than merely are not. The field was dropped again rather than shipped empty.
Filed standalone as poly-8f8m -- it is an ingest change, not redesign work.
close_reason: Closed

title: Builds results are unbounded and carry no link to their evidence
description:
db.get_build_results(conn, run_id) returns every row for a run — 13,440 for
#1842 — with no limit, offset, status filter or search. UI-2 wants a
searchable, status-filtered, paged origin table.

Today's UI dodges this: the progress view reads the chunked NN_history.json
path instead, so nothing has yet paid the cost.

NO EVIDENCE LINK EITHER

The SELECT is (build_run_id, origin, version, result, log_url, recorded_at,
status). No bundle_id, so a failure row cannot link to the evidence it
produced. progress_adapter.run_history_chunk does exactly that join inline as
a correlated subselect — so the run view has the cross-link and Builds does
not. UI-2 lists that cross-link as a requirement.

COMPARE PAYS IT TWICE

db.compare_builds calls get_build_results for both runs and builds two dicts
in Python. Works today; it is the same unbounded read, doubled.

DECIDED 2026-09-06: a paged query, not chunk reuse

The chunk endpoints are dsynth-shaped (entry/ID/elapsed/duration), exclude
in-flight rows by design, and carry no filter — a searchable table built on
them would have the client pull all 14 chunks to find one origin. So: a new
get_build_results_page, and GET /api/builds/{run_id}/results beside it.

MEASURED 2026-09-06 — 13,440 results, 598 bundles, 40 runs

The bead's closing line said to index runs(build_run_id) first. Do not. The
correlated subselect drives from bundles via idx_bundles_signature_origin
(origin=?) and reaches runs by its PRIMARY KEY; adding the index changes
neither the plan nor the time (2.0 ms either way). Same conclusion
poly-0e02.9 reached about the same index.

The cost is the ORDER BY, not the row count. build_results is keyed
(build_run_id, origin), so WHERE build_run_id=? ORDER BY origin is a
PK-prefix scan and the sort is free. The existing ORDER BY CASE status
forces a temp b-tree over the whole run before LIMIT applies:

  ORDER BY origin, offset 13000     0.26 ms
  ORDER BY status-CASE, offset 13000  5.94 ms

So the paged query orders by origin, and in-flight rows are reached by
filter rather than by sort position.

STATUS IS NOT A SECOND AXIS

enqueue_ports writes result='' status='queued'; record_results writes
status = result. So a finished row's status is a copy of its result and an
in-flight row has no result at all. One `state` filter over {queued,
building, success, failure, skipped, ignored} is the entire vocabulary, and
filtering on result alone already excludes in-flight rows.

Filter counts need no new aggregate: get_build_run already returns
success/failure/skipped/ignored/queued/building counts for the run.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE

- compare_builds: 42.6 ms for 13,440 vs 13,440, operator-triggered and not
  polled. Rewriting it is risk with no measured payoff. Revisit only if it
  moves onto a polled path.
- GET /api/builds/{run_id} stays whole-run (16.4 ms, 2.2 MiB of JSON):
  client.get_build and `dportsv3 tracker get-build` want that shape. The
  paged read is a sibling endpoint, not a change to this one.
notes: CLOSED b502dfd. get_build_results_page + GET /api/builds/{run_id}/results, 32 tests. Left deliberately: compare_builds (42.6 ms, operator-triggered) and the whole-run /api/builds/{run_id} (client.get_build depends on the shape). runs(build_run_id) measured unnecessary again.
close_reason: Closed

title: No query lists delivery rows, and the open-PR count measures the wrong population
description:
The pipeline's delivery stage has no query behind it, and the figure the
mock shows measures the wrong thing.

NO LISTING QUERY

review.open_delivery_bundle_ids() returns bare bundle ids.
review.latest_review_request_for_bundle() is one bundle at a time.
Nothing returns (issue, origin, provider, pr url, status) as a set, so
the delivery drawer is N+1 or nothing.

THE COUNT CONFLATES TWO AXES

The mock counts issues in state='resolving' and labels them "open PRs".
Those are different populations and poly-8e2 measured the divergence:
17 bundles are resolution='accepted' AND issues.state='resolved' while
their newest bundle_review_requests row is create_failed. Fix delivered,
no PR ever opened, archive says finished.

So the stage needs both numbers, not one: deliveries open upstream, and
issues awaiting a confirm build. They are not the same stage of the same
thing.

Also note the mock hardcodes a PR number in both the drawer and the
cockpit's Delivery card. Real source is the review request row.
notes:
MEASURED (19,142 delivery rows over 12,000 delivered bundles).

The N+1 the bead names is real but understated. Counting only the review
lookups it is 6.3 ms per 100 rows; the drawer also needs the origin, the
target and the issue state, so the honest figure is 8.17 ms. The listing
query returns all of it in 0.35 ms.

What makes that gap is the shape of "newest row per bundle", not the
join count. open_delivery_bundle_ids spells it as a join against a
MAX(id) aggregate, which is right there -- it wants every open bundle
and has no LIMIT to stop at. For a page it is the wrong shape twice
over: the aggregate must be materialised over the whole table before the
first row comes out, and ORDER BY id DESC then needs a temp b-tree on
top. As a NOT EXISTS predicate the planner walks the rowid backwards and
stops at the LIMIT.

  first page of 100   0.19 ms  vs  17.5 ms
  offset 10,000       8.6 ms   vs  27.6 ms
  status histogram    5.6 ms   vs   4.6 ms   (the only one the aggregate wins)

1 ms on the histogram is not worth a second spelling of the same rule,
so the predicate is used everywhere here.

CORRECTION: "the mock hardcodes a PR number in the cockpit's Delivery
card" is true of the mock only. _bundle_delivery.html has read
dr.provider_pr_id and dr.url off the review-request row since 11d-2.
Nothing to fix there.

The status vocabulary is exactly five: created, updated, merged, closed,
create_failed. `skipped` is an orchestrator outcome, not a row status --
no provider or no diff writes no row at all. That is also why
find_open_review_request's NOT IN (closed, merged, create_failed) and
open_delivery_bundle_ids' IN (created, updated) agree; they are
complements only over that vocabulary, and the first has to keep its
spelling to match the partial index uq_brr_open_branch literally.

The "resolved with a failed delivery" conjunction is already countable
from by_status["create_failed"], since a create_failed newest row IS
that population. Surfacing it in the issue archive is still poly-8e2.
close_reason: f4a6479. agentic_queries/deliveries.py: list_deliveries / count_deliveries (issue, origin, provider, PR, status in one read -- 0.35 ms per 100 rows against 8.17 for the N+1) and delivery_counts, which returns the delivery histogram and awaiting_confirm_build separately so neither can be printed as the other. Newest-row-per-bundle is a NOT EXISTS predicate rather than the MAX(id) aggregate join, which is 92x faster for a page. The mock's hardcoded PR was only in the mock.

title: Pipeline stage counts have no query source, and regressed cannot be one
description:
UI-4 needs six inventory counts. Three have a real COUNT(*) in
agentic_status (bundles, jobs by state, manual pending). The issue-side
ones have no count query at all.

WHAT IS MISSING

- issues total, and per effective state
- systemic count. Cheap: issue_state._SYSTEMIC_THRESHOLD is a plain
  times_seen cutoff, so WHERE times_seen >= N works.
- operator worklist depth (the four actionable bands)

Today these would be len() over issues_with_occurrences(), which is
capped: /agentic passes limit=500, /agentic/issues passes limit=300.
Past the cap the figure silently under-reports, which is exactly what
UI-4 says must not happen ("every number needs a named real query").

REGRESSED CANNOT BE A SQL COUNT

issue_state.derived_regression compares each occurrence's build ordinal
against the issue's green_head watermark, with a timestamp fallback. It
needs the occurrence list per issue. So "N regressed" is not a COUNT —
it is a full materialise-and-project. Decide one of:

- accept the cost and say the number is computed over a bounded window
- persist a derived flag when an occurrence lands (changes the C3
  contract; derived-on-read is deliberate, see poly-l9y)
- drop regressed from the overview and keep it in the Repairs queue

Do not ship a capped len() presented as an inventory count.
notes:
MEASURED (20k issues / 51k occurrences / 17k jobs; 12,000 unresolved,
800 resolving, 6,000 resolved, 1,200 muted). Three of the bead's
premises are wrong.

1. "issue-side counts have no count query at all" is stale.
   count_issues() landed with poly-0e02.5 and takes the same filters as
   list_issues. Total and per-STORED-state are already exact.

2. regressed does NOT need a bounded window, a persisted flag, or
   dropping. Only a `resolved` issue can regress, so SQL narrows to
   those and their occurrences, and Python streams the rows through the
   existing occurrence_past_boundary. Exact, no cap, one definition:
   17.7 ms over 6,000 resolved / 15,406 occurrence rows.
   The SQL transcription of the boundary rule costs 7.8 ms -- 10 ms is
   not worth a second copy of a rule that has already disagreed with
   itself three times (poly-l9y).

3. worklist band depth is not a COUNT, but it collapses. fix_status
   reads exactly three occurrence fields (resolution,
   verification_status, job/job_state) and issue_bucket adds
   issues.state; for an open or resolving issue effective_state
   short-circuits before it looks at occurrences, so only the LATEST
   occurrence matters. GROUP BY those four columns turns 12,800 issues
   into 64 distinct input tuples: run the policy 64 times, multiply out
   the counts. 23 ms vs 394 ms for the full materialise, identical
   answers. Indexing the feed is not the lever -- bundles(issue_key,
   ts_utc, bundle_id) + jobs(bundle_id, created_ts_utc, job_id) only
   moved the row-at-a-time version 115 -> 108 ms, because the cost was
   Python, not the plan.

   The collapse depends on that column list, so it is named in one
   place and a test asserts the grouped counts equal the full
   materialise across every bucket.

Also: the None bucket ("the runner is working it") is a real stage
count for UI-4, not an absence -- 773 issues here. It is returned
under its own key rather than dropped.
close_reason:
6548575. agentic_queries/pipeline.py: issue_inventory (1.3 ms),
regressed_issue_count (17.7 ms, exact, streamed through the real
predicate), worklist_band_counts (23 ms, GROUP BY the four columns the
projection reads -- 64 combinations instead of 12,800 issues). Both
projections agree with the full materialise; tests/test_pipeline_counts.py
asserts that, which is what catches a projection growing a fifth input.
The None bucket is counted as its own band (RUNNER_BAND) rather than
dropped. issue_state._SYSTEMIC_THRESHOLD is public now, because the
systemic count reads it in SQL.

title: UI-8 Route and template test coverage
description:
Test coverage for the migrated UI, plus the one existing assertion the nav
rename breaks.

- Focused route/template tests: navigation and active states, cross-view

  of target names, origins, issue keys, bundle and job IDs.
- Update test_view_nav_includes_agentic — it asserts the literal ">Agentic<"

- Keep existing behaviour tests green: mutations, polling, artifact and

- fix_state's action surface is currently untested for several resolutions

Gate: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q

Two of the four bullets were already done.

* test_view_nav_includes_agentic no longer exists. UI-1 renamed it to

* fix_state's action surface is covered: tests/test_bundle_action_surface.py

`' onmouseover='alert(2)` through every identifier and free-text column
-- target, origin, issue key, bundle and job id, run id, version, flavor,

message, runner stage, env action -- over 27 page loads: no injected tag,

TAGS the renderer emits, and event handlers inside a tag, is the check

title: UI-7 Accessibility, responsive behaviour and empty states
description:
Cross-cutting quality, applied across every view rather than per-view.

- Accessible landmarks, labels, keyboard-operable controls, visible focus
  states, semantic tables and lists. State never carried by colour alone.
- Contrast: verify every foreground/background pairing in BOTH themes,
  including pill text on its soft background and diff add/remove on the code
  ground. The accent needs checking on panel, on sunken strips, as button
  text, and as pill text — those are four different grounds.
- Responsive: page body never scrolls sideways; wide content (tables, diffs,
  the occurrence list, the reader) scrolls inside its own container.
- Touch targets via @media (pointer: coarse), which is the right query — it
  fires on a touch device at any width, unlike a viewport breakpoint.
- Empty states behind every table and panel: a fresh install and a sparse
  issue should both look deliberate. Distinguish "filtered to nothing" from
  "genuinely nothing" — they are different messages.

Phone layout for Repairs is explicitly parked; revisit whether the queue
should be a horizontal card strip or a vertical list with a back step.
notes:
AUDITED 26 pages x 2 themes x {1440px, 500px, coarse pointer}, plus the
same sweep against a blank install, with the drawers open. What it found,
and two things the audit itself got wrong first.

LANDMARKS. No page had a <main> and none had a skip link, so every
keyboard reader walked the header and both navs on every page. Fixed in
_base.html by splitting the body block in two: nav and body, with <main>
around the second. The split is what makes the landmark correct -- one
block would have put the navigation inside <main> and left "skip to
content" skipping nothing.

TABLES. 24 header rows across 21 templates had bare <th>. Also the
markdown renderer, which builds tables out of artifact content -- an
artifact is on a page too.

CONTROLS. Four unnamed: the manual-context textarea, the chat input, the
verify env picker, and the origin filter. Then three more after fixing
the audit: a <select>'s textContent is its options, not its name, so the
"Show N events" pickers passed a check they should have failed. The
three filter labels in _target_filter had no `for` and did not wrap their
controls, so they named nothing at all.

TOUCH. The existing @media (pointer: coarse) block covered exactly one
class, .action. 126 targets under 24px (WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 AA): every
breadcrumb, the worklist port links and ops strip, three selects, the
expand chevrons. Text links inside a sentence are exempt by that
criterion and are left alone -- padding them would break the line box.

CONTRAST. One failing pairing in the whole sheet, both themes: --faint on
--green-soft in dark is 3.98, in the diff line-number gutter. That gutter
sits on four grounds (code-bg, surface, green-soft, red-soft) and --faint
clears three. --muted is 5.82 on the worst of them and still reads quiet.

RESPONSIVE. 14 tables had no horizontal scroller; two pages scrolled the
page body sideways at 500px. All wrapped.

EMPTY STATES. Five lists said "No X match this filter" whether or not a
filter was set, so a fresh install read as a broken query. The worklist
said "Nothing needs you right now" with nothing ever ingested. The manual
queue was worse: its default view is open-only, a filter nobody chose, so
every blank install read as filtered -- that one needed a real count
(count_manual_requests) to tell the two apart.

THE AUDIT'S OWN TWO BUGS, both false negatives worth recording because
they are the shape a UI audit fails in: rewriting @media (pointer:
coarse) in the page HTML changed nothing, because the rules are in the
external sheet; and counting a control's textContent as its accessible
name passes every <select> ever written.

NOT DONE, and still parked as the bead says: the phone layout for
Repairs. The queue is legible at 500px and no longer clips, but whether
it should become a card strip or a vertical list with a back step is a
design question, not a fix.
close_reason: 0e53506. Audited 26 pages x 2 themes x {1440px, 500px, coarse pointer}, seeded and blank, drawers open: 0 findings across overflow, sub-12px type, contrast, a11y, colour-only state and touch size. Fixed: no <main> and no skip link anywhere (the shell's body block is now nav + body with <main> around the second); 7 unnamed controls; 24 bare <th> across 21 templates plus the markdown renderer; 126 touch targets under 24px (the coarse-pointer block sized exactly .action); --faint on --green-soft at 3.98 in the dark diff gutter, the sheet's only failing pair; 14 tables with no horizontal scroller; and five list pages that said 'no rows match this filter' with no filter set. tests/test_ui_quality.py (98 tests) holds the parts a regression would silently reintroduce. Phone layout for Repairs stays parked, as the bead asked.

title: UI-4 Pipeline overview
description:
New sparse system overview at /pipeline. Its job is "is the system healthy
and moving", which is a different question from "what needs me".

- Six stages as inventory counts: bundles ingested, issues fingerprinted,
  automated work in flight, operator work, delivery, outcome. Each opens a

- Secondary destinations: Jobs, Runner, Manual (existing /agentic/* routes).

Before building: confirm each count has a source. Some may need new query
functions — list any that do.

recolouring it. Drop the lifted stat-card row, stress table and preset tags
for the console's own components.

title: EPIC: Tracker UI migration — Builds / Pipeline / Repairs
description:
Replace the tracker UI with the three-view operations console from the
DeltaPorts UI migration kit: Builds (default landing), Pipeline, Repairs.
These are separate views and must not collapse into one dashboard.

CONTRACTS
- Data/behaviour: tracker-system-proposal.md from the migration kit.
  Authoritative where anything disagrees.
- Visual/interaction: a click-through mock covering all ~15 surfaces. The
  kit's own prototype specifies only the 3 top-level views; the detail
  pages (artifact reader, session viewer, chat, job detail, runner, manual,
  compare, target diff, port detail, run view) are specified by the mock.
- The kit's other HTML files are historical explorations. Ignore them.

ARCHITECTURE — UNCHANGED
FastAPI + Jinja + server-rendered HTML + small vanilla JS. No React, no SPA,
no CSS framework, no frontend build step, no second data API. Lifecycle and
action policy stay in issue_state.py / fix_state.py; templates render those
projections and never re-derive them. No filesystem parent walks, no
vendored ports data.

The process model is also unchanged and is deliberate: one uvicorn process,
no `workers`, sync routes on Starlette's threadpool. Do not reach for
workers>1 to make a slow page faster — the delivery clone lock and the
artifact-store lock are in-process threading.Locks and workers>1 silently
breaks both. Capacity for the M-hosts x N-envs future is poly-fij.9, not
this epic. The two per-render costs this redesign does add are poly-0e02.11.

DECISIONS TAKEN
- Light is the default, dark is a toggle. Three-state theming: bare :root is
  light, prefers-color-scheme:dark guarded with :not([data-theme="light"]),
  and [data-theme="dark"] so an explicit choice wins in both directions.
  This overrides the kit, which specified dark only.
- Nav reads Builds | Pipeline | Repairs. "Agentic" disappears as a label.
- Farm telemetry: only summary.stats.elapsed is measured. load and swapinfo
  are the literal "  -", pkghour/impulse/meta are 0, builder phase is the
  literal "build", builder elapsed is " --:--:--", and the builder ID is a
  zero-padded index over ports in 'building' state — there is no
  per-builder-slot model. All of it renders absent, never as a number.
  (Corrected 2026-09-05; this line previously said load/swap/phase/duration
  were shown. See poly-0e02.4.)
- The chunked NN_history.json contract stays. It already carries 13,440 rows
  via kfiles + client-side paging. Replace the rendering, not the contract.
- The progress view is rewritten, not restyled. It serves BOTH
  /target/{target} and /builds/{run_id} — pages.py:845 and pages.py:924.

KNOWN TRAPS
- Never set grid-template-* as an inline style from a view function. Inline
  beats every media query and silently kills the breakpoints.
- A grid declaring only grid-template-rows gets an implicit `auto` column
  that sizes to max-content and ignores the track it was given. Pin
  single-column grids with grid-template-columns: minmax(0,1fr).
- Reset the selected artifact when the issue changes. Artifact sets differ
  per bundle, so a carried-over relpath 404s.
- progress.css today references 63 uses of 6 CSS variables that are never
  defined (--panel-bg, --c-fail, --c-info-bg, --c-success-bg, --text-faint,
  --mono). They fall through to hardcoded fallbacks from a different, cooler
  palette. Do not reintroduce this: no colour may be defined only inside a
  media or [data-theme] block, and body must paint an explicit background.

URL CONTRACT
/ serves Builds. Only test_view_nav_includes_agentic touches /, asserting
200 plus the literal ">Agentic<"; that assertion changes with the rename.
Existing /agentic/* routes keep working.

REFERENCES
- Click-through mock, all ~15 surfaces, both themes:
  https://claude.ai/code/artifact/2c556aa9-ed25-499f-b88d-64b86272aa9a
- Query/API gap analysis: children .1 to .10 of this epic, filed 2026-09-05.
  Two gaps from that pass are NOT redesign work and are filed standalone:
  poly-lvyr (activity_log global cap) and poly-pf4a (chat not persisted).

PROGRESS — branch tracker-ui-migration, nothing pushed

  Phase 0, data correctness  DONE  5/5 (see below)
  Phase 1, foundation        DONE  4/4  .12 audiences, .9 indexes,
                                   .11 caching, UI-1 shell (poly-svnn)
  Phase 2, Builds            DONE 4/4  .3 paging (b502dfd), UI-2 (c8a8007),
                                   .4 progress contract (d7524d3),
                                   UI-3 run view (1aed3bc)
  Phase 3, Repairs           DONE 7/7  chf confirm state, kp60 untriaged
                                   actions, .5 search+paging, UI-5 (61cec16),
                                   .6 verify requests, .7 attempts,
                                   UI-6 cockpit (26d0a52)
  Phase 4, Pipeline          DONE 5/5  .1 stage counts (6548575),
                                   .2 delivery queries (f4a6479),
                                   .10 preflight (d4cc7d9),
                                   .8 no pause -> poly-0w6j (f2f63a1),
                                   UI-4 overview (12c9cfb)
  Phase 5, polish            DONE 2/2  UI-7 a11y/responsive/empty
                                   states (0e53506), UI-8 route +
                                   template coverage (946e279)

  All 22 planned children are closed. poly-0e02.14 (compare two
  occurrences) is still open and was filed DURING the migration as
  work UI-6 left out on purpose, not as part of the plan.
  Filed along the way and living outside the epic: poly-8f8m,
  poly-0w6j (operator runner pause), poly-13ku (a bundle_id with a
  slash 500s five pages).

DATA CORRECTNESS PRECONDITIONS — ALL CLOSED 2026-09-05/06
Five loop bugs meant the views would faithfully render wrong data. They are
NOT children of this epic and should not become children: each one breaks the
loop for the CLI and the runner too, and would have been worth fixing with no
UI work at all. They are linked as RELATED so they are reachable from here,
and their blocking edges into the view beads are now discharged.

- poly-awz (P1) error_signature is a constant. Measured: 28 bundles, 19
  origins, ONE distinct signature. Hidden because issue_key also hashes
  origin, but same-origin discrimination is gone — llvm19@default (configure)
  and llvm19@lite (build) collapsed into one issue, times_seen=2. An
  issue-centric workspace cannot be built on that. CLOSED f8657c8.
- poly-l9y (P2) regressed is not derived. pango resolved at green_head 12,
  failed in run 13, still reads resolved. CLOSED 6006090 — the derivation
  was sound; a row read without its occurrences was the real fault.
- poly-h6c (P2) triage never reaches done; 246 of 364 dead rows are
  runner_restart, so dead overstates failure ~3.1x. agentic_status counts it
  correctly and the label lies. CLOSED 3632088. Historical rows are NOT
  backfilled, so counts still overstate failure until they age out — this
  is load-bearing for UI-4.
- poly-9az (P1) the bundle summary reads verified when verify failed, and no
  reason is stored. CLOSED 9bd79b7.
- poly-gd5 (P2) a stale active build_runs row disables tracking, so
  occurrences arrive with build_run_id NULL and C3 falls back to wall clocks.
  Related to UI-2 and UI-6 rather than blocking: fix it, or say in the UI
  when an occurrence has no build ordinal. CLOSED 8247daa; the hook half
  is poly-i66e, still open.

AUDIENCE — SIZED 2026-09-05
About 10 operators and several dozen read-only users. Two consequences.

- TWO AUDIENCES, DESIGNED FOR NOW. Read-only means ANONYMOUS: people who
  want to see how the build is going, not accounts with a viewer role. Every
  view renders for both, switched on one boolean (can_operate) resolved from
  the tracker.public_readonly setting, and from a session once poly-fij.5
  lands. Fail closed: auth grants the capability, never restricts it. The action surface is a
  separable, omittable region in every template — interleave it with status
  and it cannot be omitted later without a rewrite. poly-0e02.12 carries the
  three tiers (public status / operator actions / agent internals) and
  blocks UI-1, so it is decided before the shell exists. This replaces the
  earlier line here that called authentication out of scope; that reasoning
  held for one or two trusted operators and does not hold now.
- Read-only load is cacheable in a way operator load is not. Dozens of
  readers request the same Builds dashboard; live polling runs at 3-5s
  (live.js intervalMs 3000/4000/5000, with backoff and pause-on-hidden), so
  roughly 10-17 req/s sustained before page loads. That is modest in
  aggregate and concentrated on the two most expensive reads in the app —
  the /agentic worklist and uncached artifact renders. poly-0e02.11 is
  raised to P1 for this reason.

Server-side rendering stays. The dominant per-request cost is data access —
decompressing a 4 MiB log, and the 500-issue worklist projection — which is
server-side under any rendering model. Do not reach for uvicorn workers as
the remedy; see poly-fij.9.

title: D10 triage_failed bundles offer no operator actions
description:
fix_state.bundle_actions() returns show=False and every capability False for
resolution=triage_failed, so the bundle detail page renders no operator-action
panel at all.

ACTION_ALLOWED permits retry, reject and verify on that same resolution, and
worklist_bucket() routes it to the decide band. The worklist asks for a
decision the detail page gives no way to make.

triage_failed is deliberately excluded from FAILURE_RESOLUTIONS (it signals
infra, not a lost fight), which is why take-over / discard / release are off.
The open question is whether retry should have followed it out: a truncated log
or an artifact-store hiccup is fixed by re-running, and that is CLI-only today.

Repro:

  from dportsv3.tracker import fix_state as fs
  b = {"resolution": "triage_failed", "verification_status": None,
       "target": "@main", "origin": "lang/rust"}
  fs.bundle_actions(b)                                 # show=False, can_retry=False
  fs.action_allowed("retry", "triage_failed", None)    # True
  fs.worklist_bucket(b)                                # "decide"

Decide one of: surface retry (and possibly verify) for triage_failed in
bundle_actions, or bucket it somewhere that does not promise an action the page
cannot offer.

tests/test_fix_state.py covers fix_status for this resolution; the action
surface is untested.

READ 2026-09-06 -- repro confirmed exactly. Three findings.

VERIFY: NO, AND IT WOULD ALWAYS FAIL

The bead's parenthetical is answered. verify replays analysis/changes.diff,
and run_verify_fix raises VerifyFixError on a 404 for it and again if it is
empty. A triage_failed bundle never produced one -- triage is what makes it.
Surfacing verify would queue a verify_requests row for a job that cannot
succeed. It stays off, and that is now a test rather than a comment.

THE GATE HAS A HOLE, AND IT IS NOT ABOUT THIS RESOLUTION

take-over and discard are gated on `r in (FAILURE_RESOLUTIONS | {None})`.
They already allow None -- an untriaged bundle nobody has looked at. A
triage_failed bundle IS untriaged; the only difference from None is that the
machinery tried and broke. Excluding it while allowing None is a stats
grouping leaking into the action policy: FAILURE_RESOLUTIONS answers "how
did the agent's attempt end", which feeds the failure counts, and it was
never meant to answer "what may an operator do".

So the third option, taken: UNTRIAGED_RESOLUTIONS -- no fix exists and
nobody is working it -- gates take-over and discard. FAILURE_RESOLUTIONS is
untouched, so the failure statistics stay honest (the poly-h6c lesson:
counting infra as failure overstated it 3.1x).

RETRY IS RETRY-WITH-CONTEXT

/retry 400s without a non-empty `context` body: it plants operator context
and re-triages. For triage_failed the operator has no feedback to give, only
a reason to re-run, so what they type is an audit note. That is acceptable
and the UI already prompts for it -- but it is not the plain re-run the bead
imagined, and worth knowing before someone builds one.

REJECT STAYS OFF

The gate permits it (r not in TERMINAL_RESOLUTIONS), but rejecting a fix
that was never produced is meaningless. This is exactly the deliberate
narrowing bundle_actions exists for.
notes: CLOSED b42db86. Third option taken: UNTRIAGED_RESOLUTIONS (failure lane + triage_failed + NULL) gates take-over/discard; FAILURE_RESOLUTIONS untouched so the failure counts stay honest. Surface offers retry/take-over/discard for triage_failed AND for a NULL resolution with no live job -- the same dead end one resolution over. Verify stays off: run_verify_fix raises without analysis/changes.diff, which triage is what produces. Reject stays off. New invariant test: if the worklist bands it, the page can act on it. 37 tests.
close_reason: Closed

title: reap_stale_queued only runs at startup, so rows created just before a restart are never reaped and block re-triage for their origin
description:
``reap_stale_queued`` runs only at runner startup, and it skips rows
younger than ``runner.stale_queued_max_age_seconds`` (3600). A row created
shortly before a restart is therefore too young at the one moment the
reaper ever looks, and nothing looks again until the next restart. It
then sits QUEUED indefinitely.

OBSERVED 2026-09-05 on the builder, after accepting a batch of bundles.

    runner restarted    11:39:59   (PID 40314 -> 139656)
    14 confirm rows     created 11:25:42 - 11:39:46 by the OLD runner
                        state=queued, .job file absent from pending/,
                        inflight/, done/, failed/ and the queue root
    at restart          those rows were 0-14 minutes old, under the
                        3600s gate, so reap_stale_queued skipped them
    at 12:39            still queued, 74 minutes old, runner idle,
                        nothing scheduled to look again

The work itself was fine: after the restart the new runner enqueued
fresh confirm jobs (done/20260905-114002Z-devel_gn-139656-confirm.job
and siblings) and all 14 origins reported confirm_green. The rows are
phantoms describing work that was redone and finished.

Symptom as an operator sees it: "15 jobs queued but the runner is idle."
The runner is correct -- it scans files, and there are no files.

WHY IT PERSISTS. runner.py:5064 calls reap_stale_queued inside the
startup block, next to reap_orphans and _reset_building_markers. There
is no other call site. So the sweep happens exactly once per process
life, and its age gate means it can only ever catch rows that were
already old when that process started.

The age gate itself is CORRECT and should stay. lifecycle.py:561
explains it: it "guards against racing with a brand-new HOOK_ENQUEUED
whose .job file is *about* to be written". Removing it would reap rows
whose file is milliseconds from existing. The bug is the pairing of a
one-shot trigger with a condition that is time-dependent -- a row can
only qualify later, and later never comes.

IMPACT IS NOT COSMETIC. QUEUED is in lifecycle.ACTIVE_WORK_STATES, which
_has_active_same_origin_job uses as the duplicate-enqueue guard for
operator-triggered retries. reap_stale_queued's own docstring names this:
a missing-file row "blocks _has_active_same_origin_job indefinitely".
So the 14 affected origins -- devel/gn, audio/mac, astro/celestia,
archivers/lazperf and the rest -- cannot be re-triaged by an operator
until the runner restarts, and the refusal is silent.

FIX SHAPE. Run the sweep periodically rather than once: a row that is
too young on one pass is caught on the next, and the race the age gate
protects against is still covered because the file has had time to
appear. A main-loop-interval or timer-driven call is enough; the query
is cheap (one indexed SELECT over QUEUED rows plus a stat per row).
Reaping at shutdown as well would not help -- the rows are equally young
then.

RELATED. Same family as poly-h6c (a completed triage job never reaches
done, so dead overstates failure ~3x). Different state, same shape: a
row outliving the work it describes, plus a sweeper that only runs at
startup. Worth fixing together -- any metric or guard built on
jobs.state is unreliable while both are open.
notes:
OUTCOME OF THE EVENTUAL REAP, recorded 2026-09-05.

When a later restart does catch these rows they are not simply deleted.
reap_stale_queued applies JobEvent.REAP_ORPHAN, and
(JobState.QUEUED, REAP_ORPHAN) -> DEAD is legal (lifecycle.py:195),
mapping through the retire_reason table to 'runner_restart'.

So the 14 phantom rows observed today -- every one of which describes
work that COMPLETED and reported confirm_green -- will be recorded as
dead/runner_restart. That is poly-h6c's complaint compounding: it
already measured 246 of 364 dead rows as runner_restart bookkeeping
rather than failure, and this adds 14 more successes to the pile.

Consequence for the fix: reaping these to DEAD is the wrong terminal
state even once the sweep runs often enough. A row whose work finished
elsewhere is not a failure. Whatever periodic sweep is added should
distinguish 'this row is a duplicate of work that completed' from
'this row died', or the metric stays wrong no matter how promptly it
runs.

reap_orphans by contrast deliberately leaves QUEUED alone -- its
docstring: 'QUEUED stays queued (those are claimable)'. Only
reap_stale_queued touches them.

title: a diffs/REMOVE is silently ignored once a port has an overlay.dops, and compose cannot distinguish that from a correct port
description:
Writing an ``overlay.dops`` suppresses the whole compat ``diffs/`` path.
Any file under ``diffs/`` that no dops op references is then silently
ignored. ``REMOVE`` is the case that can NEVER be referenced -- there is
no op that consumes a REMOVE list -- so it is always dropped, and
nothing says so.

OBSERVED 2026-09-05 on devel/llvm13, self-inflicted while converting it
from compat to dops. Its ``diffs/REMOVE`` held

    files/patch-fformat_extensions.diff

Before the conversion the compat path stripped that file. After it, the
composed port still contained it:

    compose-out/devel/llvm13/files/patch-fformat_extensions.diff  (709 bytes)

Compose reported errors=0 and applied 15 ops. Nothing in the report,
the notes, or the stage warnings mentioned REMOVE.

THE CODE

    compat.py:73   _read_remove_entries reads diffs/REMOVE and the
                   compat apply path strips each entry -- COMPAT ONLY.
    compose_discovery.py:93  notes "script-parity REMOVE list detected",
                   but this lives in compat_diff_files_script_parity,
                   i.e. the compat discovery path. A dops port never
                   reaches it.
    dops path      emits one generic note, "compat-artifacts-suppressed-
                   by-dops", which does not enumerate what was
                   suppressed.

THE DEMONSTRATION. Two ports, identical shape (overlay.dops present AND
diffs/REMOVE present), opposite correctness, indistinguishable output:

    ports-mgmt/pkg   dops   REMOVE: files/patch-src_Makefile.autosetup
                     CORRECT -- overlay.dops:44 carries the matching
                     `file remove ... on-missing noop` op, and the file
                     is absent from the composed port. Its diffs/REMOVE
                     is a vestigial leftover.
    devel/llvm13     dops   REMOVE: files/patch-fformat_extensions.diff
                     BROKEN (before the fix) -- no op, file present in
                     the composed port.

Both reported notes=['compat-artifacts-suppressed-by-dops']. There is no
way to tell them apart from the compose output. That is the bug: the
correct and the broken case are observationally identical.

THE RULE IS ALREADY KNOWN. dportsv3/migration/absorb_remove.py exists to
translate a REMOVE list into `file remove` ops, and its docstring states
the hazard exactly:

    "writing an overlay.dops flips the port to dops-mode compose, which
    suppresses the *entire* compat diffs/ path. So a port can only be
    flipped when REMOVE is its sole delta -- otherwise the other diffs/
    artifacts (Makefile.diff, ...) would silently stop applying."

It is enforced by a compose-parity gate -- but only for ports flipped by
that tool. A hand-written overlay.dops bypasses it completely, which is
how llvm13 slipped through.

SCOPE. Three ports carry diffs/REMOVE today:
    devel/boost-libs   compat -> still works, gets the note
    ports-mgmt/pkg     dops   -> correct by luck of having the op
    devel/llvm13       dops   -> was broken, fixed in DeltaPorts
                                 19ad30a33ca
Small today, but the trap is permanent and fires silently.

FIX SHAPE. At minimum, warn when a dops-mode port still has a
diffs/REMOVE: the file can never be honoured in that mode, so its
presence is either a vestige to delete or a dropped instruction. Better,
make "compat-artifacts-suppressed-by-dops" enumerate what it actually
suppressed, so an unreferenced diffs/ artifact is visible instead of
implied. Erroring is defensible too, since there is no legitimate reason
for a dops port to carry a REMOVE.

The invariant a test should pin: a port with overlay.dops and
diffs/REMOVE must not compose silently -- either the entries appear as
`file remove` ops, or compose says so.

title: a completed triage job never reaches done: it sits at triaged until a restart reaps it as dead/runner_restart
description:
A successful triage job has nowhere to go. It ends at TRIAGED and stays
there until the next runner restart sweeps it to DEAD/runner_restart, so
`dead` counts completed work as failure.

MEASURED on the builder 2026-09-05, jobs table:

    type     state       n          type    retire_reason        n
    ------------------------          -----------------------------
    triage   dead      253          triage  runner_restart     237
    triage   escalated  40          patch   patch_gave_up       59
    triage   triaged    32          patch   patch_budget_exh    42
    triage   done        0  <--     triage  abandoned           11
    patch    done      120          patch   runner_restart       5
    confirm  done      148          confirm runner_restart       4
    verify   done       81          triage  triage_failed        4
                                    patch   abandoned            1
                                    triage  origin_locked        1

patch, confirm and verify all reach DONE. Triage has reached it zero
times, ever.

246 of the 364 dead rows (68%) are runner_restart. Genuine failures --
gave_up, budget_exhausted, triage_failed, abandoned, origin_locked --
total 118. So `dead` overstates real failure by about 3.1x, and the
overstatement is concentrated entirely in triage.

THE CODE

lifecycle.TRANSITIONS reaches DONE from exactly three states:

    (VERIFYING,     VERIFY_OK)      -> DONE      lifecycle.py:132
    (VERIFYING_FIX, VERIFY_FIX_OK)  -> DONE      lifecycle.py:148
    (CONFIRMING,    CONFIRM_GREEN)  -> DONE      lifecycle.py:154
    (CONFIRMING,    CONFIRM_RED)    -> DONE      lifecycle.py:155

TRIAGED is not among them. Its only exits are:

    PATCH_START           -> PATCHING
    ESCALATE_MANUAL       -> ESCALATED
    ENV_BROKEN            -> DEAD
    WORKTREE_UNAVAILABLE  -> DEAD
    REAP_ORPHAN           -> DEAD
    ABANDON               -> DEAD

The PATCHING exit does not apply to the common case. When triage decides
auto_patch it calls enqueue_patch_job, which creates a SEPARATE row --
the table's own comment says so: "Patch jobs (created by
enqueue_patch_job after a triage decides auto_patch) arrive at CLAIMED
with no preceding triage in their own lifecycle." Observed pairs on the
builder confirm it, e.g.

    20260904-230146Z-...-biology_plink-...job         triage  triaged
    20260904-230223Z-...-biology_plink-...-patch.job  patch   done

So the triage row -- which did its work, classified the failure, and
enqueued the patch -- is left at TRIAGED permanently.

Then lifecycle.reap_orphans (lifecycle.py:509), called by the runner at
startup (runner.py:5030 "they're DEAD-with-runner_restart by
definition"), sweeps every row in _INFLIGHT_STATES to DEAD. Its docstring
names them: "CLAIMED, TRIAGING, TRIAGED, PATCHING, VERIFYING". TRIAGED is
in that set, so every completed triage is retired as an orphan on the
next restart.

THE CONTRADICTION IN THE CODE

The same state is classified two opposite ways by two consumers:

    ACTIVE_WORK_STATES  (lifecycle.py:304)  EXCLUDES TRIAGED
      -- used by the dashboard inflight count, the job-page live-poll
         indicator, and the duplicate-enqueue guard, i.e. "not active"
    _INFLIGHT_STATES    (reap_orphans)      INCLUDES TRIAGED
      -- "inflight-ish", i.e. reap it

runner.py:1638 even flags the asymmetry ("the full rationale for why
TRIAGED is excluded, and how this differs from the reap-orphans set"),
so it is known to be a special case. What is missing is the third
possibility: TRIAGED is neither active nor orphaned, it is FINISHED.

WHY IT MATTERS

Any metric over job state is wrong today. `dead` reads as failure and is
68% bookkeeping. A triage that classified correctly and handed off to a
patch job is indistinguishable, after one restart, from one that died.
This bit the analysis twice: it makes the queue view show completed
triage rows as in-flight work, and it inflates every failure count.

FIX SHAPE

Give a handed-off triage a terminal success state. Either add
(TRIAGED, PATCH_START) -> DONE on the triage row when enqueue_patch_job
creates the child, or add a TRIAGE_DONE event and transition, and remove
TRIAGED from _INFLIGHT_STATES so the reaper stops claiming finished work.
Whichever is chosen, the invariant to assert in a test is the one the
data violates: a triage job that produced a classification must not end
as DEAD/runner_restart.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-05.

Added JobEvent.TRIAGE_HANDOFF and (TRIAGED, TRIAGE_HANDOFF) -> DONE,
fired as an extra_event on the auto_patch route right after
enqueue_patch_job succeeds.

REFINEMENT OF THE FIX SHAPE. The bead offered 'add the transition, and
remove TRIAGED from _INFLIGHT_STATES so the reaper stops claiming
finished work'. Kept TRIAGED in _INFLIGHT_STATES deliberately. Once
finished triage moves to DONE, what is still sitting at TRIAGED is a
triage that classified and then died before handing off -- genuinely
incomplete, and exactly what the reaper is for. Removing the state from
the set would have stranded those forever instead. The reaper stops
claiming finished work because the work is no longer in that state, not
because the state left the set. Both directions are pinned by tests.

ALSO CHECKED: only ONE route out of TRIAGED was stranded, not two or
three. escalate_manual reaches ESCALATED, and skip / cached_health_broken
routes to ENV_BROKEN -> DEAD (steps.py, the 'route' block). auto_patch
was the only path with no exit, which matches the data: triage escalated
= 40, triage done = 0.

HISTORICAL ROWS ARE NOT BACKFILLED. The 237 existing
triage/dead/runner_restart rows stay as they are, so any count over the
current jobs table still overstates failure until they age out. That
matters for UI-4 (poly-435j), whose 'dead' figure reads this column. A
one-off migration is inferable -- a DEAD/runner_restart triage with a
patch job for the same origin created just after it did hand off -- but
rewriting job history is a call for the operator, not a side effect of
this fix.
close_reason: TRIAGE_HANDOFF now carries a handed-off triage from TRIAGED to DONE on the auto_patch route, the only route out of TRIAGED that had no exit. TRIAGED deliberately stays in _INFLIGHT_STATES so a triage that died before handing off is still reaped. Three tests: the happy path reaches DONE, a handed-off triage survives reap_orphans without runner_restart, and a crashed one is still swept. Historical rows are not backfilled -- see the note for what that costs UI-4.

title: mk disable-if comments out only the .if line, leaving an unguarded body and an if-less endif
description:
`mk disable-if` comments out the `.if` line and nothing else, which
turns a guarded block into an unguarded one and orphans its `.endif`.
It then reports success.

exec_mk_block_disable, dportsv3/engine/executors/mk_ops.py:

    original_line = text.splitlines(keepends=False)[node.span.line_start - 1]
    replacement = f"# {original_line}" if original_line else f"# {condition}"
    updated = _replace_line_range(
        text,
        start=node.span.line_start,
        end=node.span.line_end,
        new_lines=[replacement],
    )
    txn.stage_write(path, updated)
    return _success_row(op, "mk-block-disabled")

The span replaced is the condition node only, never the matching
`.endif`, and never the body.

OBSERVED 2026-09-04 on devel/stack, composing @2026Q3. The overlay
wanted misc/compat12x skipped on DragonFly, so I wrote

    mk disable-if condition "!${ARCH:Mpowerpc64*}"

Compose reported errors=0, applied=3, failed=0, and produced:

    230
    231  # .if !${ARCH:Mpowerpc64*}
    232  LIB_DEPENDS+=	libncursesw.so.8:misc/compat12x
    233  .endif

Two defects in one output. The dependency is now UNCONDITIONAL -- the
exact opposite of what disabling the block was for -- and line 233 is
an `.endif` with no `.if`, so bmake fails the port outright:
`make: "Makefile" line 233: if-less endif`. Neither is reported; the
op row says success and the port's error count is zero.

`.elif` has the same shape: commenting the `.elif` line merges its body
into the preceding branch rather than removing it.

WHY NOTHING HAS BROKEN YET. No overlay in DeltaPorts uses this op --
grep -rl '^mk disable-if' ports --include=overlay.dops returns 0 of
5010. It is a trap laid for the next author rather than live damage.
The quickref advertises it ("Comment out an .if block matching an exact
condition"), so it will be reached for.

The executor is untested. tests/test_dportsv3_emit.py only checks the
emitted op kind is mk.block.disable, and test_dportsv3_parser.py only
checks the line parses; nothing exercises the produced Makefile. A
test that composes a port with an .if/.endif and asserts .if/.endif
balance would have caught this.

WHAT IT SHOULD DO. Either comment the whole region -- `.if`, body and
`.endif` -- so the block is genuinely disabled, or refuse the op with
E_APPLY_INVALID_OPERATION when it cannot do that safely. Silently
emitting a Makefile bmake will not parse is the one behaviour to rule
out. Note the quickref's own wording implies whole-block: "Comment out
an .if BLOCK".

WORKAROUND USED. `mk replace-if` to a condition that is false on the
composed tree:

    mk replace-if from "!${ARCH:Mpowerpc64*}" \
                  to   "${OPSYS} == FreeBSD && !${ARCH:Mpowerpc64*}"

Safe there only because the block sits after `.include <bsd.port.pre.mk>`,
so ${OPSYS} is defined. Before a framework include this fails with
`Variable "OPSYS" is undefined`, so it is not a general substitute.

Related: the same file's mk.var.set / mk.var.token_remove refuse
ambiguous matches rather than guessing (E_APPLY_AMBIGUOUS_MATCH), which
is the right instinct and the opposite of what this op does.
