  subversion-family ports (devel/subversion/Makefile.addons), comms/
  opencbm and its plugin (Makefile.inc), and net/tigervnc-server
  (Makefile.common.mk). Angle-bracket includes are the framework, which
  sets only PORTREVISION?= 0 (Mk/bsd.port.mk:1359 on main), so an
  inserted assignment is honoured.

DECISIONS, settled.
- A new verb, not a "+1" meaning inside mk set: mk set's value is a
  literal string, and a special meaning would change what existing
  payloads mean and leave no way to write a literal +1.
- PORTREVISION only.
- Additive: bumps on one build line add up in apply order (@any first,
  then the line's own), and a bump after a mk set adds to that value.
  No conflict check. A bump only adds and never lowers a revision, and
  lowering is the only harmful outcome (.12); an @any bump plus a @T mk
  set is the override S2 allows; and a conflict pass would be a
  second per-line co-applicability analysis beside row 11's dead-op rule.
- Refuse slaves and quoted-include ports in v1 (above).
- Rejected, the cheaper unlock: reading another branch's Makefile from
  the dev-env host's freebsd-ports mirror (git show <branch>:<origin>/
  Makefile answers in milliseconds) only lets the agent write the right
  absolute number per line, which still pins, and it needs a new agent
  tool whose description sits in every turn.

CHANGE.
Syntax and meaning:

    mk bump PORTREVISION [by <N>]

N is an integer from 1 to 99, default 1; no on-missing clause. Plan kind
mk.var.bump, payload {"name": "PORTREVISION", "by": N}. Composed value:
the line's PORTREVISION as it stands when the op runs, plus N.

- parser.py _parse_mk_op (:321): add "bump" to the action dispatch (the
  var-op set is at :332; bump gets its own branch) and a new
  _parse_mk_bump_op: a WORD variable (the parser's expect-word helper,
  "after 'mk bump'"), then optionally the WORD "by" followed by one WORD
  (expect-word, "after 'by'"; a missing one is the helper's
  E_PARSE_EXPECTED_TOKEN). Anything else before the end of the line is
  E_PARSE_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN "unexpected token after mk bump; expected
  'by <N>' or end of line". It builds MkOpNode(action="bump", var=<var>,
  value=<the raw WORD after by, or "1">). Add bump to the "expected ..."
  list in the unexpected-action message (set|eval|shell|unset|add|
  remove|bump|...). No lexer change: "mk bump PORTREVISION by 3" lexes
  as five WORD tokens.
- semantic.py _validate_operation (:97), mk branch: an elif for "bump"
  before the "unknown mk action" else (:207). var other than
  PORTREVISION: E_SEM_INVALID_OPERATION_STATE "mk bump supports
  PORTREVISION only". value not all digits, or outside 1..99:
  E_SEM_INVALID_OPERATION_STATE "mk bump by takes an integer from 1 to
  99". Add "bump" to the set that refuses on-missing (:213).
- planner.py _map_operation (:53): "bump" maps to ("mk.var.bump",
  {"name": op.var, "by": int(op.value)}).
- mk_ops.py: factor exec_mk_var_set's write (the replacement line; the
  matched node's line range, else before _mk_var_set_insert_line, else
  at end of file) into _write_assignment(text, document, node_index:
  int | None, line: str) -> str. exec_mk_var_set calls it with
  f"{name}= {value}", with no change in behaviour. New
  exec_mk_var_bump(op, context, txn), registered as "mk.var.bump" in
  apply.py _known_registry (:153). On port_root/Makefile, checks in this
  order:

      Makefile missing           _missing_row, policy error
      MASTERDIR= at top level    E_APPLY_BUMP_UNSUPPORTED "slave port:
                                 PORTREVISION comes from or is overridden
                                 by its master; bump the master"
      two or more assignments    E_APPLY_AMBIGUOUS_MATCH "multiple
                                 assignments found for PORTREVISION"
      one, inside .if            E_APPLY_BUMP_UNSUPPORTED "PORTREVISION is
                                 assigned inside a conditional"
      one, operator not = or ?=  E_APPLY_BUMP_UNSUPPORTED "PORTREVISION
                                 uses <op>; only = and ?= can be bumped"
      one, value not an integer  E_APPLY_BUMP_UNSUPPORTED "PORTREVISION is
                                 '<value>', not an integer" (a trailing
                                 # comment and whitespace are stripped
                                 first)
      one                        _write_assignment(that node,
                                 "PORTREVISION= <v+N>"), or
                                 "PORTREVISION?= <v+N>" when it used ?=
      none, any quoted .include  E_APPLY_BUMP_UNSUPPORTED "PORTREVISION
                                 may be set by an included file (<first
                                 quoted include>)"
      none                       _write_assignment(None,
                                 "PORTREVISION= <N>")

  Depth: walk document.nodes, +1 at DirectiveIfNode and -1 at
  DirectiveEndifNode; an AssignmentNode at depth above 0 is conditional,
  and MASTERDIR counts only at depth 0. A quoted include is an
  IncludeNode whose include starts with a double quote.
  E_APPLY_BUMP_UNSUPPORTED is the one new code; its message says why.
  Success row message "mk-var-bump".
- dportsv3/engine/emit.py: mk_bump(name: str, *, by: int = 1) -> str,

- docs/dsl-v0.md: the mk_var_op grammar (:84) gains

- dportsv3/agent/dops_quickref.md: one line for the form. It is served

    When the port already builds at this upstream version and you
    changed how it builds (added a patch, edited flags), bump the
    revision with mk bump PORTREVISION, in the same target block as the

MIGRATION, a DeltaPorts commit the operator makes once the verb ships,
from today's @any mk set PORTREVISION "3" or from D8's interim
form (the op moved into a target @2026Q3,@main block):
- delete the mk set PORTREVISION op (from the interim form, drop the
  target @2026Q3,@main block too if that leaves it empty);
- put mk bump PORTREVISION in the @any block right after its last mk

That composes 2+1 = 3 on 2026Q3 and 0+1+2 = 3 on main, today's values,
and a new line gets its upstream value plus 1. Before committing,
recompute the amounts from the then-current upstream values: a line's
extra amount is (its pinned value - its upstream value - 1); a line where
that is negative needs an operator decision, because it would lower a
shipped revision. Gate: compose graphics/gdal on main and on the current
quarterly before and after (a scratch git repo named for the branch
holding the port from git archive, a copy of the overlay as delta root,
--origin, oracle off) and compare the whole composed Makefile:
byte-identical on both. Checked 2026-10-04 with a prototype of this
bead's executor, from today's form: the live overlay and its additive

EDGE CASES.
- Two bumps on one line, or a mk set then a bump: they add in apply
  order. A bump then a mk set: the mk set's absolute value wins, as any
  later mk set does.
- Upstream changes PORTVERSION and resets PORTREVISION: the bump follows
  (0 + N). The op goes when the DragonFly change goes.
- type dport: the bump edits newport's Makefile like any other.
- .sinclude and .-include lines are not IncludeNodes, so a quoted one is
  not seen by the include rule (count UNVERIFIED; rare).
- mk set PORTREVISION then mk bump on one line, under an oracle run
  (profile local or ci, bmake on PATH; dev-envs run it off): apply.py
  builds the oracle's expectation from mk.var.set payloads only, so it
  expects the mk set value while the Makefile holds value + N, a false
  oracle failure. The new oracle bead (poly-7pwa.22)
  fixes it with no change here: it drops a name any later mk.var.* op
  changes, and mk.var.bump carries its variable in payload "name". By
  reading apply.py; not run (no bmake here).

I wrote that a bump cannot be idempotent because compose runs repeatedly. It can,
for free, because COMPOSE NEVER APPLIES OPS TO ITS OWN PREVIOUS OUTPUT. Verified:
incremental compose (the agent's reapply, the repeated case) passes
copy_port_base=incremental (compose_stages.py:749) into materialize_plan_type,
which calls copy_tree(upstream_origin, output_origin) -- and copy_tree is
rmtree(dst) + copytree(src, dst) (fsutils.py:132-137). The port directory is wiped
and re-copied from pristine upstream BEFORE any op runs. A full compose reseeds
the whole tree. So  computes from upstream's value every time: N+1 on the
first compose, N+1 on the hundredth. It cannot walk upward. (Two bump ops in one
overlay would compound -- an authoring error of the same kind as two mk set lines,
not a design question.)

title: compose writes its own input tree from --origin runs too, and no report tells those writes apart from its output
description:
compose mutates the DeltaPorts SOURCE tree as a side effect of composing, in two
places, and in an agent env that tree is the job's worktree -- so the writes land
in the reviewed diff without anyone deciding to make them.

1. _apply_stale_overlay_policy (compose_stages.py:453) writes overlay.toml
   removed_in on any non-dry-run compose where a type=port overlay names an
   origin missing upstream. This is the mechanism behind poly-7pwa.6's
   stickiness: the marker is written automatically and nothing ever clears it.

2. _resolve_special_diff_selection (compose_stages.py:~145-151) copies
   special/<category>/diffs/*.diff into the port's diffs/@<target>/ when that
   directory is absent. Target-specific files, materialised into the source
   tree, by a command whose job is to produce an output tree.

Both are sticky: they persist after the compose that made them. In the agent
flow, reapply runs against /work/DeltaPorts inside the job's worktree, and
changes.diff is captured whole-tree (runner.py:4340, rel="."), so these appear
in the delivery diff as though the agent had authored them. A reviewer reading a
patch for one port sees an overlay.toml or a diffs/@main/ addition with no
explanation, because none of it is in the agent's tool trace.

SEVERITY IS LOW TODAY and I want that on the record rather than implied: (1)
requires the origin to be absent upstream, which for a port the agent is
patching means it was just built, so it is present; (2) requires the port to
have a special/ diff selection and no existing diffs/@<target>/. Neither is
common. It is filed because "compose writes to its own input" is a property
nobody would expect from the name, it is invisible in the tool trace, and it is
the root of .6.

FIX SHAPE: both writes belong behind an explicit flag or in a separate
maintenance command, not in the compose path the agent invokes on every
iteration. At minimum, compose should report them as changes to its INPUT
distinctly from its output -- there is already an I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARKED_REMOVED
warning for (1), and (2) has none.
design:
STATE. Open, P3, W3: lands on master after poly-7pwa merges (the epic's
D7; if .21 is closed and the merge still waits, wait for it; never on
poly-7pwa, which holds exactly .21's rows) and BEFORE poly-7pwa.6, so
.6's ignore/clear helper is written once on top of this bead's write
rule.

PREMISE, verified 2026-10-04 by composing fixtures on the post-carry tree
(master ab725ac plus the seven picks). It holds, with corrections.
- The property is real. A full compose writes ports/<origin>/overlay.toml
  (removed_in) for a newly stale type-port overlay. A full compose for a
  quarterly also bootstraps special/<component>/diffs/@<target>/ and
  replacements/@<target>/ from the unscoped main payload. An --origin
  compose of a stale origin writes overlay.toml too; an --origin compose of
  a present origin writes nothing.
- CORRECTION 1. The second write is special/<component>/{diffs,
  replacements}/@<target>/, not a port's diffs/. Two resolvers do it,
  _resolve_special_diff_selection and _resolve_special_replacement_selection
  (dportsv3/compose_stages.py). Both return early for @main, and
  apply_special_stage returns before them on an --origin compose. A
  bootstrap with nothing to copy creates an empty directory git does not
  see.
- CORRECTION 2. "(2) has none" is wrong: I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARKED_REMOVED,
  I_COMPOSE_SPECIAL_TARGET_BOOTSTRAPPED and the "auto-bootstrapped target
  dirs" hint report the writes. What no report does is tell them apart as
  changes to the INPUT tree.
- CORRECTION 3. Nothing reaches an agent's diff today. Every in-job compose
  is reapply, an --origin compose (dportsv3/agent/worker.py
  materialize_dports and reset_port, through dev-env's reapply helper).
  The job's origins exist upstream on its line, so the stale policy never
  fires for them, and the agent has no shell tool (dportsv3/agent/tools.py,
  _TOOLS).
- A FOURTH CASE the bead missed: a full compose whose --freebsd-root is not
  on the target's branch. _check_freebsd_git_state records
  E_COMPOSE_TARGET_BRANCH_MISMATCH (or E_COMPOSE_GIT_BRANCH_CHECK_FAILED)
  and returns True, so preflight reads upstream presence from the wrong
  line and writes markers from it. With poly-7pwa.6's clear it would also
  delete valid ones: composing @main against a 2026Q3 checkout would clear
  108 of the 1088 @main markers (19 of them on dops ports); @2026Q3
  against main would clear 2. Method: for each overlay.toml entry @main,
  git ls-tree 2026Q3 <origin>/Makefile in freebsd-ports, and the converse.

WHERE IT BITES.
- Operator commits. DeltaPorts 03581ae8b63, "special: add @2026Q3
  patches", carries 948 overlay.toml marker writes next to 35
  special/@2026Q3 files.
- The absorb_remove gate. absorb_remove_gated calls check_parity with
  baseline_root set to the real DeltaPorts tree, and migration/parity.py
  composes --origin with dry_run=False, so a gate run on a stale origin
  writes removed_in into both delta roots, the real tree among them --
  against parity.py's own "read-only with respect to both delta roots"
  docstring, which this bead makes true (pinned by
  test_the_parity_gate_leaves_both_delta_roots_unchanged).
  No CLI or code path calls absorb_remove_gated or absorb_makefile_gated
  today, only tests. absorb_makefile_gated cannot reach the write: it
  returns before check_parity when the upstream Makefile is missing.
- Two pending changes would bring it to the agent: poly-7pwa.6's marker
  clear, if it ran on --origin composes, and poly-7pwa.8 Tier 2, which
  composes the job's origin for ANOTHER line where the port may be absent.
  Either would write overlay.toml into the job's worktree, and changes.diff
  is whole-tree (dportsv3/agent/runner.py, rel = ".").

RULE (adopted with the epic's D3, 2026-10-04). Only a full compose, without
--dry-run, whose freebsd checkout passed the branch check writes the delta
tree. An --origin compose reads the delta tree and never writes it.
Everything that must not write already runs --origin: reapply,
apply-and-build, the absorb parity gates and .8 Tier 2. Every full compose
is an operator sweep, env creation (dev-env builder, initial compose) or
regen without an origin. So no flag and no new command. The special
bootstrap already runs only on a full compose, copies within the delta tree
and reads nothing from the freebsd checkout, so it needs no branch gate.

title: two open fixes for one origin on two build lines merge at Accept into a union no line built
description:
Every exclusion in the agentic pipeline is keyed per (target, origin); the file
two jobs would both write is keyed per origin alone.

- origin skip-lock: per (target, origin) -- tracker/agentic_queries/skip.py
- retry/attempt history: per (target, origin) -- agent/decision.py
- delivery dedupe and the branch name: per (origin, target, signature), the
  branch template carries {target_safe} -- settings.py delivery keys

So two runners on two envs, one per build line, may hold patch jobs for the SAME
origin at the same time. Both edit ports/<origin>/overlay.dops. Both started from
the same DeltaPorts base. Each is validated against its own target only, because
that is all an env can do.

Whichever delivery lands second either conflicts in the overlay, or -- worse and
more likely, because the two edits usually touch different blocks -- merges
cleanly and lands its @any ops onto the first line's target having never been
composed there. The result is a tree where each build line was individually
verified and the union of the two changes was verified nowhere.

THIS IS THE ONE FINDING IN THE EPIC THAT GETS WORSE AS THE MULTI-TARGET WORK
SUCCEEDS. The others are static defects that a careful agent plus better
guidance can avoid. This one is a race that only appears once two build lines
are actually being worked in parallel, which is the stated goal.

NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and worth settling before designing a fix: whether the two
envs share one DeltaPorts checkout or each holds its own. The pre-job clean
assertion (agent/steps.py, "refuse to start a patch job if ports/<origin>/ has
leftover edits") is per-worktree, so if envs have separate worktrees the
conflict surfaces at delivery rather than during the attempt; if they share one,
it surfaces as the second job refusing to start, which is the better outcome and
possibly already the behaviour. Measure that first -- the answer decides whether
this is a locking problem or a merge-policy problem.

FIX SHAPE (after the above is settled): either extend the skip-lock to cover
(origin) across targets for the duration of a patch attempt -- serialising the
two build lines per port, cheap and boring -- or require the second delivery to
re-verify the union. The first is far simpler and costs only parallelism on the
same port, which is rare.

WHAT THE FILED QUESTION SETTLED, verified 2026-10-04.
- Envs do not share a DeltaPorts checkout. dev-env create clones
  DeltaPorts into each env's own /work/ports-main
  (dev-env/dports_dev_env/builder.py:128) from one host-side bare mirror,
  and each job gets a linked worktree of its env's ports-main
  (worker.create_job_worktree, worker.py:2708 on the post-carry tree).
  The pre-job clean assertion is per worktree and cannot see another
  env's edits.
- _has_active_same_origin_job (runner.py:1862-1887) is not an execution
  lock. Its only caller is the operator-context retriage guard
  (runner.py:1912), and it matches the run's own target or none.
  Measured: over a state.db holding an active @main patch job for
  lang/rust, it returns that job when asked from a @main run and None
  from a @2026Q3 run.
- The skip-lock is set only by an operator's take-over or discard
  (tracker/routes/bundle_actions.py:693, :856); the runner never takes one
  per attempt.
- Execution is already serial. One runner per queue root (a flock,
  runner.acquire_runner_lock, runner.py:2101-2133; one queue root per host
  by default, paths.queue_root; a second runner on another queue root is
  unsupported, not prevented, :2116-2119), and the main loop runs one job
  to completion before claiming the next.

THE LOCK FIX SHAPE IS MOOT. Extending the skip-lock to the origin for the
duration of a patch attempt adds nothing. Attempts are already serial, and
serial does not help: the second job branches from its own env's base, not
from the first job's result. The window that matters runs from the first
fix's verification until its change is in the base the second job branches
from (review, merge, dev-env update): days, not one attempt.

THE HAZARD THAT SURVIVES needs no concurrency. Take two fixes for one
origin, one per build line:
- each job branches from its own env's ports-main HEAD, which moves only
  on an operator's dev-env update or sync-dirty (nothing in the runner
  refreshes it), so neither sees the other's change;
- each changes.diff is git diff <base> (runner._capture_branch_diff,
  runner.py:4325-4354), verified on its own line only;
- the branch template carries the target (delivery.branch_template,
  settings.py:614-621), so they are two deliveries;
- with delivery.type = github, Accept fetches origin/<base> and applies
  with git apply --3way --index (delivery/github.py:164-170,
  delivery/_git.py:185-266). With local-patch (an outbox the operator
  applies by hand, delivery/local_patch.py) or with delivery off (the
  shipped default, settings.py:578-586), whoever applies the second diff
  forms the same union by hand.
Measured 2026-10-04. Method: ports-mgmt/pkg copied from DeltaPorts into
scratch git repos, one clone per env; each fix's diff taken with git diff
<base>; Accept simulated with fetch, checkout -B and git apply --3way
--index; plans built with the engine's build_plan.
  S1  edits at different places, both @any: B applies cleanly after A is
      merged. The union carries, on @main, a file.materialize and, on
      @2026Q3, a mk.var.token_add that no job planned on that line.
  S2  two @any PORTREVISION sets at different places: clean. Both stay in
      @any, and by apply order the later one wins on every line.
  S3  both append at the end of the @any block: a 3-way conflict, loud.

2026Q1, 2026Q2 and 2026Q3 envs. Once poly-7pwa.14 lands, each line's jobs
run in their own env (held until it is selected), which makes two open
fixes for one origin on two lines more likely, not less.

HOW OFTEN AN OVERLAY MOVES UNDER AN OPEN FIX. Measured 2026-10-04 over
DeltaPorts history since 2026-01-01 (HEAD c030e103838; git log
--name-only, 1026 commits; a port counts as touched when a commit changes
a file under ports/<origin>/). Of the 196 commits titled "<origin>: fix
build failure on DragonFly" (the delivery title,
delivery/orchestrator.py:431), 8 had their port touched by another commit
within the 7 days before, and 9 within the 30 days before (4.1 and 4.6
percent). None of those earlier commits used the delivery title. For 3 of
the 9 ports it was a "chore(migration)" commit; for devel/readline (the
ninth, outside the 7-day window) three "convert to DOPS" commits by a
human author; for the other 5, Fred [bot] commits with other titles.
Whether those 5 were agent- or human-directed is UNVERIFIED: they and the
delivery commits share the author "Fred [bot]" (delivery.committer_name),
who authors 745 of the 1026 commits, so authorship cannot tell agent work
from human work.

CANDIDATE RULES. Both are kept; choose one when a trigger fires.
1. One open fix per origin across build lines, until it is merged and the
   other env updated. Where: the triage and patch enqueue path, or
   poly-fij's claim once it exists. Cost: the second line's fix waits
   days.
2. A pre-image check at Accept, github provider only. A bundle diff's
   index lines name each file's pre-image blob, so once
   prepare_clean_branch has fetched origin/<base>, a file whose blob there
   differs from its pre-image was 3-way-merged onto a version nobody
   built. It flags all three scenarios above, and could add a section to
   the pull request body. Caveat: re-verifying cannot clear it, because a
   diff's pre-images never change; a clearable version needs verify to
   record the base it built.

cross-env scheduler.

title: the compat implicit payload copy is target-blind and keeps the @target path component, so a compat-mode scoped port would get both targets' patches
description:
LATENT: 0 ports affected today. Filed because it is the trap the third
multi-target port walks into, and because the discrepancy is with the
documented behaviour rather than with taste.

compose_discovery.py:100-113, compat_dragonfly_files_script_parity, takes NO
target and collects the payload recursively:

    rows = [
        (src, src.relative_to(dragonfly_dir))
        for src in sorted(path for path in dragonfly_dir.rglob("*") if path.is_file())
    ]

So for a port with target-scoped payload dirs it returns every target's files,
each keyed by a relative path that still carries the scope component --
`@main/patch-configure.def`, `@2026Q3/patch-auto.def.c` -- and compose_stages
.844 hands that straight to run_compat_merge as `payload_files`. A compat-mode
port would therefore get BOTH targets' patches copied into the composed tree,
under literal `@main/` and `@2026Q3/` subdirectories of `dragonfly/`.

THAT CONTRADICTS THE DOCUMENTED INTENT. docs/implementation-plan-v3.md:1339:
"Copy files from ports/<origin>/dragonfly/@target/** into output origin tree",
and architecture-v3.md:203 "implicit payload in dragonfly/@target/... remains
supported" -- one target's scoped files, flattened. The dops path gets this
right because the ops name src and dst explicitly; only the compat auto-copy
is target-blind.

WHY IT IS LATENT. Measured across the whole tree: exactly two ports have
target-scoped payload dirs (lang/rust, ports-mgmt/pkg) and both carry an
overlay.dops, so both compose in dops mode, where the compat auto-copy is
suppressed (I_COMPOSE_MODE_DOPS_SUPPRESSES_COMPAT). Nothing hits this path
today.

HOW IT STOPS BEING LATENT, either of:
- a third port adopts the scoped convention while still in compat mode (no
  overlay.dops yet) -- the natural order, since the scoped dirs are how you
  discover you need per-target handling
- an existing scoped port loses or is reverted off its overlay.dops

Both are one commit away, and the symptom is a build reading patches from a
directory named `@main` that bsd.port.mk's do-patch will not glob, i.e. the
patches silently stop applying.

NOTE the sibling function immediately below, resolve_layered_compat_makefile
(line 116), DOES take a target and layers Makefile.DragonFly.<target> over
.@any over legacy. The target-awareness is present one function down; the
payload resolver just never got it.

and dragonfly/@2026Q3/patch-X, composed for @main, must produce exactly
dragonfly/patch-X from the @main source and nothing from @2026Q3.

title: removed_in still skips a port after upstream restores it, so its overlay is silently lost on that build line
description:
A port may carry `overlay.toml` with `removed_in = ["@main", ...]`, meaning its
overlay is not applied for those targets at all. compose_stages.py:549-552 sets
removed_for_target and `continue`s; the dops apply stage (686-689) and the
compat apply stage (828-831) then skip the port outright. Nothing in
dportsv3/agent/ has ever heard of overlay.toml or removed_in --
probe_overlay_facts does not look at it, no tool exposes it, no playbook
mentions it.

MEASURED IN THE TREE TODAY:

  1093 ports carry removed_in
   251 of those ALSO carry a live overlay.dops
   108 are removed_in ["@main"] only -- a live overlay on the quarterlies,
       skipped on main

PROVEN END TO END, not reasoned about. devel/plasma has removed_in ["@main"]
and an overlay.dops that plans clean with 2 @any ops. Composing it for @main:

  dportsv3 compose --target @main --origin devel/plasma ...

  "applied_ops": 0, "total_ops": 0, "errors": 0, "warnings": 0
  notes: ["removed-for-target", "stale-skipped", "stale-skipped"]
  and the command reports SUCCESS

Every op in the overlay was discarded and compose said nothing -- zero errors,
zero warnings, exit clean.

THE JOB THAT CANNOT SUCCEED. A patch job is created from a dsynth failure on a
target. For one of these 108 ports on @main the port composes as pure
freebsd-ports, fails to build, and a patch job is filed. The agent then edits
ports/<origin>/overlay.dops; validate_dops passes (the overlay is well-formed);
materialize_dports reports ok (compose succeeds, having applied nothing);
dsynth_build fails exactly as before. The agent burns its whole budget on a
file the build for that target does not read. Terminal symptom identical to
poly-7pwa.1, cause total rather than partial.

AND THE RIGHT ANSWER IS NOT EXPRESSIBLE. When such a port does need an overlay
on that target after all, the fix is to drop that target from removed_in --
the inverse of what compose_stages.write_overlay_removed_in does. The agent
cannot do it and does not know the list exists. Note _reject_orphan_dops_write
only guards `*.dops`, so an overlay.toml write is not blocked; this is missing
knowledge and a missing tool surface, not a blocked path.

WHAT IS NEEDED, roughly:
- probe_overlay_facts reads overlay.toml and OverlayFacts carries removed_in
- the runner refuses, or at minimum loudly warns, before spending a patch
  attempt on a port whose overlay is removed for the job's target; "this
  overlay does not apply to the target you are building" is knowable before
  the first turn, for free
- if the agent is allowed to conclude "this port needs its overlay back on
  @main", it needs a way to say so -- an op, a tool, or an escalation

VERIFICATION SHAPE: the devel/plasma compose above is the fixture. It must
become loud. A test that composes a removed-for-target port with a non-empty
overlay and asserts a warning is emitted fails against today's code.
design:
STATE. Open, P3, W3: lands right after poly-7pwa.16, on the same branch,
on top of its write rule. Decided (D3, below); not gated any more.

PREMISE, verified 2026-10-04 against DeltaPorts c030e103838 and
freebsd-ports main, 2026Q3, 2026Q2 and origin/2026Q1. It holds as this
bead's notes correct it.
- Nothing is broken today. The 1093 ports/*/*/overlay.toml files hold 3561
  removed_in entries (@main 1088, @2026Q3 982, @2026Q2 808, @2026Q1 683),
  removed_in is their only key, and 0 entries name a line on which the
  origin exists. Method: for each entry, git ls-tree <branch>
  <origin>/Makefile in freebsd-ports (main, 2026Q3, 2026Q2 and
  origin/2026Q1).
- Every marker is on a type port overlay: 842 compat (by
  infer_compat_port_type) and 251 dops (header type port), all of which
  plan.
- Nothing has ever cleared one. All 1093 files come from five DeltaPorts
  sweep commits: 8948ebe0a12 @2026Q1, fe218b65a3f @2026Q2, 03581ae8b63 and
  16dfbc3b2e0 @2026Q3, edb5585a79b @main (2026-09-27). Together they add
  3561 target lines and remove none. Method: git log -p over
  ports/*/*/overlay.toml, counting added and removed target lines.
- Upstream does bring ports back. Since 2023-10-01, 62 origins whose
  removal line was later deleted from freebsd-ports MOVED are present on
  main today, and 41 of them have a DeltaPorts directory. Their 42
  restorations: median 6.5 days gone over all rows, 11 days over the 37
  real absences (5 rows are same-day reverts or a withdrawn scheduled
  removal); 13 came back after more than 30 days, 8 after more than 90.
  Method: git log -p main -- MOVED since 2023-10-01, deleted lines
  "origin||date|reason" whose origin exists on main today, gap = deleting
  commit date minus the line's date. The bug bites only when a sweep marked
  the port while it was gone; "a few cases a year" is an UNVERIFIED
  projection that depends on the sweep cadence (five sweeps in seven
  months).

HISTORY. DeltaPorts 1d3e313d8f5 (2026-03-18) introduced removed_in with the
bullet "Add removed_in field to overlay.toml for per-target port
exclusion", a hand-written exclusion; its test,
test_compose_removed_in_skips_port_for_target, excludes a port that EXISTS
upstream ("Port exists upstream but is declared removed for @main"), and
the field had no writer. 6f74c3602c5 (2026-03-25), "Auto-mark stale
overlays during compose", added write_overlay_removed_in, and every marker
in the tree today came from that writer. (Another bullet of 1d3e313d8f5,
"Fix stale overlay pruning ... when a port is missing from one target's
upstream tree", is about pruning, not removed_in.)

DECISION, made by the user 2026-10-04 (the epic's D3, option a). removed_in
records that the origin was missing upstream for a line, and it skips the
port only while that holds. A full compose that may write the delta tree
(poly-7pwa.16's rule, including its freebsd branch-check gate) removes the
target from removed_in once the port is back. This reverses the original
2026-03-18 meaning.

COST, recorded as the decision requires. A hand-written removed_in no
longer keeps an overlay off a line where its port exists: on a type port,
lock or mask overlay it is ignored, and the next full compose clears it.
A dport marker still skips, because a dport origin is never upstream. None
exists today (all 1093 markers are type port and none names a present
origin), and no doc describes manual use. In overlay.dops the same intent
is expressed with target blocks for the lines that need the ops.

CHANGE, on top of poly-7pwa.16.
1. dportsv3/compose_discovery.py, beside write_overlay_removed_in, its
   inverse:
       def clear_overlay_removed_in(port_path: Path, target: str
               ) -> tuple[bool, str | None]
   Missing manifest, or target not in _removed_in_targets(payload) (from
   .16): (False, None). A read error: (False, error). Otherwise remove the
   target, keeping the rest sorted as the writer does; drop the removed_in
   key when nothing remains; if the table is then empty, unlink
   overlay.toml (write_overlay_removed_in created it, and all 1093 hold
   only removed_in), reporting an OSError as
       f"Failed to remove file: {manifest} ({exc})"
   else write it with write_toml_file. Return (True, None) on a change.
2. dportsv3/compose_stages.py, preflight_stage, the removed_in check:
       if target in read_overlay_removed_in(ctx.path):
           if ctx.origin not in upstream_origins:
               ctx.removed_for_target = True
               report.notes.append("removed-for-target")
               continue
           _note_stale_removed_in(
               ctx=ctx, report=report, stage=stage, target=target,
               origin_compose=selected_origins is not None,
               delta_write_skip=delta_write_skip,
               delta_writes=delta_writes)
   then fall through, so the overlay is planned and applied like any other.
   A comment says why: removed_in records absence; skipping a present port
   would build it as pure upstream with its overlay silently gone.
3. A new helper beside _apply_stale_overlay_policy:
       def _note_stale_removed_in(*, ctx: ComposePortContext,
               report: ComposePortReport, stage: ComposeStageResult,
               target: str, origin_compose: bool,
               delta_write_skip: str | None,
               delta_writes: list[str]) -> None
   - delta_write_skip is None: call clear_overlay_removed_in(ctx.path,
     target).
     error: stage.add_error("E_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_FAILED",
     f"{ctx.origin}: {error}"); report.errors += 1; return.
     changed: warning I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_CLEARED with
         f"{ctx.origin}: present upstream again; removed {target} "
         f"from overlay.toml removed_in"
     note "removed-for-target-cleared";
         delta_writes.append(
             f"ports/{ctx.origin}/overlay.toml (removed_in -{target})")
     return.
   - otherwise: note "removed-for-target-ignored"; and only when not
     origin_compose, warning I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_IGNORED with
         f"{ctx.origin}: overlay.toml removed_in lists {target}, but the "
         f"origin is present upstream again, so the overlay was applied; "
         f"the stale marker was left in place ({delta_write_skip})"
   An --origin compose is the agent's reapply: it gets the overlay, the
   note in --json, and no warning it could not act on.
4. dportsv3/compose_reporting.py, build_compose_report_overview, after the
   I_COMPOSE_COMPAT_SCOPED_PAYLOAD hint: when the
   I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_IGNORED count is > 0, append the hint
       removed_in named a build line on which the port exists upstream
       again: its overlay was applied, and a full compose removes the
       stale marker
   No hint for CLEARED: the delta_writes: line already names the write.
5. docs/dportsv3-user-guide.md, "Stale overlay errors", code names in
   backticks as the guide does. 5c35255 ends the "two runs read
   differently" bullet with an em-dash clause, "because the removed_in
   check precedes the upstream-presence check, ... overlay.toml is where it
   is written.", and follows it with the bullet "removed_in is only ever
   added to, never cleared, ...". Replace that clause and that bullet with:
       ... exits 0 and warns about nothing: removed_in skips a port only
       while it is still missing upstream for that target, so a quiet
       removed-for-target means exactly that.
     - removed_in records that the port was missing; it does not outlive
       that. If the port reappears upstream, compose applies the overlay
       again. A full compose removes the target from removed_in
       (I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_CLEARED, note removed-for-target-cleared),
       deleting overlay.toml when nothing else is left in it; a dry run
       warns I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_IGNORED instead, and an --origin compose
       only notes removed-for-target-ignored. If the old overlay no longer
       applies to the restored port, compose now fails on it.
     - removed_in is written by compose; it is not a switch for keeping an
       overlay off one build line. In overlay.dops, put the ops under
       target blocks for the lines that need them instead.
6. tests/test_removed_for_target_report.py,
   test_the_transition_every_real_port_goes_through: its docstring says
   the steady-state report cannot mention "absent upstream" because "the
   continue precedes the upstream check and compose genuinely does not
   know by then", which stops being true. Replace the text from
   "-- and shows why" to the end of that sentence with:
       . A quiet removed-for-target means "still absent upstream": the
       marker skips a port only while that holds (poly-7pwa.6).
   No assertion changes.

EDGE CASES.
- A port back upstream whose old overlay no longer applies now fails the
  compose (exit 2; E_COMPOSE_APPLY_FAILED for dops; for compat
  E_COMPOSE_COMPAT_FAILED "devel/back: patch failed (Makefile.diff): ...";
  both run 2026-10-04 and pinned below) where it composed silently as pure
  upstream. Intended: a loud failure on the line the port
  is back on is the point of this bead. An operator sweep shows it; so does
  dev-env's initial compose, which exits 1 and leaves the env ready for
  inspection. The marker is already cleared, so the failure repeats until
  the overlay is fixed or scoped away from that line.
- --origin compose (reapply, the absorb parity gates): the overlay
  applies, nothing is written, a note and no warning.
- --dry-run, and a full compose on the wrong branch: the overlay applies,
  the marker stays, and I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_IGNORED names the reason.
- A dport marker still skips. A hand-written marker on a lock or mask
  overlay whose origin exists is ignored, then cleared (none exists).
- --strict and --prune-stale-overlays are unaffected.

WHAT NOT TO BUILD.
- No warning for an overlay skipped while its port is missing upstream.
  This SUPERSEDES the second half of the FIX SHAPE in this bead's notes
  ("warn rather than stay silent when a non-empty overlay is skipped"):
  it would fire on every full compose for every marked overlay with
  content for the target, 257 on @main, 238 on @2026Q3, 187 on @2026Q2
  and 157 on @2026Q1. Method: an overlay.dops op under @any or the target,
  or a compat .diff, dragonfly/ file, Makefile.DragonFly* or newport/.
  Nothing is lost in those cases: the port is not in the tree at all.
- Nothing in dportsv3/agent/: no OverlayFacts field, probe, tool, runner
  refusal, brief line or playbook text. A patch job exists only for a port
  dsynth built on the job's line, so the port is upstream there, and after
  this change removed_in cannot skip it. Items 1-3 of the original WHAT IS
  NEEDED are moot. The original VERIFICATION SHAPE is wrong: devel/plasma
  is absent upstream on main, so it must stay quiet.
- No parsing of skipped overlays, and so no port_type for them.

PROMPT COST. 0 characters. Reapply is an --origin compose: no
I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_* warning and no hint, and the note is only in --json
ports[].notes, which no agent path reads. On a full compose the warning
text is --json only (193 characters with its code prefix, as
stages[].warnings stores it, 163 without, for devel/back on a dry run);
the text output carries the code count and the 145-character hint.

TESTS. New tests/test_removed_in_upstream_restored.py, synthetic trees.
Fixture _tree(root, kind="dops", ops='mk set VAR "from-overlay"\n'): a
freebsd git repo on branch main with devel/back and devel/present
(Makefile "VAR= upstream\n"); in the delta, ports/devel/back with an
overlay.dops (port devel/back, type port, reason "fixture", target @any,
then ops) or, for kind "compat", a Makefile.DragonFly ("DFLY= yes\n"); and
overlay.toml removed_in = ["@main"]. Every compose runs through
dportsv3.cli.main with --target @main, --output <root>/out, --delta-root
<root>/delta, --freebsd-root <root>/freebsd and --oracle-profile off. A
"full compose" (no --origin) adds --replace-output --json unless the case
names other flags or text output. Every case except the last fails on the
.16 tree:
- test_a_port_restored_upstream_gets_its_overlay_back, parametrized over
  kind "dops" and "compat" (842 of the 1093 markers are compat): full
  compose. Exit 0; "removed-for-target" not in notes;
  dops: applied_ops 1 and the composed Makefile contains from-overlay;
  compat: out/devel/back/Makefile.DragonFly is a file.
- test_a_full_compose_clears_the_marker_of_a_port_that_is_back:
  overlay.toml is gone; note removed-for-target-cleared; one warning
  starting "I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_CLEARED: devel/back:"; preflight metadata
  delta_writes == ["ports/devel/back/overlay.toml (removed_in -@main)"].
- test_clearing_keeps_the_rest_of_the_manifest: overlay.toml is
  type = "port" with removed_in ["@2026Q3", "@main"]; afterwards it parses
  to {"type": "port", "removed_in": ["@2026Q3"]}.
- test_reapply_applies_the_overlay_and_writes_and_warns_nothing: output
  seeded by copying freebsd; compose --origin devel/back --json. Exit 0;
  applied_ops 1; note removed-for-target-ignored; no warning starts with

- test_a_dry_run_names_the_stale_marker_and_leaves_it: full compose
  --dry-run, text output. Exit 0; stdout contains
  "I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_IGNORED=1" and "hint: removed_in named a build line
  on which the port exists upstream again"; overlay.toml byte-identical.
- test_a_full_compose_on_the_wrong_branch_clears_nothing: freebsd then
  switched to a new branch 2026Q3 (still holding devel/back); compose @main
  --replace-output --json. Exit 2; overlay.toml byte-identical; no
  I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_CLEARED; the single I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_IGNORED
  ends "(the freebsd checkout is not on branch main)". This pins D3's
  gate where the clear lives; removing .16's branch condition fails it.
- test_a_restored_port_whose_overlay_no_longer_applies_fails_loudly,
  parametrized over (kind, code): ("dops", "E_COMPOSE_APPLY_FAILED") with

      --- Makefile.orig
      +++ Makefile
      @@ -1 +1 @@
      -OLDVAR= gone
      +OLDVAR= new
  Full compose --replace-output --json. Exit 2; an error starting with the
  case's code names devel/back (before: exit 0, no error).
- test_the_marker_still_skips_a_port_missing_upstream_and_stays_quiet:
  devel/back removed from freebsd; full compose. Exit 0; note
  removed-for-target; applied_ops 0; preflight warnings == []; overlay.toml
  still present; no out/devel/back. Passes before and after: it guards
  against adding noise.
Rewrite tests/test_dportsv3_compose.py
test_compose_removed_in_skips_port_for_target: delete the comment "Port
exists upstream but is declared removed for @main" and the two lines that
create freebsd/devel/gone, and put in their place
    # devel/gone is absent upstream: removed_in skips a port only while that
    # holds. A port upstream again applies its overlay (poly-7pwa.6).
Every assertion stays.
Measured on a prototype: 9 of the 10 new cases fail on the .16 tree and
all 10 pass after; without row 3a, the three 5c35255 tests named in
poly-7pwa.7 fail here; the compose-related set (as in .16) passes.

DEPENDS ON. poly-7pwa.16 (delta_write_skip, delta_writes and
_removed_in_targets). poly-7pwa.21 rows 3 and 3a: this edits the guide
text 5c35255 adds, and without row 3a's fixture three 5c35255 tests fail
here.
acceptance_criteria:
- A port with removed_in ["@T"] that exists upstream on T composes with
  its overlay applied in a full compose, a dry run and an --origin compose,
  for a dops overlay and for a compat one.
- A full compose without --dry-run, on T's branch, removes T from
  removed_in (deleting overlay.toml when it held nothing else), warns
  I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_CLEARED, notes removed-for-target-cleared and lists
  the write in delta_writes.
- A dry run, or a full compose on the wrong branch, leaves overlay.toml
  byte-identical and warns I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_IGNORED with the reason;
  the text output carries the IGNORED hint.
- An --origin compose writes nothing and emits no I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARK_*
  warning; reapply's text output gains 0 characters.
- A port with removed_in ["@T"] that is missing upstream on T is skipped
  exactly as before: note removed-for-target, exit 0, no new warning,
  marker kept.
- A port with removed_in ["@T"] that is back upstream on T and whose
  overlay no longer applies fails a full compose (exit 2):
  E_COMPOSE_APPLY_FAILED for dops, E_COMPOSE_COMPAT_FAILED for compat.
- tests/test_removed_in_upstream_restored.py: 10 cases pass (8 functions,
  two of them parametrized over dops and compat); on the .16 tree 9 fail
  and only the quiet guard passes.
- test_compose_removed_in_skips_port_for_target is rewritten as specified,
  every assertion kept, and passes. tests/test_removed_for_target_report.py
  passes 7 of 7 with only its one docstring sentence changed.
- The guide no longer says removed_in is never cleared or that compose
  cannot know the port is absent upstream, and it says removed_in is not a
  switch (use target blocks).
- Nothing in dportsv3/agent/ changes.
- The compose test files pass; then the full suite with DPORTS_DELTA_ROOT
  set (only the two known tracker CLI tests may fail).
notes:
CORRECTION, and it is a substantial one. An independent audit challenged the
consequence claim and it does not hold as filed. I had the mechanism right and
the reachability wrong, which is the more important half.

WHAT removed_in ACTUALLY MEANS. It is not a deliberate 'this port needs no
overlay on this build line'. It is a STALENESS marker, written automatically by
_apply_stale_overlay_policy (compose_stages.py:420-462) when a type=port overlay
names an origin that is NOT PRESENT in upstream freebsd-ports for that target.
devel/plasma, the fixture I used, simply does not exist in freebsd-ports@main --
I checked after the audit pointed at the stale path, and I should have checked
before choosing it as an example.

SO THE UNWINNABLE-JOB CLAIM IS NOT REACHABLE TODAY. Measured across the tree:

  removed_in contains @main AND the port has a live overlay.dops : 249
  ...of those still present in freebsd-ports@main                :   0

Zero. If the port is not upstream it cannot be composed, so dsynth cannot build
it, so no patch job can be filed for it on that target. The attempt I described
burning its budget cannot currently be started for any port in the tree. The
P1 rating was wrong; downgraded to P3, alongside the other latent one (.9).

Also corrected: the first compose that discovers the staleness is NOT silent --
it raises E_COMPOSE_STALE_OVERLAY and that compose reports ok=False
(compose_stages.py:440-443), plus I_COMPOSE_STALE_MARKED_REMOVED when the
marker is written. The silent zero-warning behaviour I reproduced is the
STEADY STATE, every run after the marker is already persisted. Accurate for the
tree as it stands, but 'compose says nothing' overstated it.

WHAT SURVIVES, and is still worth fixing:

- the silent steady state is real: an overlay with valid ops contributes
  nothing and compose reports success with 0 errors and 0 warnings
- dportsv3/agent/ has genuinely never heard of overlay.toml or removed_in
- and the actual defect, which the original filing missed: removed_in IS
  WRITE-ONLY. write_overlay_removed_in (compose_discovery.py:46-72) only ever
  adds -- payload['removed_in'] = sorted({*current, target}) -- and nothing
  anywhere removes a target from the list. Verified by grep: the only callers
  are the read and that one writer.

THE REACHABLE FAILURE, restated. A port is dropped from upstream freebsd-ports
on a branch, gets marked removed_in for that target, and is LATER RESTORED
upstream. It now composes as pure freebsd-ports with its DragonFly overlay
permanently and silently disabled, because nothing clears the marker. If it
then fails to build, a patch job is filed and that job is unwinnable exactly as
originally described. Upstream resurrections are uncommon but not rare, and the
disablement is permanent and silent once it happens.

FIX SHAPE, narrower than filed: clear the target from removed_in when the
origin reappears upstream (the same preflight already knows upstream_origins,
compose_stages.py:545), and warn rather than stay silent when a non-empty
overlay is skipped. The agent-side knowledge (probe_overlay_facts reading
overlay.toml) is then defence in depth rather than the primary fix.
2026-10-04: D3 = option (a). Design rewritten on top of .16 (ignore + clear).
The notes' warn-on-skip and the original agent-side items are superseded (WHAT
NOT TO BUILD). The restored-port-that-no-longer-applies case is run and pinned
for dops and compat.
close_reason: landed on master as 14fabe8 (2026-10-04, not pushed): removed_in skips a port only while its origin is missing upstream; a full compose on the right branch clears it (D3)

title: The built console has a Deliveries surface the mock never drew
description:
The ONLY divergence found so far that runs the other way: the build has a
surface the mock does not, rather than missing one it does.

  mock pipelineNav    Overview · Jobs · Runner · Manual
  built secondary nav Overview · Jobs · Deliveries · Runner · Manual

The route is /pipeline/deliveries and it landed 2026-09-06, one day AFTER the
mock version this epic names as its source (published 2026-09-05, read
2026-09-07). So the mock is behind the build here; nothing is wrong with the
page.

WHY IT STILL NEEDS A DECISION RATHER THAN A SHRUG. This epic exists because
poly-0e02 shipped 22 children and none of them compared the result to the
mock, so divergences accumulated unrecorded until two whole views were
different applications. A surface the mock does not contain is exactly the
same failure mode running forwards: if the mock is the authority, every page
it lacks is either a gap in the mock or an unapproved addition, and nobody can
tell which later without asking whoever was there.

TWO HONEST OPTIONS, and the repo rule ("a divergence that survives is a
decision, and gets written down") wants one of them chosen rather than left:
- PORT IT INTO THE MOCK, as poly-qqx9.10 did for the job detail, so the
  console keeps one authoritative source and the rest of this epic can measure
  against it.
- RECORD IT AS A DELIBERATE ADDITION the mock will not carry, and say why.

Cheap either way. What is not acceptable is the third outcome, where the next
person doing a side-by-side re-discovers it and files this bead again.

FOUND BY: the element-by-element table in the job-detail side-by-side
(artifact 88bZw6sd4ZmokTb26oqQXu), where it was the one row marked "near"
rather than same-or-differs -- and the only row of eleven with no bead behind
it.
notes:
ALREADY DECIDED, and the decision is in this bead's own parent. The epic's
"DELIBERATE DIVERGENCES TO KEEP, not defects to fix" list has carried the
line since it was written:

  • A standalone Deliveries list, which the mock has no route for.

So option 2 was taken before this bead existed, and filing it was the exact
outcome its last paragraph names as unacceptable -- the next person doing a
side-by-side re-discovering it. That person was me. The job-detail comparison
read the mock's nav against the build's and never read the epic's own
divergence list first.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE PREMISE, which matters more than the duplicate. This
bead argued "the route landed 2026-09-06, one day AFTER the mock version, so
the mock is behind rather than the build wrong". That reading is dead: the
artifact was republished 2026-09-13 (the epic's own NOTES record it, design
unchanged, two footer switches added) and the copy read for this comparison
on 2026-09-24 still has no Deliveries route. Two republishes later it is not
a lag. It is a standing divergence, which is what the epic already called it.

THE WHY, which the epic recorded the decision without: it follows from the
divergence two bullets above it. Delivery is two axes, not the mock's one
node -- poly-8e2 measured 17 live counterexamples to the conflation the
mock's "1 open PRs / awaiting confirm build" makes. The Deliveries page is
where the two are held apart, and its own lede says so: "An issue resolves
when a build proves the fix, not when a PR merges -- so a resolved issue here
can still show a delivery that never reached the provider." A single mock
node cannot say that, which is why porting it into the mock (option 1) would
mean redrawing the node the epic has already decided not to follow.

Appended to the epic so the next side-by-side reads the reason, not just the
ruling. Closed as a duplicate of that line.

title: Drop the unused artifacts table
description:
schema.py:191 creates an artifacts table (bundle_id, relpath, kind, mtime,
size) on every state.db. Nothing reads or writes it:

  grep -E '(FROM|INTO|UPDATE|JOIN)[[:space:]]+artifacts\b' over the tree
  returns nothing.

It is the pre-content-addressing ancestor of artifact_refs, which carries
backend/sha256/fs_path and is the table everything actually uses. On a
live builder: artifacts 0 rows, artifact_refs 31,606.

Worth removing because the two names are one character apart in a schema
of 27 tables, and the empty one is the first hit when someone goes looking
for artifact storage. It cost a reader time on 2026-09-24.

Removing the CREATE only stops NEW databases from getting it, so the
table stays on every deployed host. Dropping it for real wants a
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS in MIGRATIONS, which runs before SCHEMA (schema.py:633
catches the OperationalError on a fresh db).

0 rows confirmed on ONE host only. Confirm elsewhere before the DROP
lands, or take the CREATE out and leave existing tables alone.
notes:
DONE 2026-09-24.

THE CAUTION IN THE DESCRIPTION IS DISCHARGED, not worked around. It asked
for 0 rows to be confirmed on every host before dropping. Stronger answer:

  git log -S "INTO artifacts" -- dportsv3/   ->   no commits

Nothing in the history of the tree ever wrote it, so there are no rows to
lose on any host. The DROP is safe unconditionally.

ONE CODE DEPENDENCY, not just the CREATE: identifiers.py _REFERENCES
listed ("artifacts", "bundle_id") in the bundle_id rename-carry map, so a
rename would have tried to update a dropped table. Removed. The scanner
next to it, stored_unsafe_identifiers, reads a different list (_ID_COLUMNS
-- bundles, jobs, runs, issues) and never touched it.

NOT PUT IN MIGRATIONS. That tuple documents itself as "the non-destructive
path for an existing state.db" and init_db runs it tolerantly, swallowing
OperationalError to absorb duplicate-column errors -- which would also
swallow a real failure here. Followed _RETIRE_STORED_REGRESSED's precedent
instead: a separate one-shot tuple, _DROP_DEAD_TABLES, run untolerated
after SCHEMA. IF EXISTS carries the idempotence.

Three tests in test_schema_migration_ordering.py: a db carrying the legacy
table has it dropped while artifact_refs survives, a second init_db is a
no-op, and SCHEMA is asserted not to contain the CREATE again -- the drop
runs after SCHEMA, so a re-added CREATE would leave the drop doing nothing
visible.

4201 tests pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: run_shell exists but 38 call sites hand-build the shell argv instead
description:
ChrootRunner.run_shell exists as the idiomatic way to run a shell snippet in
an env, and almost nothing uses it. Call sites hand-build the same argv and
interpolate values into the script instead of passing them as positional
arguments.

    chroot.py:47
    def run_shell(self, script, *args, ...):
        return self.run(["/bin/sh", "-c", script, "_", *args], ...)

Counts across both packages, tests excluded:

    run_shell callers                     2
    hand-built ["/bin/sh", "-c", ...]     38

    dportsv3/agent/worker.py             25
    dev-env/dports_dev_env/cli.py         7
    dev-env/dports_dev_env/chroot.py      3
    dportsv3/agent/runner.py              1
    dportsv3/agent/health.py              1
    dev-env/dports_dev_env/session.py     1

Of the 38, only 6 pass a positional argument at all. The rest interpolate
into the script string, which is why shlex.quote appears 33 times across the
two packages: every site that interpolates has to remember to quote, and
nothing checks that it did.

This is not a live bug. Origins, targets and paths are tame strings and the
sites that interpolate them do call shlex.quote. It is a standing invitation
to a quoting bug in the next one written, and the framework already has the
shape that removes the question.

## Not in scope

The centralization itself is sound and was audited: in-chroot work goes
through ChrootRunner.run (dev-env) or _exec / _run_dev_env (agent), and every
raw subprocess call outside those is host-side work - mounts, git, fs, pgrep,
host-side grep - which belongs there. health.py rebuilds the `dev-env exec`
argv rather than importing _exec, deliberately, so the module stays importable
without the dev-env package.

## Shape of the work

Convert the 38 sites to run_shell, passing interpolated values as "$1", "$2"
and dropping the matching shlex.quote. Mechanical and individually testable;
worth doing per file rather than in one sweep. worker.py holds two thirds of
them and is where a quoting bug would hurt most, since its scripts carry
agent-supplied paths.
notes:
Revised after reading every site. The count conflated two mechanisms and
included three non-call-sites.

ChrootRunner family - can use run_shell today:

    dev-env/cli.py        7
    dev-env/chroot.py     1   command_exists, already uses "$1"
    dev-env/session.py    1   exec_command, already passes *argv
                          9

_exec family - CANNOT use run_shell. _exec shells out to `dev-env exec`
and is a module function in dportsv3/agent/worker.py, not a ChrootRunner
method. These need an equivalent agent-side helper before any conversion:

    agent/worker.py      25
    agent/runner.py       1
    agent/health.py       1
                         27

Not call sites at all: chroot.py:55 is run_shell's own body, chroot.py:69 is
an os.execv, and the health.py entry is a static script with nothing
interpolated.

One site is a real unquoted interpolation rather than a style point.
cli.py's wrkdir_script builds

    'cd "$DPORTS_COMPOSE_ROOT/' + o + '" && make ...'

joined over build_origins with no shlex.quote anywhere. Tame today because
origins are category/port, but it is the exact shape the bead is about.
## Landed

ChrootRunner family converted, 9 sites: cli.py 7, chroot.py command_exists,
session.py exec_command. run_shell callers 2 -> 11; hand-built sites in
dev-env 11 -> 2, and those two are run_shell's own body and an os.execv.

Every interpolated value now arrives as a positional argument, so shlex is
gone from cli.py and session.py entirely. The dead build_args / reapply_args
locals went with it.

wrkdir_script was the one real defect, not a style point: it joined
'cd "$DPORTS_COMPOSE_ROOT/' + o + '"' over build_origins with no quoting. Now
a `for o in "$@"` loop.

Two equivalences worth recording, both checked against sh:
  reapply a && reapply b  ->  reapply "$@"     (the helper loops and exits
                                                on first failure either way)
  dtest ARGS > LOG        ->  log=$1; shift; dtest "$@" > "$log"

Test fakes in test_dev_env_apply_and_build.py and test_dev_env_job_worktree.py
grew a run_shell mirroring the real body, so recorded argv still matches what
the chroot would see. Assertions now split argv into (script, args) via a
_shell helper instead of substring-matching an interpolated command line.

Suite 4016 passed.

## Remaining

The 27 _exec sites are untouched and still need an agent-side equivalent of
run_shell before any of them can convert. That is the larger half and the one
carrying agent-supplied paths.

title: The worklist never updates on its own: no staleness signal, so a queue left open silently goes stale
description:
/agentic is a static render. No dpLive, no refresh, no polling of any kind -- grep over agentic_index.html and repairs-rail.js finds none. Four other surfaces do poll (agentic-runner.js, agentic-job.js, agentic-bundle.js, run.js); the queue is not one of them.

So a worklist left open is a photograph. Nothing in it moves when a verify finishes, when a confirm build lands, or when another operator accepts something. It looks correct the whole time, which is the part that matters: there is no cue that it is out of date.

It usually goes unnoticed because the cockpit reloads the page for you after most operator actions. Two gaps where it does not:

- accept with delivery create_failed deliberately skips the reload so the error sticks on screen -- and then the queue beside it is stale too.
- anything the RUNNER finishes. poly-x3pg.11 made a verify legible in the queue; you still have to reload to see it move from 'verifying' to 'verified'.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE, and the reasoning, so this is not re-litigated from scratch

A staleness SIGNAL, not an auto-refresh.

1. The queue holds operator state -- scroll position, expanded groups, the selection, the active filter. poly-x3pg.6 and poly-x3pg.9 exist to preserve that across a deliberate navigation; swapping the rail out every few seconds fights them. A row changing band under the cursor is worse than a stale row.
2. Re-rendering the queue is the expensive thing. tracker.shell_facts_seconds exists because the worklist band projection measures 25.8 ms per render on 20,000 issues, and it is memoised for 15 s precisely to avoid paying that often. Polling a full re-render per operator spends exactly what that setting was created to save, against one uvicorn process with no workers and sync routes on a threadpool.
3. There is almost nothing to see. The states that change unattended are slow -- a verify is minutes, a confirm build longer. Sub-minute freshness buys nothing a reload does not.

So: a dpLive poll against a cheap endpoint returning a change counter (MAX(id) over activity_log or the events table, one indexed read), and when it moves, an unobtrusive 'the queue has changed - reload' affordance in the ops strip. The operator reloads between decisions rather than mid-click. Same idiom the run view already uses: it reloads itself when run_id changes rather than patching rows in place.

REJECTED, deliberately: auto-swapping .repair-rail from a fragment endpoint. It is the obvious ask and it is the one that would annoy an operator daily.
acceptance_criteria: A queue left open says when it has fallen behind, without moving anything the operator is looking at. The check costs one indexed read, not a worklist render. Reloading stays the operator's decision.

title: Does the fix-review conversation survive into the manual handoff?
description:
Left open by poly-pf4a, which decided where the chat LIVES (bundle_chat_turns, keyed on the occurrence) and deliberately did not decide what carries it onward.

The conversation is evidence now: it is the operator's reasoning about a fix, stored beside the artifacts that fix produced. The manual handoff is what a human gets when the loop gives up on a port. If the questions already asked and answered about an attempt are not in it, the next person re-asks them.

Against: the handoff is meant to be readable, and a long Q&A thread is not obviously part of 'here is what went wrong'. It may belong as a reference rather than inline.

Decide what the handoff carries, not where the chat lives -- that is settled.
acceptance_criteria: Either the handoff carries the thread (or a pointer to it) and says why, or it deliberately does not and the bead records the reason.

title: The Repairs queue expands issues into occurrence rows; the mock has no such thing
description:
The sixth divergence from poly-x3pg.7, left open there because it is a decision rather than a defect.

The queue renders a multi-occurrence issue as a .wl-group whose .wl-children are one row per occurrence, expanded by wlToggle and (since poly-x3pg.6) opened server-side when one of them is selected. The mock has no group and no children: the queue is strictly one row per issue, and occurrences live in the detail pane's occurrence bar -- a collapsed strip reading 'OCCURRENCES . 3  <id>  <when> . <state> . reached <stage>   <sibling> got furthest' with a CHANGE control that drops the full list, each row carrying id, timestamp, state, what it reached, attempt count and a FURTHEST mark.

The tracker already renders that bar: _occurrence_selector.html is the same thing under a different name, and it is in the pane today. So the two surfaces list the same occurrences side by side on one screen.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY AT STAKE
- The pane's version puts the choice next to the evidence and directly above the action bar that acts on it. The queue's version puts it ~1200px away in the other column.
- The pane's version says more per occurrence: what it reached, how many attempts, which got furthest. The queue's says id, status pill, age.
- The queue's version is the only one that lets you compare two issues' occurrence lists without opening either.
- The group expansion is a large part of what makes rows tall, and it is the reason the rail needs scroll- and open-state persistence at all.

Deleting the group would retire .wl-group / .wl-children / wlToggle, the data-issue open-state persistence in repairs-rail.js, and the server-side open in agentic_index.html.
design: Mock: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/2c556aa9-ed25-499f-b88d-64b86272aa9a -- footer switch 'queue at 500' shows the queue at the real cap.
acceptance_criteria: One place picks which occurrence to act on, not two. Whichever survives says what an occurrence reached and which got furthest, because that is what decides which one is worth reading.

title: Repairs split: the occurrence selector navigates out of the split
description:
_occurrence_selector.html links every sibling occurrence to
request.url_for('agentic_bundle_detail', ...), so switching occurrence from the
Repairs right pane drops you onto the standalone page and loses the queue. The
same partial is correct on the standalone page, which is where the URL was
written.

Found while fixing poly-icif, which gave the artifact reader a cockpit_page_url
the split overrides with its own ?occ= URL. The occurrence selector wants the
same treatment: build the href from cockpit_page_url with occ= swapped, so it
selects within whichever page hosts the cockpit.

Low priority: it navigates somewhere real and correct, it just leaves the split.
notes:
Revisited after reading the code (2026-09-10).

Confirmed scope: _occurrence_selector.html:29 is the ONLY remaining link out of
the split among the cockpit's eight partials. Checked _bundle_summary,
_bundle_operator_actions, _bundle_delivery, _bundle_operator_activity,
_bundle_artifacts, _bundle_chat, _bundle_jobs -- none address an occurrence.
(The header's 'Open issue' and 'Port history' leave deliberately: different
resources.)

Better shape than this bead first proposed. Rather than swapping occ= inside
cockpit_page_url, invert it: the host supplies ONE base -- how this page
addresses an occurrence, with the bundle id appended -- and both partials
derive from it. cockpit_page_url is then just base ~ this bundle's id, so
there are not two variables that have to agree.

  split:      <agentic_index url> ~ '?occ='   ->  /agentic?occ=<id>
  standalone: url_for('agentic_bundle_detail') per id (the default)

Also found, same root assumption and not noted before: the current row carries
aria-current="page". True standing alone, false in the split, where the
cockpit is a section and the subnav's Worklist already claims the page. Two
'this is the page' claims in one document. builds_dashboard.html and
pipeline.html already use aria-current="true" for an in-page selection.
tests/test_cockpit.py:138 and test_tracker_agentic_views.py:686 both assert
aria-current="page" against the standalone page, so they stay correct.

Small: one variable, two call sites.
close_reason: Closed

title: FastAPI on_event is deprecated: the tracker's startup and shutdown hooks will stop firing
description:
server.py:187 and :194 use @app.on_event("startup") / ("shutdown").
FastAPI emits a DeprecationWarning for both on every test run and points
at lifespan handlers.

What is behind those hooks is not decorative: startup runs the schema
init, the delivery preflight and _log_unsafe_identifiers; shutdown is
where the orchestrator releases its clone. When FastAPI drops on_event
these stop being called, and the failure mode is silence -- the server
starts, and nothing that was supposed to run at startup ran.

Mechanical: one @asynccontextmanager taking the startup body, a yield,
then the shutdown body, passed as app = FastAPI(lifespan=...).

Also visible in the same run: fastapi's own testclient warns that httpx
with starlette.testclient is deprecated in favour of httpx2. That one is
theirs, not ours, and is worth watching rather than acting on.

title: The status rail's live region is inert: nothing ever writes to it
description:
_base.html:81 renders
on every page. No JS references it -- grep over static/ finds one hit, a comment in agentic-bundle.js:158 that uses the word "toast" for the inline statusEl it writes instead. So the page carries an announced-to-nobody landmark. A screen reader user gets no announcement for any operator action; a sighted user gets the inline status line, which is what actually reports accept/deliver/verify results today. Two ways to close it, and they are not equivalent: 1. Wire it. Route the same strings agentic-bundle.js writes to statusEl through a helper that also writes #toast. The inline line stays -- it is where a sighted operator is already looking -- and the live region becomes the announcement. This is the one that adds something. 2. Delete it. Honest, and better than the status quo, because an empty role=status is a promise the page does not keep. Prefer 1. The actions that most need announcing are the slow ones: verify enqueues a job that takes minutes and the page polls, and a create_failed delivery deliberately does not reload -- that error message lives nowhere else in the UI.
notes:
Implemented 2026-09-13, option 1 (wire it). Verified in headless Chrome: setting op-status writes the toast's textContent and adds .visible.

- _base.html defines window.dpToast beside the element it writes, in an inline script ahead of the page's scripts block -- every page's own JS is deferred, so the writer is already defined when any of it runs. Shows and announces the same string; role=status announces a text change whether or not the box is visible, so the 6s hide is purely visual.
- agentic-bundle.js mirrors #op-status into it with a MutationObserver, rather than threading a helper through the thirty call sites that write that line. Trade-off taken deliberately: one place instead of thirty edits to a file otherwise untouched, and a message added later is announced without anyone remembering to. The visible line is unchanged, which is the point -- it is where a sighted operator is already looking.
- dpToast ignores empty and repeated strings, so a re-render of the same status does not re-announce.

Tests in test_ui_quality.py, which is where the other UI-7 landmark properties live.
close_reason: Closed

title: M5 Builds is close, and the gap is three details
description:
The one view that came across. Same nav, same subnav shape, same
heading and subtitle verbatim, same active/history split, same run row
with its progress bar and Building/Queued/Failed counts, same result
table with filter chips and a search box. Rendered side by side you
have to look for the differences.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DIFFERENT

1. The fifth subnav item. Mock: Active | History | Compare | Target Diff
   | Live Progress. Ours: ... | Targets. Two separate things happened --
   the mock's "Live Progress" is the run view we built as UI-3 and reach
   from a run row instead, and our "Targets" is the old per-target
   rollup the mock has no entry for. Decide which belongs in the nav; if
   both do, that is five plus one, not a swap.

2. The result table's first two columns. Mock leads with NO. (a 52px
   ordinal, 001, 002, ...) and STATUS as a coloured square plus
   uppercase mono word. Ours drops the ordinal and uses a pill. The
   ordinal is worth having -- it is the build order, which is how an
   operator reads a dsynth log -- and it is a real column, not
   decoration, so it comes from the row's position in the run.

3. The Evidence column. Mock renders "Open repair" per failed row,
   linking to the occurrence. Ours renders an em dash for every row
   because the demo fixture never links build_results to bundles. Check
   against real data whether the join is right before calling this a
   template gap -- it may be the fixture that is wrong and not the page.

Header filters differ cosmetically: the mock's target/build-type
selectors are .control buttons in .heading-actions, ours are selects.
Ours submit without JS, which the mock's do not. Keep ours.

CONSTRAINTS

Adding a leading ordinal column shifts every colspan in that table,
including the empty-state row UI-7 added. The scoped headers stay.
notes:
ALL THREE CHECKED. One is a fixture bug and two are declines with
reasons, so this bead is smaller than it looked.

1. LIVE PROGRESS is already there, in the place the mock puts it that
   has a run to show. builds_dashboard.html:133 renders a "Live progress"
   control in the selected run's toolbar, which is the mock's own
   .detail-toolbar button. What the mock ALSO has is a nav entry, and
   that is the version that needs a default run invented for it -- the
   subnav's own comment already says so. Our fifth item stays Targets,
   which the mock has no route for at all and which is how you reach a
   live view per target.

2. THE ORDINAL would number the wrong thing here. The mock's "001, 002"
   is dsynth build order, which is how an operator reads the log. The
   dashboard's table is ORDER BY origin ASC -- deliberately, so search
   and paging are stable -- so an ordinal in it counts position in an
   alphabetical list and means nothing. The run view IS in arrival order
   and already has the column (UI-3). Adding one here would be a number
   that looks like the mock's and is not.

3. EVIDENCE: the page is right and the demo fixture was wrong. Proved
   against a fresh DB -- one build_result and one bundle sharing an
   origin, and get_build_results_page returns bundle_id='bnd-1'. The
   fixture's bundles carry origins like devel/tiff while its
   build_results carry devel/tiff-0, so BUNDLE_FOR_RESULT_SQL correctly
   matches nothing. Fix the fixture and pin the join with a test, since
   nothing covered it.

The remaining differences are cosmetic and ours are the better half: the
mock's four filter chips against our six states, and its single toolbar
row against our two, which is what keeps the controls usable at 500px.
close_reason: Committed. Three items, one bug and two declines. Evidence: the page was right and the demo fixture was wrong -- its bundles carried origins the build_results did not, so BUNDLE_FOR_RESULT_SQL correctly matched nothing; fixed, and the join is pinned by a test that also covers the success case getting no link. The ordinal is declined: the dashboard table is ORDER BY origin so a number there would count an alphabetical position while looking like dsynth build order, and the run view that IS in arrival order already has it. The Live Progress nav entry is declined: the button already exists in the selected run's toolbar, which is where it has a run to show, and a nav entry would need a default invented. Both declines are pinned by tests so the reasoning is where the difference is.

title: An operator cannot pause the runner, and runner_status is the wrong place to say so
description:
The runner pauses itself for three reasons -- dev-env health broken, no
env resolved, dsynth holding the build lock -- all in _gate_blocked()
(runner.py, the loop's single gate). An operator has no way to stop it
short of killing the process, which loses whatever job is in flight.

poly-0e02.8 dropped the mocked Pause button rather than shipping one,
and recorded why the obvious implementation does not work.

RUNNER_STATUS IS NOT THE FIELD

runner_status.status is written by the runner on essentially every tick
(idle / processing / paused / stopped). A tracker write of 'paused'
there would be overwritten by the next loop, and the runner would have
no way to tell its own pause from the operator's -- both are the same
string in the same column.

THE PATTERN ALREADY EXISTS

The loop drains three tracker-written channels every tick:
process_user_context_updates, process_verify_requests,
process_build_requests. Operator intent reaching the runner is a solved
shape here; a pause is a fourth one, or a single-row control table the
gate reads.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE

* somewhere durable for the intent, with who and when (an operator pause
  that vanishes on runner restart is a trap)
* a fourth condition in _gate_blocked(), ordered against the other three
  -- an operator pause should presumably outrank a health pause, so
  resuming does not undo it
* a tracker endpoint behind forbid_anonymous, like every other write
* a stage string the Runner page can show, so 'paused' says by whom
* the resume path, including what happens to a job already claimed

Not in the UI migration epic: it is a feature with a state machine, not
a view.
notes:
Implemented 2026-09-13. All five 'what it would take' items, and the bead's own diagnosis was right on every count.

- SOMEWHERE DURABLE. runner_control, a single row (id=1, CHECK) with paused/reason/requested_by/requested_at. Not runner_status.status, for exactly the reason the bead gives: the runner rewrites that every tick, so a tracker write would be overwritten and the runner could not tell its own pause from the operator's. Durable because a pause that vanishes on runner restart is a trap.
- A FOURTH CONDITION IN _gate_blocked(), ORDERED FIRST. The bead guessed it should outrank the health pause; it has to. Ordered the other way, a health pause clearing logs 'runner resumed: health ready' and starts claiming again while the operator's hold still stands. Read fresh every gate through _operator_pause(), a fourth tracker-written channel beside process_verify_requests and process_user_context_updates. An unreadable row means NOT paused: a runner that stops working because it could not read a table is a worse failure than one that keeps going.
- AN ENDPOINT BEHIND forbid_anonymous. PUT /api/runner/pause {paused, reason?}. Emits runner_paused / runner_resumed.
- A STAGE STRING. 'operator_paused by <who>: <reason>', so 'paused' on the Runner page says which of the now four kinds it is.
- THE RESUME PATH, AND THE CLAIMED JOB. The gate runs before claim_next_job_batch, so a pause stops the runner CLAIMING and never touches the job it already has -- that job runs to its end. This is the whole point: killing the process is what loses in-flight work. The page says so in those words.

Reason is optional. An urgent pause should not be gated behind typing; the activity log has the who and when either way.

Two tests in test_runner_page.py asserted the deliberate ABSENCE of a pause (poly-0e02.8 dropped a mocked one).
